label: thm:energy
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:energy}
There is an explicit constant $c_{\mathrm{cert}}>1.14268353624$
(\Cref{cor:numerical}) such that
\[
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\ \inf_{J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N}
 \frac1{N^3}\sum_{i=1}^N[(I-J)^{-1}]_{ii}^2\ \ge\ c_{\mathrm{cert}} .
\]
For the sine--Jacobi matrices $J_N^\star$ of \Cref{thm:sine-finite},
\[
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1{N^3}\sum_{i=1}^N[(I-J_N^\star)^{-1}]_{ii}^2=c_{\sin},
 \qquad c_{\sin}<1.14269218 .
\]

name: Green energy of the Chebyshev fiber

label: thm:main-centered
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Near-optimality of the sine--Jacobi method

label: def:methods
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:methods}
A recurrence $\mathcal R$ of length $N$ is a list of coefficients
$(\alpha_j,\beta_j,\gamma_j)_{0\le j<N}$ with
\[
 \gamma_j>0,\qquad \beta_0=0,\qquad \beta_j\ge0,\qquad
 \alpha_j=1+\beta_j .
\]
Its residual polynomials are $p_{-1}=0$, $p_0=1$, and
$p_{j+1}(\lambda)=(\alpha_j-\gamma_j\lambda)p_j(\lambda)-\beta_jp_{j-1}(\lambda)$.
The recurrence is {terminal-exact} on $[\mu,L]$ if
$p_N(\lambda)=\epsilon_N^\star T_N(z(\lambda))$ identically; these recurrences form
the class $\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)$. Its {irreducible} subclass has
$\beta_j>0$ for $1\le j<N$, and its {centered} subclass consists of
the irreducible recurrences with $\alpha_j=(L+\mu)\gamma_j/2$ for all $j$.

For real $p\times p$ matrices $H_0,\dots,H_{N-1}$, the recurrence acts by
\[
 \mathbf p_{-1}=0,\qquad \mathbf p_0=I,\qquad
 \mathbf p_{j+1}=(\alpha_jI-\gamma_jH_j)\mathbf p_j-\beta_j\mathbf p_{j-1};
\]
with $H_j=H$ for all $j$ this gives $\mathbf p_N=p_N(H)$. For symmetric
$H$ with $\mu I\preceq H\preceq LI$ and real $p\times p$ matrices
$B=(B_0,\dots,B_{N-1})$, let $\mathsf D_{\mathcal R,H}[B]$ be the
derivative of $\mathbf p_N$ at $(H,\dots,H)$ in the direction $B$. The
{Hessian-drift gain} is
\[
 A_N(\mathcal R)=
 \sup_{\substack{p\ge1,\ H=H^T\\\mu I\preceq H\preceq LI}}
 \ \sup_{B\ne0}
 \frac{\|\mathsf D_{\mathcal R,H}[B]\|_{\mathrm{HS}}}
 {(\sum_j\|B_j\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2)^{1/2}},
 \qquad
 \mathscr G(\mu,L)=\liminf_{N\to\infty}\ \inf_{\mathcal R\in\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)}
 \frac{\Delta A_N(\mathcal R)}{N^{3/2}\epsilon_N^\star}.
\]
head: environment
name: Terminal-exact recurrences and their gain

label: thm:jacobi
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:jacobi}
For $J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$ with diagonal $b_i$ and off-diagonal entries
$J_{j,j+1}=\sqrt{v_j}$, one has $P_j(z_0)>0$ for $0\le j\le N$, and the
coefficients
\[
 \gamma_j=\frac2\Delta\frac{P_j(z_0)}{P_{j+1}(z_0)},\qquad
 \alpha_j=(z_0-b_{j+1})\frac{P_j(z_0)}{P_{j+1}(z_0)},\qquad
 \beta_j=v_j\frac{P_{j-1}(z_0)}{P_{j+1}(z_0)}\quad(\beta_0=0)
\]
define a recurrence $\mathcal R_J\in\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)$ with residual
polynomials $p_j(\lambda)=P_j(z(\lambda))/P_j(z_0)$. The map
$J\mapsto\mathcal R_J$ is a bijection
$\overline{\mathcal Y}_N\to\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)$. It maps $\mathcal Y_N$ onto the irreducible
recurrences and $\mathcal X_N$ onto the centered ones. All six classes are
nonempty.

name: Recurrences and Jacobi matrices

label: thm:gain
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: The gain of a Jacobi matrix

label: cor:symmetric-gain
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:symmetric-gain}
Let $A_N^{\rm sym}$ be the gain of \Cref{def:methods} with every $B_j$
required to be symmetric. For every $J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$,
\[
 \frac{2\epsilon_N^\star}{\Delta}\sqrt{\mathcal E_N(J)}
 \le A_N^{\rm sym}(\mathcal R_J)\le A_N(\mathcal R_J).
\]
Both inequalities are equalities for $J_N^\star$. Consequently,
\Cref{thm:main-centered} holds with $A_N$ replaced by $A_N^{\rm sym}$.
head: environment
name: Symmetric perturbations

title: Proof
body_md:
The upper bound restricts the perturbation class. For the lower bound,
take dimension one and $H=\mu$, so $Z=1$ in \Cref{lem:gain-kernel}.
Choose scalar $B_j$ proportional to $\widehat P_j(1)P_j(1)$, with
$\sum_jB_j^2=1$. The response norm is
$2\epsilon_N^\star\Delta^{-1}\sqrt{\mathcal E_N(J)}$ by the cofactor formula for $G$.
\Cref{thm:sine-finite} gives equality for the sine matrix; its upper
bound and \Cref{thm:energy} then give the asymptotic assertion.
head: environment

label: cor:centering-packing
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{cor:centering-packing}
Let $J$ be a real symmetric tridiagonal $M\times M$ matrix with positive
off-diagonal entries and $\|J\|<1$, $G=(I-J)^{-1}$, $d_i=G_{ii}$. There
are points $y_1<\dots<y_M$ and bounded closed intervals $I_i\ni y_i$
with pairwise disjoint interiors and $|I_i|=1/d_i$ such that
$G_{ij}=\sqrt{d_id_j}\,e^{-|y_i-y_j|}$.

label: thm:packing
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: thm:transfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:transfer}
Put
\[
 k=\frac{\pi^2}4,\qquad \Lambda_j=\frac2{\pi^2(j+\frac12)^2}\quad(j\ge0),
 \qquad H_*(s)=\log\cosh\sqrt s .
\]
Then $\sum_j\Lambda_j=1$, $\sum_j\Lambda_j^2=\frac23$,
$\sum_j\log(1+s\Lambda_j/2)=H_*(s)$, and for every $J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deltaN}
 \sum_{j\ge0}|\lambda_j(K_{m_J})-\Lambda_j|
 \le\delta_N:=\frac2{\sqrt N}+\frac1N+\frac8{\pi^2(2N-1)} .
\end{equation}
Consequently, uniformly in $J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$ and $s\ge0$,
\[
 |H_{m_J}(s)-H_*(s)|\le\frac s2\delta_N,\qquad
 \bigl|\operatorname{tr} K_{m_J}^2-\tfrac23\bigr|\le2\delta_N,\qquad
 |\kappa(m_J)-k|\le\frac{4\delta_N}{\Lambda_0^2}\quad
 (\delta_N<\Lambda_0/2).
\]
head: environment
name: Uniform spectral transfer

label: thm:sine-finite
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:sine-finite}

Let $J_N^\star$ be the symmetric tridiagonal matrix with zero diagonal
and off-diagonal entries
\[
 J_{i,i+1}^\star=\frac{\sin(i\pi/N)}
 {2\sqrt{\sin((i-\frac12)\pi/N)\,\sin((i+\frac12)\pi/N)}}
 \qquad(1\le i<N).
\]
Then $J_N^\star\in\mathcal X_N$, and the recurrence
$\mathcal R_N^\star=\mathcal R_{J_N^\star}$ is centered and satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sine-gain}
 A_N(\mathcal R_N^\star)=\frac{2\epsilon_N^\star}{\Delta}\sqrt{\mathcal E_N(J_N^\star)}
 \qquad(0<\mu<L).
\end{equation}
The rescaled Green diagonal $D_N(t)=N^{-1}d_i$ on
$[(i-1)/N,i/N)$ converges in $L^2(0,1)$ to
\[
 \phi_*(t)=\frac4{\pi^2}\sin(\pi t)\,
 \mathbf K\bigl(\sin^2\tfrac{\pi t}2\bigr)\mathbf K\bigl(\cos^2\tfrac{\pi t}2\bigr),
 \qquad
 \mathbf K(s)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\,\mathrm d\theta}{\sqrt{1-s\sin^2\theta}},
\]
so that $N^{-3}\mathcal E_N(J_N^\star)\toc_{\sin}:=\int_0^1\phi_*^2$ and
$\mathscr G(\mu,L)\le2\sqrt{c_{\sin}}$.
head: environment
name: The sine--Jacobi matrices

label: def:sine
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:sine}
The function $\phi_*$ is continuous and positive on $(0,1)$. Let
$X_*:(0,1)\to\mathbb R$ be the strictly increasing function with $X_*'=1/\phi_*$
and $X_*(\frac12)=0$. Put $m_*(x)=\phi_*(t)^2$ if $x=X_*(t)$ for some
$t\in(0,1)$, $m_*(x)=0$ otherwise, and $n_*=\sqrt{m_*}$.
head: environment
name: The sine density

label: prop:target
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:target}
The map $X_*$ is an increasing bijection of $(0,1)$ onto $\mathbb R$ with
$X_*(1-t)=-X_*(t)$, and
\[
 \int m_*=\int\sqrt{m_*}=1,\qquad E(m_*)=c_{\sin},\qquad
 \lambda_j(K_{m_*})=\Lambda_j\quad(j\ge0).
\]
With $\Sigma_1(a)=\sum_{j\ge0}a^{j(j+1)}$ and
$\Sigma_2(a)=1+2\sum_{j\ge1}(-1)^ja^{j^2}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sine-theta}
 n_*(x)=8\varpi\,e^{-\pi\varpi/2}\,\Sigma_1(e^{-\pi\varpi})^2\,
 \Sigma_2(e^{-\pi\varpi})^2,\qquad \varpi=e^{2|x|} .
\end{equation}
In particular $n_*(x)=\exp(-\frac\pi2e^{2|x|}+O(|x|))$ as
$|x|\to\infty$.
head: environment
name: Properties of the sine density

label: def:classes
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:classes}
For $\varsigma>0$ and $m\in\mathcal M^1_c$ with ground parameter $\kappa=\kappa(m)$,
the {observation vector} is
\[
 \mathbf o_\varsigma(m)=\bigl(H_m(s_0),\,H_m(s_1),\,H_m(\varsigma\kappa),\,
 \operatorname{tr} K_m^2\bigr),
\]
and its target is
$\mathbf o_\varsigma^*=(H_*(s_0),H_*(s_1),H_*(\varsigma k),\frac23)$. The relaxed
class is
\[
 \mathcal A_{\mathrm{obs}}(\varsigma)=\{m\in\mathcal M^{1}_c:\ \kappa(m)=k,\
 \mathbf o_\varsigma(m)=\mathbf o_\varsigma^*\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Observations and the relaxed class

label: thm:ground
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:ground}
Let $m\ge0$ be integrable and not zero, and $\kappa=\kappa(m)$. The
eigenvalue $\lambda_0(K_m)$ is simple, and there is $u>0$,
$u\in H^1(\mathbb R)\cap C^1(\mathbb R)$ with $u'$ locally absolutely continuous and
$|u'|\le u$, such that $-u''+u=\kappa mu$ almost everywhere. For every
$f\in H^1(\mathbb R)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:ground-square}
 \int(f'^2+f^2)-\kappa\int mf^2=\int\Bigl(f'-\frac{u'}uf\Bigr)^2,
\end{equation}
whose right-hand side vanishes exactly for multiples of $u$. Every positive
$\tilde u\in H^1(\mathbb R)\cap C^1(\mathbb R)$ with $\tilde u'$ locally absolutely continuous
and $-\tilde u''+\tilde u=\kappa m\tilde u$ almost everywhere is a positive
multiple of $u$. The {ground coordinate} $q=1-u'/u$, which therefore
depends only on $m$, is locally absolutely continuous and satisfies
\[
 0\le q\le2,\qquad q'=\kappa m-Q(q)\ \text{a.e.},\qquad Q(q)=q(2-q),
 \qquad q(-\infty)=0,\quad q(+\infty)=2,
\]
$Q(q),q'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\int Q(q)\,\mathrm d x=\kappa\int m-2$. If
$\operatorname{supp} m\subset[x_-,x_+]$, then $q=0$ on $(-\infty,x_-]$ and $q=2$ on
$[x_+,\infty)$; if moreover $m$ is bounded, $q$ is Lipschitz. In particular,
$\kappa(m)=\max\{\kappa'>0:\int(f'^2+f^2)\ge\kappa'\int mf^2\ \text{for all }f\in H^1(\mathbb R)\}$.
head: environment
name: Ground state

label: lem:filter
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{lem:filter}
Let $m\ge0$ be integrable and not zero, with $M=\int m$, ground
parameter $\kappa$ and ground coordinate $q$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The linear filter $r_\circ(x)=\kappa\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}m(y)\,\mathrm d y$ is
absolutely continuous, $r_\circ'=\kappa m-2r_\circ$, $r_\circ(\pm\infty)=0$,
$\|r_\circ'\|_1\le2\kappa M$, and $0\le r_\circ\le q$. The function $h=q-r_\circ$
satisfies $h'=q^2-2h$, $0\le h\le q$, and
\[
 S(m):=\int_\mathbb R r_\circ^2=\frac{\kappa^2}4\operatorname{tr} K_m^2 .
\]
More generally, for $c>0$ and $0\le\tilde m\in L^1(\mathbb R)$,
\[
 \int_\mathbb R\Bigl(c\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}\tilde m(y)\,\mathrm d y\Bigr)^2\,\mathrm d x
 =\frac{c^2}4\iint e^{-2|y-z|}\tilde m(y)\tilde m(z)\,\mathrm d y\,\mathrm d z .
\]
\item For $s\ge0$ there is a unique bounded locally absolutely continuous
solution $r_s$ of $r_s'=sm-2r_s-r_s^2$ with $r_s(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$.
It satisfies
\[
 0\le r_s\le\frac s\kappa r_\circ\le\frac s\kappa q,\qquad r_s(+\infty)=0,\qquad
 \int_\mathbb R r_s=H_m(s),\qquad \|r_s'\|_1\le sM+(2+\|r_s\|_\infty)H_m(s).
\]
The function $V_s=\exp\int_{-\infty}^xr_s$ is the unique bounded solution of
$V_s(x)=1+\frac s2\int_{-\infty}^x(1-e^{-2(x-y)})m(y)V_s(y)\,\mathrm d y$; it is $C^1$,
$V_s'$ is locally absolutely continuous, $V_s''+2V_s'=smV_s$ almost
everywhere, $V_s(-\infty)=1$ and $V_s(+\infty)=\exp H_m(s)$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Filters

label: def:base
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:base}
A {calibration} consists of $\varsigma>0$, $b>0$, $\omega\ge0$, and
a continuous $g:[0,2]\to\mathbb R$ with $0\le g(h)\le2-h$. Put
\[
 \mathcal J_\varsigma(h)=-\int_0^h\frac{g}{2+\varsigma g},\qquad
 F_\varsigma(q,h)=\frac{2(q-h)^2-(q^2-2h)g(h)}{2+\varsigma g(h)},\qquad
 \Gamma_\varsigma(q)=\min_{0\le h\le q}F_\varsigma(q,h).
\]
For $\kappa>0$, the {comparison amplitude} $\nu_\kappa(q)$ is the
positive root of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-root}
 \kappa\nu^3-3Q(q)\nu-2bQ(q)-2\kappa\omega\Gamma_\varsigma(q)=0
 \quad(0<q<2),\qquad \nu_\kappa(0)=\nu_\kappa(2)=0,
\end{equation}
$d_\kappa=\kappa\nu_\kappa^2-Q$, and the {base value} of a density
$m$ with $\kappa(m)=\kappa$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-value}
 \mathcal B_\kappa(m)=-b+\frac{2b}\kappa+\frac3{2\kappa}\int_0^2\nu_\kappa\,\mathrm d q
 -\omega \mathcal J_\varsigma(2)-\omega S_\varsigma(m).
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Calibration

label: lem:base-identity
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Exact base identity

label: thm:contact
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:contact}
Let $b_\circ$ be smooth, positive and nondecreasing on $[0,1]$, and
$\varsigma>0$. Then $X_\circ(2)<\infty$, $m_\circ$ is continuous, bounded,
symmetric about $X_\circ(2)/2$, has ground parameter $k$ and ground
coordinate $q_\circ$ with $q_\circ=X_\circ^{-1}$ on $[0,X_\circ(2)]$. The function
$h_c=q_\circ-f_\circ$ increases strictly on $[0,\infty)$ from $h_c(0)=0$ to
$h_c(+\infty)=2$, and $g_\circ(h_c(x))=f_\circ(x)+\check f_\circ(x)$, $g_\circ(2)=0$,
defines a continuous $g_\circ$ with $0\le g_\circ(h)\le2-h$. For $g=g_\circ$
and every $0<q<2$, the function $F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ has a unique minimizer
on $[0,2]$, namely $h_c(x)$ with $q_\circ(x)=q$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contact}
 \Gamma_\varsigma(q)=
 \frac{Q(q)(f_\circ+\check f_\circ)-2f_\circ\check f_\circ}
 {2+\varsigma(f_\circ+\check f_\circ)}\quad\text{at }q_\circ=q,
 \qquad \Gamma_\varsigma(2-q)=\Gamma_\varsigma(q).
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Contact potential

label: prop:exact-reference
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:exact-reference}
Let $b_\circ$ and $\varsigma$ be as in \Cref{thm:contact}, and let $b>0$,
$\omega\ge0$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:self-consistent}
 b_\circ(Q(q))\,Q(q)=b\,Q(q)+k\omega\Gamma_\varsigma(q)\qquad(0<q<2)
\end{equation}
for the calibration $(\varsigma,b,\omega,g_\circ)$. Then $\nu_\circ=\nu_k$, and
$m_\circ(x)=\bar m_k(x-X_\circ(1))$, where $\bar m_k$ is the comparison density of the
calibration (\Cref{def:local-profile}). If moreover $\int m_\circ=1$, then $E(m_\circ)=\mathcal B_k(m_\circ)$, and
\[
 E(m_\circ)=\min\bigl\{E(m):\ m\in\mathcal M^1_c,\ \kappa(m)=k,\
 H_m(\varsigma k)=H_{m_\circ}(\varsigma k)\bigr\}.
\]
head: environment
name: Exactness at a self-consistent reference

label: prop:baseline
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: A one-determinant lower bound

title: Proof
body_md:
If $E(m)<\infty$, the first assertion follows from
\eqref{eq:base-deficit}; otherwise it is immediate. For the packed
densities, \Cref{thm:transfer} gives $\kappa(m_J)\to k$ uniformly in $J$.
Since $\int m_J=1$, $0\le\partial_sH_{m_J}(s)\le1/2$, and hence
\[
 |H_{m_J}(\varsigma\kappa(m_J))-H_*(\varsigma k)|
 \le\frac\varsigma2|\kappa(m_J)-k|+\frac{\varsigma k}2\delta_N\to0.
\]
Joint continuity of $\nu_\kappa(q)$ on compact parameter sets
(\Cref{lem:base-identity}) gives
$\mathcal B_{\kappa(m_J)}(m_J)\to\mathcal B_*$ uniformly. Apply
\eqref{eq:base-deficit} and $E(m_J)=N^{-3}\mathcal E_N(J)$.
head: environment

label: thm:common-measure
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: One measure for all filters

label: def:states
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:states}
The {state} of $m$ at $x$ is $Y=(q,u_0,u_1,h)$ with
$u_i=r_{s_i}/s_i$ and $h=q-r_\circ$. By \Cref{thm:ground,lem:filter} it is
absolutely continuous on compact intervals, $Y'$ is integrable,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:state-flow}
 Y'=\mathsf b(Y)n^2-\mathsf d(Y),\qquad
 \mathsf b=(\kappa,1,1,0),\qquad
 \mathsf d=\bigl(Q(q),\,2u_0+s_0u_0^2,\,2u_1+s_1u_1^2,\,2h-q^2\bigr),
\end{equation}
and $Y\to Y_-=(0,0,0,0)$ at $-\infty$, $Y\to Y_+=(2,0,0,2)$ at
$+\infty$.
head: environment
name: States

label: prop:state-region
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:state-region}
Let $\kappa>0$. There are continuous functions $V$ and
$0\le\vartheta_-\le\vartheta_+\le1$ on $[0,1]^2$, given explicitly in
\Cref{lem:range}, such that the set
\[
 \Omega_\kappa=\{Y_-\}\cup\Bigl\{\Bigl(q,\frac{qU}\kappa,\frac{qV(U,T)}\kappa,q\vartheta\Bigr):
 0<q\le2,\ (U,T)\in[0,1]^2,\ \vartheta_-(U,T)\le\vartheta\le\vartheta_+(U,T)\Bigr\}
\]
is compact, and the state of every $m$ as in \Cref{lem:filter} with
$\kappa(m)=\kappa$ lies in $\Omega_\kappa$ at every point. Every point of
$\Omega_\kappa$ with $q>0$ corresponds, through \eqref{eq:common}, to some
probability measure on $[0,1]$.
head: environment
name: The state region

label: def:local-profile
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:local-profile}
For a calibration and $\kappa>0$, let $X_\kappa(q)=\int_1^qd_\kappa^{-1}$ and
$\bar m_\kappa(X_\kappa(q))=\nu_\kappa(q)^2$ on $(X_\kappa(0),X_\kappa(2))$,
$\bar m_\kappa=0$ elsewhere ($X_\kappa(0)$ and $X_\kappa(2)$ are finite by
\Cref{lem:local-profile}). Its state at $X_\kappa(q)$ is denoted by
$\bar Y(q)=(q,\bar u_0,\bar u_1,\bar h)$. Its {right filters} are the
functions of $q$
\[
 R_s(q)=\check r_s(-X_\kappa(q)),\qquad R_\circ(q)=\check r_\circ(-X_\kappa(q)),
\]
where $\check r_s,\check r_\circ$ are the filters of \Cref{lem:filter} of the
reflected density $\bar m_\kappa(-x)$.
head: environment
name: Comparison density

label: thm:comparisons
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:comparisons}

Let $m\ge0$ be integrable and not zero, with $E(m)<\infty$,
$\kappa(m)=\kappa$, ground coordinate $q$ and filters $r_s,r_\circ$. Put
\[
 a_s(q,r)=-\frac{sQ(q)+\kappa rR_s(q)}{d_\kappa(q)\bigl(2+r+R_s(q)\bigr)},
 \qquad
 a_\circ(q,r)=\frac{\kappa\bigl[2rR_\circ(q)-Q(q)(r+R_\circ(q))\bigr]}{2d_\kappa(q)}
\]
for $0<q<2$, and $a_s=a_\circ=0$ at $q\in\{0,2\}$. Then
$-sQ/(2d_\kappa)\le a_s(q,r_s)\le0$, $-\kappa Q/d_\kappa\le a_\circ(q,r_\circ)\le0$, and
\[
 H_m(s)-H_{\bar m_\kappa}(s)=\int a_s(q,r_s)\bigl(n^2-\nu_\kappa(q)^2\bigr)\,\mathrm d x,
 \qquad
 S(m)-S(\bar m_\kappa)=\int a_\circ(q,r_\circ)\bigl(n^2-\nu_\kappa(q)^2\bigr)\,\mathrm d x ,
\]
with integrable integrands.
head: environment
name: Signed comparisons

label: prop:certificate-mechanism
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:certificate-mechanism}
Suppose that $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,n)\ge0$ for all $Y\in\Omega_\kappa$
with $0<q<2$ and all $n\ge0$, and that $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,0)\ge0$ for
$Y\in\Omega_\kappa$ with $q\in\{0,2\}$. Then every $m\in\mathcal M^{1}_c$ with
$\kappa(m)=\kappa$ satisfies
\[
 E(m)\ge\mathcal B_\kappa(m)+\sum_{i=0}^1\xi_i\bigl[H_m(s_i)-H_{\bar m_\kappa}(s_i)\bigr]
 +\chi\bigl[S(m)-S(\bar m_\kappa)\bigr]-\mathcal P_\kappa,
 \qquad
 \mathcal P_\kappa=\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\eta+\frac{\tau(\kappa-2)}\kappa .
\]
head: environment
name: Integrating the residual

label: thm:master
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:master}
With the data above, $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,n)\ge0$ for all $n\ge0$ if
and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:master}
 \mathcal C\bigl(\nu_\kappa,\ a-\eta-\mathsf b_\Psi\bigr)
 \le\frac{\eta d_\kappa+\tau Q}\kappa+\mathsf b_\Psi\nu_\kappa^2-\mathsf d_\Psi .
\end{equation}
For every $F\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ with $F(0)=F(2)$, the replacement
$\Psi\mapsto\Psi-F(q)$, $\eta\mapsto\eta+\kappa F'(q)$ changes neither
the two sides of \eqref{eq:master} nor $\mathcal P_\kappa$. If
$\eta=-\tau Q/d_\kappa+\nu_\kappa e$ on $(0,2)$ for a bounded function $e$
that is continuous outside a finite set, then the right side of
\eqref{eq:master} is
$\nu_\kappa e\,d_\kappa/\kappa+\mathsf b_\Psi\nu_\kappa^2-\mathsf d_\Psi$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:centered-price}
 \mathcal P_\kappa=\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\nu_\kappa e\,\mathrm d q
 +\tau\Bigl(1-\int\bar m_\kappa\Bigr).
\end{equation}

name: Pointwise criterion

label: def:dual
title: Definition

label: def:admissible

head: environment
name: Admissibility and value

label: thm:primal-map
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:primal-map}
Let $\kappa>0$ and let $D:(0,2)\to(0,\infty)$ be measurable with
$D\in L^\infty$ and $1/D\in L^1(0,2)$. Put
$X(q)=\int_1^qD^{-1}$ and let $m$ equal $(D(q)+Q(q))/\kappa$ at
$x=X(q)$ and zero outside $[X(0),X(2)]$. Then $m$ is bounded, compactly
supported, has ground parameter $\kappa$ and ground coordinate
$X^{-1}$ on its support, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:primal-masses}
 \int m^{j/2}=\int_0^2\Bigl(\frac{D+Q}\kappa\Bigr)^{j/2}\frac{\,\mathrm d q}D
 \qquad(j=1,2,3).
\end{equation}

label: def:primal
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:primal}
A primal certificate consists of rationals $c_0,\dots,c_{16}$, a matrix
$C\in\mathbb Q^{6\times6}$ and a rational $\varrho>0$. Put
\[
 \phi_0(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{16}c_jT_j(2t-1),\qquad
 \phi_i(t)=T_{j_i}(2t-1),\quad (j_1,\dots,j_6)=(0,1,2,3,6,7),
\]
and, for $a\in\mathbb R^6$, $\phi_a=\phi_0+\sum_ia_i\phi_i$. Let $m_a$ be the
density of \Cref{thm:primal-map} with $\kappa=k$ and the symmetric speed
\[
 D_a(t^3)=t^2e^{\phi_a(t)}\quad(0<t\le1),\qquad D_a(2-q)=D_a(q),
\]
and
\[
 F(a)=\Bigl(\int m_a-1,\ \int\sqrt{m_a}-1,\
 \bigl(H_{m_a}(s)-H_*(s)\bigr)_{s=s_0,s_1,\varsigma_{\mathrm{cal}}k},\
 S(m_a)-\frac{k^2}6\Bigr).
\]

label: thm:no-touching
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:no-touching}
Fix scales $0<\sigma_1<\dots<\sigma_r$ and put
\[
 \mathbf O(m)=\bigl(\kappa(m),\ \operatorname{tr} K_m^2,\ (H_m(\sigma_j),H_m'(\sigma_j))_{j=1}^r\bigr),
 \qquad H_m'(s)=\partial_sH_m(s).
\]
Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $\mathbf O(m_*)$ and $\Phi\in C^1(U)$ with
$\Phi(\mathbf O(m_*))=E(m_*)$. Then for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is
$v\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\|v\|_\infty<\varepsilon$ such that
$m=m_*+v$ satisfies $m\ge0$, $\int m=\int\sqrt m=1$, $\mathbf O(m)\in U$ and
$E(m)<\Phi(\mathbf O(m))$. The same holds if some coordinates of $\mathbf O$ are
omitted, and if the scales $\sigma_j$ are continuously differentiable
functions of $\kappa(m)$ with $\sigma_j(\kappa(m_*))>0$.

label: lem:trace
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:trace}
Let $J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$ and $G=(I-J)^{-1}$. Then $G$ is positive definite
with eigenvalues $(1-\xi_j)^{-1}$, $\xi_j=\cos((j-\frac12)\pi/N)$,
$1\le j\le N$, and
\[
 \operatorname{tr} G=N^2,\qquad \operatorname{tr}(G^2)=\frac{2N^4+N^2}3 .
\]
The eigenvalues of $G/N^2$, in decreasing order, are
\[
 r_{N,j}=\frac1{2N^2\sin^2((2j+1)\pi/(4N))}\qquad(0\le j<N).
\]
head: environment
name: Spectral identities of the fiber

label: proof:lem:trace
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:trace}
The characteristic polynomial of $J$ is $P=2^{1-N}T_N=\prod_j(z-\xi_j)$
with the distinct roots $\xi_j\in(-1,1)$ of $T_N$, so $G$ has the stated
eigenvalues, and
$\operatorname{tr} G=\sum_j(1-\xi_j)^{-1}=P'(1)/P(1)$,
$\operatorname{tr} G^2=\sum_j(1-\xi_j)^{-2}=(P'/P)^2(1)-P''(1)/P(1)$. The equation
$(1-x^2)T_N''-xT_N'+N^2T_N=0$ at $x=1$ gives $T_N'(1)=N^2T_N(1)=N^2$, and its
derivative $(1-x^2)T_N'''-3xT_N''+(N^2-1)T_N'=0$ at $x=1$ gives
$T_N''(1)=N^2(N^2-1)/3$. Hence $\operatorname{tr} G=N^2$ and
$\operatorname{tr} G^2=N^4-N^2(N^2-1)/3$. Finally
$1-\xi_{j+1}=2\sin^2((2j+1)\pi/(4N))$.

label: proof:thm:jacobi
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:jacobi}
Since $\|J\|=\cos\frac\pi{2N}<1<z_0$, every $z_0I-J_{[1:j]}$ is positive
definite, so $P_j(z_0)>0$. Evaluating \eqref{eq:continuant} at $z_0$ and
dividing by $P_{j+1}(z_0)$ gives $\alpha_j-\beta_j=1$; the formulas also give $\gamma_j>0$,
$\beta_j\ge0$ with equality exactly when $v_j=0$, and $\alpha_0=1$,
$\beta_0=0$. Evaluating \eqref{eq:continuant} at $z(\lambda)$, with
$z(\lambda)-b_{j+1}=(z_0-b_{j+1})-2\lambda/\Delta$, and dividing by $P_{j+1}(z_0)$
shows that $P_j(z(\lambda))/P_j(z_0)$ satisfies the residual recurrence of
$\mathcal R_J$; hence it is $p_j$, and $p_N(\lambda)=T_N(z(\lambda))/T_N(z_0)$. So
$\mathcal R_J\in\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)$.

Conversely, let $\mathcal R\in\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)$, put $a_j=\Delta\gamma_j/2$,
$c_j=\prod_{i<j}a_i^{-1}$, $b_{j+1}=z_0-\alpha_j/a_j$ and
$v_j=\beta_j/(a_ja_{j-1})\ge0$. Then $\widetilde P_j(z)=c_jp_j(\Delta(z_0-z)/2)$
satisfies \eqref{eq:continuant} with these coefficients, so it is the
$j$-th leading minor of the Jacobi matrix $J$ with diagonal $b_i$ and
off-diagonal entries $\sqrt{v_j}$. Terminal exactness makes
$\widetilde P_N$ a multiple of $T_N$; being monic, $\widetilde P_N=2^{1-N}T_N$,
so $J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$. Since $\alpha_j-\beta_j=1$, $p_j(0)=1$ and
$\widetilde P_j(z_0)=c_j$; inserting this into the formulas of the theorem
returns $(\alpha_j,\beta_j,\gamma_j)$. Inserting the formulas of the theorem
into the definitions of $b_{j+1},v_j$ returns the entries of $J$, the
off-diagonal ones by the nonnegative square root. The two maps are
therefore inverse to each other.

Since $\beta_j>0$ exactly when $v_j>0$, and $b_{j+1}=0$ exactly when
$\alpha_j=z_0a_j=\frac{L+\mu}2\gamma_j$, the bijection maps $\mathcal Y_N$ onto the
irreducible and $\mathcal X_N$ onto the centered recurrences. The zero-diagonal
matrix with $v_1=\frac12$ and $v_j=\frac14$ ($j\ge2$) has $P_1=T_1$ and
$P_j=2^{1-j}T_j$ ($j\ge2$) by \eqref{eq:continuant} and the Chebyshev
recurrence, so it lies in $\mathcal X_N$, and all six classes are nonempty.

label: lem:gain-kernel
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Derivative of the terminal residual

label: proof:lem:gain-kernel
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:gain-kernel}
The iterates are polynomials in the entries of $H_0,\dots,H_{N-1}$. Let
$U_j$ be the derivative of $\mathbf p_j$ at $(H,\dots,H)$ in the direction
$B$. Since $\mathbf p_j=p_j(H)=P_j(Z)/P_j(z_0)$ at the base point,
$U_{-1}=U_0=0$ and
$U_{j+1}=(\alpha_jI-\gamma_jH)U_j-\beta_jU_{j-1}-\gamma_jB_jp_j(H)$. By the formulas
of \Cref{thm:jacobi}, $P_{j+1}(z_0)(\alpha_jI-\gamma_jH)=P_j(z_0)(Z-b_{j+1}I)$,
$P_{j+1}(z_0)\beta_j=v_jP_{j-1}(z_0)$ and $P_{j+1}(z_0)\gamma_j=2P_j(z_0)/\Delta$; so
$W_j=P_j(z_0)U_j$ satisfies
\[
 W_{j+1}=(Z-b_{j+1}I)W_j-v_jW_{j-1}-\frac2\Delta B_jP_j(Z),\qquad W_{-1}=W_0=0 .
\]
The solution of the homogeneous recurrence with $W_l=0$, $W_{l+1}=X$ is
$W_j=\widehat P_{l,j}(Z)X$, by the continuant recurrence of $\widehat P_{l,j}$.
By linearity, $W_N=-\frac2\Delta\sum_l\widehat P_{l,N}(Z)B_lP_l(Z)$, and
$\mathsf D[B]=U_N=W_N/P_N(z_0)$ is \eqref{eq:gain-kernel}.
head: environment

label: proof:thm:gain
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:gain}
Put $\bar c=2/(\Delta P_N(z_0))$, $c_l(x,y)=\widehat P_l(x)P_l(y)$ and
$C_*^2=\max_{[-1,1]^2}\sum_lc_l^2$. Diagonalize $Z=O\operatorname{diag}(z_i)O^T$ with
$z_i\in[-1,1]$ and put $\widetilde B_l=O^TB_lO$. By \eqref{eq:gain-kernel} the
$(i,i')$ entry of $O^T\mathsf D[B]O$ is $-\bar c\sum_lc_l(z_i,z_{i'})(\widetilde B_l)_{ii'}$,
and the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality in $l$ gives
$\|\mathsf D[B]\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\le\bar c^2C_*^2\sum_l\|B_l\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2$. For a
maximizer $(x_*,y_*)$, $p=2$, $Z=\operatorname{diag}(x_*,y_*)$, that is,
$H=\frac\Delta2(z_0I-Z)$, and
$B_l=c_l(x_*,y_*)E_{12}/C_*$, with $E_{12}$ the matrix unit, give
$\mathsf D[B]=-\bar cC_*E_{12}$ and $\sum_l\|B_l\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2=1$; this proves the
equality in \eqref{eq:full-gain} and attainment in dimension two.

Deleting row and column $l+1$ from $I-J$ leaves the blocks
$I-J_{[1:l]}$ and $I-J_{[l+2:N]}$, so $d_{l+1}=P_l(1)\widehat P_l(1)/P_N(1)$.
With $P_N(1)/P_N(z_0)=T_N(1)/T_N(z_0)=\epsilon_N^\star$, the value of the maximum at
$(1,1)$ gives the inequality in \eqref{eq:full-gain}. Taking the infimum over
the fiber, which is in bijection with $\mathfrak E_N$, and the lower limit in
$N$, gives $\mathscr G(\mu,L)\ge2\sqrt{\underline{\mathsf e}}$, since the square root is
continuous and increasing.

label: lem:green
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:green}
Let $J$ be a real symmetric tridiagonal $M\times M$ matrix, $M\ge2$,
with zero diagonal, positive off-diagonal entries and $\|J\|<1$, and let
$G=(I-J)^{-1}$, $d_i=G_{ii}$. Put $t_0=t_M=0$ and
$t_i=J_{i,i+1}G_{i,i+1}$ for $1\le i<M$. Then $t_i>0$, $d_i=1+t_{i-1}+t_i$,
and with
\[
 x_1=0,\qquad x_{i+1}-x_i=\tfrac12\log(1+1/t_i)\quad(1\le i<M),
\]
one has
\[
 G_{ij}=\sqrt{d_id_j}\,e^{-|x_i-x_j|}\qquad(1\le i,j\le M).
\]
head: environment
name: Green factorization

label: proof:lem:green
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:green}
Put $A=I-J\succ0$, $a_i=J_{i,i+1}>0$, $\theta_i=\det A_{[1:i]}$ and
$\varphi_i=\det A_{[i:M]}$, with $\theta_0=\varphi_{M+1}=1$; all are positive. The
inverse of a tridiagonal matrix is
\[
 G_{ij}=\frac{\theta_{i-1}\varphi_{j+1}}{\theta_M}\prod_{r=i}^{j-1}a_r
 \qquad(i\le j)
\]
\cite{Meurant}, and the Laplace expansion of $\det A$ along its first $i$
rows gives $\theta_i\varphi_{i+1}-a_i^2\theta_{i-1}\varphi_{i+2}=\theta_M$ $(1\le i<M)$. Hence $G_{ij}>0$,
$G_{ij}G_{jl}=G_{il}d_j$ for $i\le j\le l$, and
$d_id_{i+1}-G_{i,i+1}^2=\theta_{i-1}\varphi_{i+2}/\theta_M=G_{i,i+1}/a_i$. The diagonal of
$AG=I$ reads $d_i=1+t_{i-1}+t_i$, and
$G_{i,i+1}^2/(d_id_{i+1})=t_i/(1+t_i)=e^{-2(x_{i+1}-x_i)}$. The quotients
$c_{ij}=G_{ij}/\sqrt{d_id_j}>0$ satisfy $c_{il}=c_{ij}c_{jl}$ for $i\le j\le l$,
so $c_{ij}=\prod_{r=i}^{j-1}c_{r,r+1}=e^{-(x_j-x_i)}$.

label: thm:centering-transfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:centering-transfer}
Let $J$ be a real symmetric tridiagonal $M\times M$ matrix with positive
off-diagonal entries and $\|J\|<1$. There is a unique lower bidiagonal
matrix $\mathsf B$ with positive diagonal and subdiagonal such that
$\mathsf B\mathsf B^T=(I+J)/2$. Define the $2M\times2M$ matrix $\widehat J$
on the index sets $\mathrm o=(1,3,\dots,2M-1)$ and
$\mathrm e=(2,4,\dots,2M)$ by
\[
 \widehat J_{\mathrm o,\mathrm e}=\mathsf B,\qquad
 \widehat J_{\mathrm e,\mathrm o}=\mathsf B^T,\qquad
 \widehat J_{\mathrm o,\mathrm o}=\widehat J_{\mathrm e,\mathrm e}=0.
\]
Then $\widehat J$ is tridiagonal with zero diagonal and positive
off-diagonal entries, $\|\widehat J\|<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lift-green-block}
 \bigl[(I-\widehat J)^{-1}\bigr]_{\mathrm o,\mathrm o}=2(I-J)^{-1},
\end{equation}
and $\det(xI-\widehat J)=2^{-M}\det((2x^2-1)I-J)$. For $M=N$ the map
$J\mapsto\widehat J$ is a bijection $\mathcal Y_N\to\mathcal X_{2N}$ with inverse
$J=2\mathsf B\mathsf B^T-I$.
head: environment
name: The centering lift

label: proof:thm:centering-transfer
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:centering-transfer}
The matrix $\Sigma=(I+J)/2$ satisfies $0\prec\Sigma\prec I$ and is tridiagonal;
its Cholesky factor $\mathsf B$ is the unique lower triangular matrix with
positive diagonal and $\mathsf B\mathsf B^T=\Sigma$, it is bidiagonal, and
$\mathsf B_{i+1,i}=\Sigma_{i,i+1}/\mathsf B_{ii}>0$ \cite[\S\S4.2--4.3]{GolubVanLoan}. In
the interlaced order the entries of $\widehat J$ above the diagonal are
$\mathsf B_{ii}$ and $\mathsf B_{i+1,i}$, so $\widehat J$ is a Jacobi matrix with
zero diagonal and positive off-diagonal entries. Grouping the odd
indices before the even ones, $\widehat J$ becomes
$\mathscr J=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&\mathsf B\\\mathsf B^T&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$,
and $\mathscr J^2=\operatorname{diag}(\mathsf B\mathsf B^T,\mathsf B^T\mathsf B)$ has the
eigenvalues of $\Sigma$ in $(0,1)$; so $\|\widehat J\|<1$. The Schur complement
of the lower right block of $xI-\mathscr J$ gives
$\det(xI-\widehat J)=x^M\det(xI-x^{-1}\Sigma)=\det(x^2I-\Sigma)$ for $x\ne0$, and by
continuity for all $x$. The system $(I-\mathscr J)(r,s)=(f,0)$ reads
$r-\mathsf Bs=f$, $s=\mathsf B^Tr$, so $(I-\Sigma)r=f$ and $r=2(I-J)^{-1}f$, which
is \eqref{eq:lift-green-block}.

For $J\in\mathcal Y_N$, $T_N(2x^2-1)=T_{2N}(x)$ gives
$\det(xI-\widehat J)=2^{1-2N}T_{2N}(x)$, so $\widehat J\in\mathcal X_{2N}$. Conversely, for
$C\in\mathcal X_{2N}$ the block $\mathsf B=C_{\mathrm o,\mathrm e}$ is lower bidiagonal with
positive diagonal and subdiagonal, $J=2\mathsf B\mathsf B^T-I$ is a Jacobi
matrix with positive off-diagonal entries, and the same determinant
identity gives $\det(yI-J)=2^{1-N}T_N(y)$ for $y\ge-1$, hence for all $y$;
so $J\in\mathcal Y_N$. By uniqueness of the Cholesky factor the two maps are
inverse to each other.
head: environment

label: proof:cor:centering-packing
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:cor:centering-packing}
For $M=1$, take $y_1=0$ and $I_1=[-1/d_1,0]$. Assume $M\ge2$ and
apply \Cref{lem:green} to the lift $\widehat J$, with points
$x_1<\dots<x_{2M}$, numbers $t_r$ and diagonal $D_r=1+t_{r-1}+t_r$ of
$(I-\widehat J)^{-1}$, and put $y_i=x_{2i-1}$. By \eqref{eq:lift-green-block},
$D_{2i-1}=2d_i$ and $2G_{ij}=\sqrt{(2d_i)(2d_j)}\,e^{-|y_i-y_j|}$. Since
$\frac12\log(1+1/t)=\operatorname{artanh}(1/(2t+1))\ge1/(2t+1)$,
\[
 x_{2i}-x_{2i-2}\ge\frac1{2t_{2i-2}+1}+\frac1{2t_{2i-1}+1}\ge\frac4{2D_{2i-1}}=\frac1{d_i}
 \qquad(2\le i\le M-1),
\]
by the inequality $\frac1a+\frac1b\ge\frac4{a+b}$. Put $I_1=[y_1-1/d_1,y_1]$,
$I_M=[y_M,y_M+1/d_M]$ (for $M\ge2$), and for $2\le i\le M-1$ let $I_i$ be the
interval of length $1/d_i$ in $[x_{2i-2},x_{2i}]$ whose left end point is
$\max\{x_{2i-2},y_i-1/d_i\}$; it lies in $[x_{2i-2},x_{2i}]$ and contains $y_i$,
because $x_{2i-2}<y_i<x_{2i}$ and $x_{2i}-x_{2i-2}\ge1/d_i$. These intervals lie in
the consecutive ranges $(-\infty,x_1]$, $[x_{2i-2},x_{2i}]$ and $[x_{2M-1},\infty)$,
which have pairwise disjoint interiors.

label: lem:features
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:features}
\begin{enumerate}
\item $\mathcal H$ is a separable Hilbert space; every $u\in\mathcal H$ has a continuous
representative with $u(x)\to0$ as $|x|\to\infty$; and
$\langle u,\mathsf k_x\rangle_\mathcal H=u(x)$, $\langle v_x,v_y\rangle_\mathcal H=e^{-|x-y|}$,
$\|\mathcal P_x-\mathcal P_y\|_1=2\sqrt{1-e^{-2|x-y|}}$.
\item The integral defining $\mathcal K_\sigma$ exists as a Bochner integral
in the trace class, $\|\mathcal K_\sigma\|_1\le|\sigma|(\mathbb R)$ and
$\operatorname{tr}\mathcal K_\sigma=\sigma(\mathbb R)$; for $\sigma\ge0$, $\mathcal K_\sigma$ is
positive.
\item For $0\le m\in L^1(\mathbb R)$, $K_m$ is positive and trace class, its
nonzero eigenvalues coincide with those of $\mathcal K_m$ with
multiplicity, and $\operatorname{tr} K_m=\int m$. For $\sigma=\sum_{i=1}^Mw_i\delta_{y_i}$
with $w_i\ge0$, the nonzero eigenvalues of $\mathcal K_\sigma$ coincide with
those of the matrix $(\sqrt{w_iw_j}\,e^{-|y_i-y_j|})_{i,j=1}^M$.
\item For positive trace-class operators $A,B$ on a separable real Hilbert
space,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trace-lipschitz}
 \sum_{j\ge0}|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|_1 .
\end{equation}
\item If $\pi$ is a finite positive Borel measure on $\mathbb R^2$ of total mass
$M_\pi$ whose marginals are $\sigma$ and $\sigma'$, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:coupling-spectrum}
 \|\mathcal K_\sigma-\mathcal K_{\sigma'}\|_1
 \le2\sqrt{2M_\pi\int|x-y|\,\mathrm d\pi(x,y)} .
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Feature operators

label: proof:lem:features
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:features}
(i) The Sobolev facts follow from \cite[Proposition~8.1 and Theorem~8.2]{Brezis}.
In particular, $(u^2)'=2uu'\in L^1$, so $u^2$ has limits at both
infinities; these limits vanish because $u\in L^2$. The distributional
identity $(-\partial_t^2+1)\mathsf k_x=\delta_x$ gives
$\langle u,\mathsf k_x\rangle_\mathcal H=u(x)$, first for smooth compactly supported $u$
and then by density in $H^1$. Thus $\langle v_x,v_y\rangle_\mathcal H=e^{-|x-y|}$.
For unit vectors $v,w$ with $r=\langle v,w\rangle$, the operator
$v\otimes v-w\otimes w$ has nonzero eigenvalues
$\pm\sqrt{1-r^2}$ (diagonalize on $\operatorname{span}\{v,w\}$). This proves the
trace-norm formula, including the case $v=w$.

(ii) The map $x\mapsto\mathcal P_x$ is continuous in trace norm, has a
separable range, and satisfies $\|\mathcal P_x\|_1=1$. It is therefore
Bochner integrable against every finite signed measure, with
$\|\mathcal K_\sigma\|_1\le|\sigma|(\mathbb R)$. Positivity follows by integrating
$\langle \mathcal P_xu,u\rangle=|\langle u,v_x\rangle|^2$. Continuity of the trace on the
trace class gives $\operatorname{tr}\mathcal K_\sigma=\int\operatorname{tr}\mathcal P_x\,\mathrm d\sigma=\sigma(\mathbb R)$.

(iii) Define $A_m:L^2(\mathbb R)\to\mathcal H$ by
$A_mf=\int v_x\sqrt{m(x)}f(x)\,\mathrm d x$. The Bochner integral exists and
$\|A_mf\|_\mathcal H\le\|m\|_1^{1/2}\|f\|_2$. Part (i) gives
\[
 A_m^*u=\sqrt{2m}\,u,\qquad A_mA_m^*=\mathcal K_m,\qquad A_m^*A_m=K_m.
\]
For an orthonormal basis $(e_j)$ of $\mathcal H$, Tonelli's theorem yields
\[
 \|A_m^*\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
 =\sum_j\int m(x)|\langle e_j,v_x\rangle_\mathcal H|^2\,\mathrm d x
 =\int m(x)\|v_x\|_\mathcal H^2\,\mathrm d x=\int m.
\]
Thus $A_m$ is Hilbert--Schmidt, both products are positive trace class,
and their nonzero eigenvalues coincide with multiplicity: $A_m$ and
$\lambda^{-1}A_m^*$ identify the eigenspaces at $\lambda>0$.
For an atomic measure, use instead
$Ca=\sum_i\sqrt{w_i}a_iv_{y_i}$; then $CC^*=\mathcal K_\sigma$ and
$(C^*C)_{ij}=\sqrt{w_iw_j}e^{-|y_i-y_j|}$.

(iv) Write $A-B=D_+-D_-$ for its positive and negative parts. The min--max
principle gives eigenvalue monotonicity under operator order. Since
$A\preceq B+D_+$,
\[
 \sum_j(\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B))_+
 \le\sum_j[\lambda_j(B+D_+)-\lambda_j(B)]=\operatorname{tr} D_+.
\]
Exchange $A$ and $B$ and add; $\operatorname{tr} D_++\operatorname{tr} D_-=\|A-B\|_1$ proves
\eqref{eq:trace-lipschitz}. Finite-dimensional spaces may be enlarged
by a zero summand to implement the stated padding convention.

(v) The marginal identities for Bochner integrals give
$\mathcal K_\sigma-\mathcal K_{\sigma'}=\int(\mathcal P_x-\mathcal P_y)\,\mathrm d\pi$.
Part (i), $1-e^{-2a}\le2a$, and Cauchy--Schwarz imply
\[
 \|\mathcal K_\sigma-\mathcal K_{\sigma'}\|_1
 \le2\int\sqrt{1-e^{-2|x-y|}}\,\mathrm d\pi
 \le2\sqrt{2M_\pi\int|x-y|\,\mathrm d\pi}.\qedhere
\]

label: proof:thm:packing
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:packing}
Split $J$ at its zero off-diagonal entries into irreducible diagonal
blocks $J^{(1)},\dots,J^{(q)}$; each is real symmetric tridiagonal with
positive off-diagonal entries and $\|J^{(p)}\|\le\|J\|<1$, and
$G=(I-J)^{-1}$ is block diagonal with blocks $(I-J^{(p)})^{-1}$. For a
block of size at least two, \Cref{cor:centering-packing} gives points
$y_i$ and closed intervals $I_i\ni y_i$ of lengths $1/d_i$ with disjoint
interiors such that $G_{ij}=\sqrt{d_id_j}e^{-|y_i-y_j|}$ inside the block.
For a block of size one with entry $b$, $d_i=(1-b)^{-1}>0$; put $y_i=0$
and $I_i=[-1/d_i,0]$. Translate the blocks, in their order, so that the
union of the intervals of each block lies at distance at least $2\log N$
from the union of the intervals of every other block; translations
preserve the factorization within a block. Define $m_J$ as in the
statement. Since the $I_i$ have disjoint interiors and
$|I_i|=1/d_i$,
\[
 \int m_J=\sum_i\frac{d_i^2}{N^2}\cdot\frac1{d_i}=\frac{\operatorname{tr} G}{N^2}=1,\qquad
 \int\sqrt{m_J}=\sum_i\frac{d_i}N\cdot\frac1{d_i}=1,\qquad
 E(m_J)=\sum_i\frac{d_i^3}{N^3}\cdot\frac1{d_i}=\frac{\mathcal E_N(J)}{N^3},
\]
by \Cref{lem:trace}; $m_J$ is bounded with compact support, so
$m_J\in\mathcal M_c$.

Put $w_i=d_i/N^2$, so that $\sum_iw_i=1$, and
$\sigma_J=\sum_iw_i\delta_{y_i}$. The measure
$\pi=\sum_i\frac{d_i^2}{N^2}\mathbf1_{I_i}(x)\,\mathrm d x\otimes\delta_{y_i}$ has
marginals $m_J\,\mathrm d x$ and $\sigma_J$ and mass one. Since
$\int_{I}|x-y|\,\mathrm d x\le|I|^2/2$ for $y\in I$,
\[
 \int|x-y|\,\mathrm d\pi\le\sum_i\frac{d_i^2}{N^2}\cdot\frac1{2d_i^2}=\frac1{2N},
\]
and \eqref{eq:coupling-spectrum} gives
$\|\mathcal K_{m_J}-\mathcal K_{\sigma_J}\|_1\le2/\sqrt N$. By
\Cref{lem:features}(iii) and (iv),
$\sum_j|\lambda_j(K_{m_J})-\lambda_j(\widetilde G)|\le2/\sqrt N$, where
$\widetilde G_{ij}=\sqrt{w_iw_j}\,e^{-|y_i-y_j|}$. For $i,j$ in the same
block $\widetilde G_{ij}=G_{ij}/N^2$; for $i,j$ in different blocks
$G_{ij}=0$ and $|y_i-y_j|\ge2\log N$, so
$0<\widetilde G_{ij}\le\sqrt{w_iw_j}/N^2$. Each matrix unit has trace norm
one, so
\[
 \Bigl\|\widetilde G-\frac G{N^2}\Bigr\|_1\le\sum_{i,j}\frac{\sqrt{w_iw_j}}{N^2}
 =\frac1{N^2}\Bigl(\sum_i\sqrt{w_i}\Bigr)^2\le\frac{N\sum_iw_i}{N^2}=\frac1N .
\]
Both matrices are positive semidefinite, and \eqref{eq:trace-lipschitz}
together with the triangle inequality gives
\eqref{eq:block-spectral-error}.

label: proof:thm:transfer
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:transfer}
By \Cref{lem:trace}, $\lambda_j(G/N^2)=r_{N,j}$ for $j<N$ and zero for
$j\ge N$. For $0\le j<N$ the argument $a=(2j+1)\pi/(4N)$ lies in
$(0,\pi/2)$, where $\frac2\pi a\le\sin a\le a$; hence
\[
 \Lambda_j=\frac{8}{\pi^2(2j+1)^2}=\frac1{2N^2a^2}\le r_{N,j}
 \le\frac{\pi^2}{8N^2a^2}=\frac2{(2j+1)^2}.
\]
For fixed $j$, $r_{N,j}\to\Lambda_j$ because $\sin a/a\to1$. Since
$\sum_jr_{N,j}=\operatorname{tr} G/N^2=1$ and $r_{N,j}\le2/(2j+1)^2$, dominated
convergence gives $\sum_j\Lambda_j=1$. Similarly
$\sum_jr_{N,j}^2=\operatorname{tr}(G^2)/N^4=\frac23+\frac1{3N^2}$ by \Cref{lem:trace},
and $r_{N,j}^2\le4/(2j+1)^4$, so $\sum_j\Lambda_j^2=\frac23$. Since
$r_{N,j}\ge\Lambda_j$ for $j<N$,
\[
 \sum_j|r_{N,j}-\Lambda_j|
 =\Bigl(1-\sum_{j<N}\Lambda_j\Bigr)+\sum_{j\ge N}\Lambda_j
 =2\sum_{j\ge N}\Lambda_j,
\]
and $\frac1{(2j+1)^2}\le\frac1{(2j-1)(2j+1)}=\frac12\bigl(\frac1{2j-1}-\frac1{2j+1}\bigr)$
gives, by telescoping, $\sum_{j\ge N}\Lambda_j\le\frac8{\pi^2}\cdot\frac1{2(2N-1)}$.
Hence $\sum_j|r_{N,j}-\Lambda_j|\le8/(\pi^2(2N-1))$, and with
\eqref{eq:block-spectral-error} and the triangle inequality this proves
\eqref{eq:deltaN}.

For the determinant, $P(z)=\prod_j(z-\xi_j)=2^{1-N}T_N(z)$ and
$T_N(1)=1$ give
\[
 \prod_{j<N}\Bigl(1+\frac s2r_{N,j}\Bigr)
 =\prod_{j=1}^N\frac{1+s/(2N^2)-\xi_j}{1-\xi_j}
 =\frac{T_N(1+s/(2N^2))}{T_N(1)}=T_N\Bigl(1+\frac s{2N^2}\Bigr).
\]
Use $T_N(\cosh t)=\cosh(Nt)$ with
$t_N=2\operatorname{arsinh}(\sqrt s/(2N))$. Then
$\cosh t_N=1+s/(2N^2)$ and $Nt_N\to\sqrt s$, giving
$\sum_j\log(1+sr_{N,j}/2)\to\log\cosh\sqrt s=H_*(s)$, also for $s=0$.
The map
$x\mapsto\log(1+sx/2)$ is $(s/2)$-Lipschitz on $[0,\infty)$, so
\[
 \Bigl|\sum_j\log(1+sr_{N,j}/2)-\sum_j\log(1+s\Lambda_j/2)\Bigr|
 \le\frac s2\sum_j|r_{N,j}-\Lambda_j|\longrightarrow0,
\]
which proves $\sum_j\log(1+s\Lambda_j/2)=H_*(s)$; the series converges
because its terms are at most $s\Lambda_j/2$. The same Lipschitz bound
and \eqref{eq:deltaN} give $|H_{m_J}(s)-H_*(s)|\le\frac s2\delta_N$. Since
$\sum_j\lambda_j(K_{m_J})=\int m_J=1$ and $\sum_j\Lambda_j=1$, all
$\lambda_j(K_{m_J})$ and $\Lambda_j$ lie in $[0,1]$, so
\[
 \Bigl|\operatorname{tr} K_{m_J}^2-\frac23\Bigr|
 =\Bigl|\sum_j(\lambda_j(K_{m_J})-\Lambda_j)(\lambda_j(K_{m_J})+\Lambda_j)\Bigr|
 \le2\delta_N .
\]
Finally, $|\lambda_0(K_{m_J})-\Lambda_0|\le\delta_N<\Lambda_0/2$ gives
$\lambda_0(K_{m_J})>\Lambda_0/2$ and
\[
 |\kappa(m_J)-k|=\frac{2|\lambda_0(K_{m_J})-\Lambda_0|}{\lambda_0(K_{m_J})\Lambda_0}
 \le\frac{4\delta_N}{\Lambda_0^2},
\]
where $k=2/\Lambda_0=\pi^2/4$.

label: proof:thm:sine-finite
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:sine-finite}
{Spectrum.} Put $w_i=p_i\sin(h/2)$. Since
$2\sin(h/2)\sin\theta_i=\cos((i-1)h)-\cos(ih)$, the sum $\sum_iw_i$
telescopes to $\frac12(1-\cos(Nh))=1$. For functions $f$ on the nodes
$\{x_1,\dots,x_N\}$, written $f_i=f(x_i)$, define
\[
 (\mathcal L_Nf)_i=\frac{\sin(ih)f_{i+1}+\sin((i-1)h)f_{i-1}}{2p_i}
 \qquad(1\le i\le N),
\]
where the coefficient of $f_0$ at $i=1$ and that of $f_{N+1}$ at $i=N$
vanish. Since
$w_i(\mathcal L_N)_{i,i+1}=\frac12\sin(h/2)\sin(ih)=w_{i+1}(\mathcal L_N)_{i+1,i}$,
$\mathcal L_N$ is symmetric in $\ell^2(w)$. The matrix
$D^{1/2}\mathcal L_ND^{-1/2}$, $D=\operatorname{diag}(w_i)$, is symmetric tridiagonal with
zero diagonal and entries
$\sqrt{w_i/w_{i+1}}\,\sin(ih)/(2p_i)=\sin(ih)/(2\sqrt{p_ip_{i+1}})$, that is,
it equals $J_N^\star$; these entries are positive for $1\le i<N$.

Let $f=T_j$, so that $f_i=\cos(j\theta_i)$, and use $\theta_{i\pm1}=\theta_i\pm h$,
$ih=\theta_i+h/2$, $(i-1)h=\theta_i-h/2$. The terms with the vanishing
coefficients may be evaluated by the same formula, so for every $i$
\begin{align*}
 2p_i(\mathcal L_NT_j)_i
 &=\sin(\theta_i+\tfrac h2)\cos(j\theta_i+jh)
  +\sin(\theta_i-\tfrac h2)\cos(j\theta_i-jh)\\
 &=\cos(j\theta_i)\cos(jh)\cdot2\sin\theta_i\cos\tfrac h2
  -\sin(j\theta_i)\sin(jh)\cdot2\cos\theta_i\sin\tfrac h2 .
\end{align*}
With $U_{j-1}(\cos\theta)=\sin(j\theta)/\sin\theta$ this reads
\[
 \mathcal L_NT_j=\cos\tfrac h2\cos(jh)\,T_j-\sin\tfrac h2\sin(jh)\,xU_{j-1}
 \quad\text{on the nodes}.
\]
For $j\ge1$ both $T_j$ and $xU_{j-1}$ have degree $j$ and leading
coefficient $2^{j-1}$, and $\mathcal L_NT_0=\cos\frac h2$. Hence, for
$0\le j<N$, $\mathcal L_N$ maps the restrictions to the nodes of the
polynomials of degree at most $j$ into themselves, and multiplies the
coefficient of $x^j$ by $\cos\frac h2\cos(jh)-\sin\frac h2\sin(jh)=\cos((j+\frac12)h)$.
The $N$ nodes are distinct, so the restrictions of the polynomials of
degree less than $N$ form all of $\mathbb R^N$, and $\ell^2(w)$ is an inner
product on them. Let $\phi_{N,j}$ be the orthonormal polynomials of
$\ell^2(w)$ with positive leading coefficients, $0\le j<N$. Then
$\mathcal L_N\phi_{N,j}$ has degree at most $j$, and for $l<j$,
$\langle \mathcal L_N\phi_{N,j},\phi_{N,l}\rangle_w=\langle \phi_{N,j},\mathcal L_N\phi_{N,l}\rangle_w=0$
because $\mathcal L_N\phi_{N,l}$ has degree at most $l$. Hence
$\mathcal L_N\phi_{N,j}=\cos((j+\frac12)h)\phi_{N,j}$. The vectors
$U_{\cdot j}=(\sqrt{w_i}\phi_{N,j}(x_i))_i$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of
$J_N^\star$ with eigenvalues $\cos((j+\frac12)h)$, $0\le j<N$; these are
the $N$ distinct roots of $T_N$, so the monic characteristic polynomial
of $J_N^\star$ is $2^{1-N}T_N$ and $J_N^\star\in\mathcal X_N$. By
\Cref{thm:jacobi}, $\mathcal R_N^\star$ is centered.

{Reversal.} Since $\sin((N-i)h)=\sin(ih)$,
$\sin\theta_{N-i}=\sin\theta_{i+1}$ and $\sin\theta_{N+1-i}=\sin\theta_i$,
the entries satisfy $J^\star_{N-i,N+1-i}=J^\star_{i,i+1}$. Hence
$RJ_N^\star R=J_N^\star$ for the reversal permutation $R$, which maps
$J^\star_{[s+2:N]}$ onto $J^\star_{[1:N-s-1]}$, and
$\widehat P_s=P_{N-s-1}$ for $0\le s<N$.

{Leading principal polynomials.} Put $A_0=1$ and
$A_s=\prod_{r=0}^{s-1}\frac{\sin((r+\frac12)h)}{\sin((r+1)h)}>0$ for
$1\le s\le N-1$, and
\[
 C_s(\cos\theta)=\sum_{j=0}^sA_jA_{s-j}\cos((s-2j)\theta)\qquad(0\le s\le N-1).
\]
We show that for $1\le s\le N-2$
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rogers}
 \sin((s+1)h)\,C_{s+1}=2\sin((s+\tfrac12)h)\,xC_s-\sin(sh)\,C_{s-1}.
\end{equation}
Using $2\cos\theta\cos(n\theta)=\cos((n+1)\theta)+\cos((n-1)\theta)$, the
three functions in \eqref{eq:rogers} are combinations of
$\cos((s+1-2k)\theta)$, $0\le k\le s+1$, with coefficients
\[
 [C_{s+1}]_k=A_kA_{s+1-k},\qquad
 [2xC_s]_k=A_kA_{s-k}+A_{k-1}A_{s+1-k},\qquad
 [C_{s-1}]_k=A_{k-1}A_{s-k},
\]
where $A_{-1}=0$ and $A_n=0$ for $n<0$. It suffices to compare these
coefficients. For $k=0$ the comparison reads
$\sin((s+1)h)A_{s+1}=\sin((s+\frac12)h)A_s$, which is the definition of
$A_{s+1}$; the case $k=s+1$ is the same. For $1\le k\le s$ put
$l=s+1-k\ge1$; dividing by $A_{k-1}A_{l-1}$ and using
$A_n/A_{n-1}=\sin((n-\frac12)h)/\sin(nh)$, then multiplying by
$\sin(kh)\sin(lh)$, the comparison becomes, with $\alpha=kh$,
$\beta=lh$, $\delta=h/2$,
\[
 \sin(\alpha+\beta)\sin(\alpha-\delta)\sin(\beta-\delta)
 +\sin(\alpha+\beta-2\delta)\sin\alpha\sin\beta
 =\sin(\alpha+\beta-\delta)\bigl[\sin(\alpha-\delta)\sin\beta
 +\sin(\beta-\delta)\sin\alpha\bigr].
\]
Both sides equal
$\cos(\alpha-\beta)\cos\delta\sin\sigma-\sin\sigma\cos\sigma$,
where $\sigma=\alpha+\beta-\delta$, by the product-to-sum identities.
This proves \eqref{eq:rogers}.

The coefficient of $x^s$ in $C_s$ is $2^sA_s$, since $\cos(n\theta)=T_n(x)$
has leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$ and the degree $s$ occurs
for $j=0$ and $j=s$. Put $\widetilde P_s=C_s/(2^sA_s)$. Then
$\widetilde P_0=1$, $\widetilde P_1=x$, and dividing \eqref{eq:rogers} by
$2^{s+1}\sin((s+1)h)A_{s+1}=2^{s+1}\sin((s+\frac12)h)A_s$ gives
\[
 \widetilde P_{s+1}=x\widetilde P_s
 -\frac{\sin(sh)A_{s-1}}{4\sin((s+\frac12)h)A_s}\widetilde P_{s-1}
 =x\widetilde P_s-\frac{\sin^2(sh)}{4\sin\theta_s\sin\theta_{s+1}}\widetilde P_{s-1}.
\]
The last coefficient is $(J^\star_{s,s+1})^2$, and $J_N^\star$ has zero
diagonal, so $\widetilde P_s$ and $P_s$ satisfy the same recurrence
\eqref{eq:continuant} with the same initial values: $P_s=C_s/(2^sA_s)$
for $0\le s\le N-1$. All coefficients $A_jA_{s-j}$ are positive and
$|\cos((s-2j)\theta)|\le1$, so $|P_s(x)|\le P_s(1)$ for $x\in[-1,1]$.

{The gain.} By reversal, $|\widehat P_s(x)|=|P_{N-s-1}(x)|\le
P_{N-s-1}(1)=\widehat P_s(1)$ on $[-1,1]$, so
$\sum_s\widehat P_s(x)^2P_s(y)^2\le\sum_s\widehat P_s(1)^2P_s(1)^2$ for
$x,y\in[-1,1]$. The maximum in \eqref{eq:full-gain} is attained at
$(1,1)$, and the endpoint evaluation in the proof of \Cref{thm:gain}
gives \eqref{eq:sine-gain}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:legendre}
Let $\mathsf P_j$ be the Legendre polynomials, and let
\[
 \upsilon_j(t)=\sqrt{\pi(j+\tfrac12)\sin\pi t}\;\mathsf P_j(\cos\pi t),\qquad
 \mu_j=\pi^2(j+\tfrac12)^2=2/\Lambda_j .
\]
Then $(\upsilon_j)$ is an orthonormal
basis of $L^2(0,1)$, and each $\upsilon_j$ solves
$-\upsilon''-\frac{\pi^2}{4\sin^2\pi t}\upsilon=\mu_j\upsilon$ on $(0,1)$. Put
\[
 l(t)=\frac2\pi\sqrt{\sin\pi t}\,\mathbf K\bigl(\sin^2\tfrac{\pi t}2\bigr),
 \qquad \bar l(t)=l(1-t).
\]
Then $l,\bar l$ extend continuously to $[0,1]$ with value zero at both
ends, $l'\bar l-l\bar l'=2$ on $(0,1)$, and the operator with kernel
$G_*(t,s)=\frac12l(\min(t,s))\,\bar l(\max(t,s))$ is
$\sum_j\mu_j^{-1}\langle \cdot,\upsilon_j\rangle\upsilon_j$. The kernel is continuous on
$[0,1]^2$, $G_*(t,t)=\sum_j\upsilon_j(t)^2/\mu_j$ for every $t$, and
$\int_0^1G_*(t,t)\,\mathrm d t=\frac12$.

label: proof:lem:legendre
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:legendre}
{The basis.} Legendre orthogonality and density of polynomials in
$L^2(-1,1)$ show that $(p_j)$ is an orthonormal basis. The substitution
$z=\cos\pi t$ proves that $V$ is unitary; hence $(\upsilon_j)=(Vp_j)$
is an orthonormal basis of $L^2(0,1)$.

{The equation.} Let $s=\sin^2(\pi t/2)$, so $\cos\pi t=1-2s$ and
$\sin\pi t=2\sqrt{s(1-s)}$. For $F\in C^2(0,1)$, the chain rule gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:legendre-transform}
 \Bigl(-\partial_t^2-\frac{\pi^2}{4\sin^2\pi t}\Bigr)\bigl\{\sqrt{\sin\pi t}\,F(s)\bigr\}
 =\pi^2\sqrt{\sin\pi t}\,\bigl\{\tfrac14F-(1-2s)F'-s(1-s)F''\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
For $F(s)=\mathsf P_j(1-2s)$, $\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d x}=-\frac12\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d s}$ and
$1-x^2=4s(1-s)$ turn the Legendre equation into
$s(1-s)F''+(1-2s)F'+j(j+1)F=0$, so the brace in
\eqref{eq:legendre-transform} equals $(\frac14+j(j+1))F=(j+\frac12)^2F$, and
$\upsilon_j$ solves the stated equation.

{Zero-energy solutions.} For $0\le s<1$, the binomial series
$(1-u)^{-1/2}=\sum_nc_nu^n$, $c_n=\binom{2n}n4^{-n}$, and
$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2n}\theta\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac\pi2c_n$ give
$\mathbf K(s)=\frac\pi2\sum_nc_n^2s^n$. Since $c_{n+1}/c_n=(n+\frac12)/(n+1)$,
the coefficients $a_n=\frac\pi2c_n^2$ satisfy $(n+1)^2a_{n+1}=(n+\frac12)^2a_n$,
which is the coefficient form of
\[
 s(1-s)\mathbf K''+(1-2s)\mathbf K'-\tfrac14\mathbf K=0 .
\]
This equation is invariant under $s\mapsto1-s$, so $\mathbf K(1-s)$ also
solves it. By \eqref{eq:legendre-transform}, $l$ and $\bar l$, which equal
$\frac2\pi\sqrt{\sin\pi t}$ times $\mathbf K(s)$ and $\mathbf K(1-s)$, solve
$-y''-\frac{\pi^2}{4\sin^2\pi t}y=0$ on $(0,1)$, and both are positive.

{Endpoint behavior.} Our elliptic integral uses the parameter:
$\mathbf K(s)=K_{\mathrm{DLMF}}(\sqrt s)$. The convergent endpoint
expansion \cite[Eq.~19.12.1]{DLMF2026}, with complementary modulus
$\sqrt s$, gives
\[
 \mathbf K(s)=\frac\pi2+O(s),\qquad
 \mathbf K(1-s)=\log4-\frac12\log s+O(s\log(1/s))
 \quad(s\downarrow0).
\]
As $t\downarrow0$, $\sin\pi t=\pi t(1+O(t^2))$ and $s=(\pi t/2)^2(1+O(t^2))$,
so $\frac12\log\frac1s=\log\frac1t+O(1)$ and
\[
 l(t)=\sqrt{\pi t}\,(1+O(t^2)),\qquad
 \bar l(t)=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\sqrt t\log\frac1t+O(\sqrt t).
\]
In particular $l(t)\to0$ and $\bar l(t)\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, and by
$\bar l(t)=l(1-t)$ also as $t\uparrow1$.

{Wronskian.} $W=l'\bar l-l\bar l'$ satisfies $W'=l''\bar l-l\bar l''=0$,
since both functions solve the same equation, so $W$ is constant. Since
$(\bar l/l)'=-W/l^2$,
\[
 \frac{\bar l}l(t)=\frac{\bar l}l(\tfrac12)+W\int_t^{1/2}\frac{\,\mathrm d u}{l(u)^2}
 =\frac W\pi\log\frac1t+O(1)\qquad(t\downarrow0),
\]
by $l(u)^2=\pi u(1+O(u^2))$. On the other hand
$\bar l/l=\mathbf K(1-s)/\mathbf K(s)=\frac2\pi\log\frac1t+O(1)$. Hence $W=2$.

{The inverse.} Let $\mathcal G$ be the operator with kernel $G_*$,
which is continuous on $[0,1]^2$ as a product of continuous functions of
$\min(t,s)$ and $\max(t,s)$. For bounded continuous $g$ on $(0,1)$, the
function
$u=\mathcal Gg=\frac12\bar l(t)\int_0^tlg+\frac12l(t)\int_t^1\bar lg$ is $C^2$ on
$(0,1)$, with
\[
 u'=\tfrac12\bar l'\!\int_0^tlg+\tfrac12l'\!\int_t^1\bar lg,\qquad
 u''=-\frac{\pi^2}{4\sin^2\pi t}u-\tfrac12Wg=-\frac{\pi^2}{4\sin^2\pi t}u-g ,
\]
since the terms $\pm\frac12l\bar lg$ cancel in $u'$. Apply this to $g=\upsilon_j$ and set
$f=\mathcal G\upsilon_j-\upsilon_j/\mu_j$. Then $f=al+b\bar l$, since
it solves the homogeneous equation and $W=2$. At $0$, both
$\mathcal G\upsilon_j$ and $\upsilon_j/\mu_j$ are $O(\sqrt t)$:
the first integral term is $O(t^{5/2}\log(1/t))$ and the second is
$O(\sqrt t)$. Thus $b=0$, because $\bar l(t)/\sqrt t\to\infty$.
Reflection gives $f(t)=O(\sqrt{1-t})$ at $1$, and hence $a=0$.
Consequently $\mathcal G\upsilon_j=\mu_j^{-1}\upsilon_j$ for every $j$.
The bounded kernel and completeness of the basis give
$\mathcal G=\mathscr H^{-1}=\sum_j\mu_j^{-1}\langle \cdot,\upsilon_j\rangle\upsilon_j$.

{The diagonal.} By Mercer's theorem \cite[\S98]{RieszNagy} for the
continuous symmetric kernel $G_*$ of the positive operator $\mathcal G$,
$G_*(t,s)=\sum_j\mu_j^{-1}\upsilon_j(t)\upsilon_j(s)$ with absolute and uniform
convergence on $[0,1]^2$. On the diagonal this gives
$G_*(t,t)=\sum_j\upsilon_j(t)^2/\mu_j$, and integration gives
$\int_0^1G_*(t,t)\,\mathrm d t=\sum_j\mu_j^{-1}=\frac12\sum_j\Lambda_j=\frac12$ by
\Cref{thm:transfer}.
head: environment

label: proof:prop:target
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:prop:target}
{The map $X_*$.} With $s=\sin^2(\pi t/2)$,
$l\bar l=\frac4{\pi^2}\sin(\pi t)\mathbf K(s)\mathbf K(1-s)=\phi_*$, and
$(\log(l/\bar l))'=W/(l\bar l)=2/\phi_*$. Since $l(\frac12)=\bar l(\frac12)$,
\[
 X_*(t)=\tfrac12\log\frac{l(t)}{\bar l(t)}=-\tfrac12\log\varpi(t),\qquad
 \varpi(t)=\frac{\mathbf K(\cos^2(\pi t/2))}{\mathbf K(\sin^2(\pi t/2))}.
\]
Thus $X_*$ is continuous and strictly increasing, $X_*(1-t)=-X_*(t)$, and
$\varpi(t)\to\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$ because $\mathbf K(1-s)\to\infty$ and
$\mathbf K(s)\to\frac\pi2$. Hence $X_*(t)\to-\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$ and
$X_*(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\uparrow1$, and $X_*$ is a bijection onto $\mathbb R$.

{Normalizations and spectrum.} The substitution $x=X_*(t)$,
$\,\mathrm d x=\,\mathrm d t/\phi_*(t)$, and $m_*(X_*(t))=\phi_*(t)^2$ give
\[
 \int m_*=\int_0^1\phi_*,\qquad \int\sqrt{m_*}=\int_0^1\,\mathrm d t=1,\qquad
 E(m_*)=\int_0^1\phi_*^2=c_{\sin} ,
\]
and $\int_0^1\phi_*=\int_0^1l\bar l=2\int_0^1G_*(t,t)\,\mathrm d t=1$ by
\Cref{lem:legendre}. For $s<t$,
\[
 \sqrt{\phi_*(s)\phi_*(t)}\,e^{-(X_*(t)-X_*(s))}
 =\sqrt{l(s)\bar l(s)l(t)\bar l(t)}\sqrt{\frac{l(s)\bar l(t)}{\bar l(s)l(t)}}
 =l(s)\bar l(t)=2G_*(s,t).
\]
The map
\[
 U:L^2(\mathbb R)\to L^2(0,1),\qquad (Uf)(t)=f(X_*(t))/\sqrt{\phi_*(t)},
\]
is unitary, since $\int_0^1|f(X_*(t))|^2\,\mathrm d t/\phi_*(t)=\int|f|^2$ and
$g\mapsto(\sqrt{\phi_*}\,g)\circ X_*^{-1}$ is its inverse. For
$g\in L^2(0,1)$ and $f=U^{-1}g$, the substitution $y=X_*(s)$ gives
\[
 (UK_{m_*}f)(t)=\frac1{\sqrt{\phi_*(t)}}\int_0^1\phi_*(t)e^{-|X_*(t)-X_*(s)|}
 \phi_*(s)\sqrt{\phi_*(s)}g(s)\frac{\,\mathrm d s}{\phi_*(s)}
 =\int_0^12G_*(t,s)g(s)\,\mathrm d s ,
\]
so $UK_{m_*}U^{-1}=2\mathcal G$, and by \Cref{lem:legendre}
$\lambda_j(K_{m_*})=2/\mu_j=\Lambda_j$.

{Theta form.} Fix $t\le\frac12$, so that $\varpi=\varpi(t)\ge1$, and put
$z=\sin^2(\pi t/2)$ and $a=e^{-\pi\varpi}$. For $0<q<1$ let
$\vartheta_3(q)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}q^{j^2}$,
$\vartheta_4(q)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}(-1)^jq^{j^2}$,
$\vartheta_2(q)=\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}q^{(j+1/2)^2}$. Jacobi's
theta--elliptic identities \cite[\S20.9(i)]{DLMF2026}, in our parameter
convention, read
\[
 z=\frac{\vartheta_2(a)^4}{\vartheta_3(a)^4},\qquad
 1-z=\frac{\vartheta_4(a)^4}{\vartheta_3(a)^4},\qquad
 \mathbf K(z)=\frac\pi2\vartheta_3(a)^2,
 \quad a=\exp\!\left(-\pi\frac{\mathbf K(1-z)}{\mathbf K(z)}\right).
\]
These are also given in \cite[\S4.6]{FGS}; the equivalent modular
transformation follows from Gaussian Poisson summation
\cite[Chapter~5]{SteinShakarchi}.
Using $\sin\pi t=2\sqrt{z(1-z)}$ and
$\mathbf K(1-z)=\varpi\mathbf K(z)$,
\[
 \phi_*(t)=\frac8{\pi^2}\varpi\sqrt{z(1-z)}\,\mathbf K(z)^2
 =\frac8{\pi^2}\varpi\,\frac{\vartheta_2(a)^2\vartheta_4(a)^2}{\vartheta_3(a)^4}
 \cdot\frac{\pi^2}4\vartheta_3(a)^4=2\varpi\,\vartheta_2(a)^2\vartheta_4(a)^2 .
\]
Since $(j+\frac12)^2=\frac14+j(j+1)$ and the terms with $j$ and $-1-j$ agree,
$\vartheta_2(a)=2a^{1/4}\Sigma_1(a)$; and $\vartheta_4(a)=\Sigma_2(a)$. With
$x=X_*(t)=-\frac12\log\varpi\le0$, that is $\varpi=e^{2|x|}$, and
$n_*(x)=\phi_*(t)$, this is \eqref{eq:sine-theta} for $x\le0$; since
$\phi_*(1-t)=\phi_*(t)$ and $X_*(1-t)=-X_*(t)$, $n_*$ is even, which gives
$x\ge0$.

{Asymptotics.} For $\varpi\ge1$, $j(j+1)\ge2j$ and
$j^2\ge3j-2$ give
\[
 0\le\Sigma_1(a)-1\le\frac{a^2}{1-a^2}\le\frac{e^{-2\pi\varpi}}{1-e^{-2\pi}},\qquad
 |\Sigma_2(a)-1|\le\frac{2a}{1-a^3}\le\frac{2e^{-\pi\varpi}}{1-e^{-3\pi}} .
\]
Hence, for $\varpi\ge1$, $1\le\Sigma_1(a)\le M_1$ and
$0<1-2e^{-\pi}/(1-e^{-3\pi})\le\Sigma_2(a)\le M_2$, with $M_1,M_2$ of
\Cref{lem:sine-sum}; so $\log\Sigma_1$ and $\log\Sigma_2$ are bounded, and
$\log n_*(x)=-\frac\pi2e^{2|x|}+2|x|+O(1)$.

label: lem:uniform-diagonal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:uniform-diagonal}
For every $N\ge2$ and $i$, $0<[(I-J_N^\star)^{-1}]_{ii}\le64N$.
head: environment
name: Uniform bound for the sine diagonal

label: proof:lem:uniform-diagonal
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:uniform-diagonal}
Put $c=\cos\frac\pi{2N}$. Since $\sin y\ge\frac{2y}\pi$ on
$[0,\frac\pi2]$, $1-c=2\sin^2\frac\pi{4N}\ge\frac1{2N^2}$. For $N=2,3$, the
diagonal entries of the positive definite matrix
$(I-J_N^\star)^{-1}$ are at most its norm $(1-c)^{-1}\le2N^2\le6N$.

Let $N\ge4$. The vector $(\sqrt{p_i})_i$ satisfies
$(J_N^\star\sqrt p)_i=\frac{\sin(ih)+\sin((i-1)h)}{2\sqrt{p_i}}=c\sqrt{p_i}$, by
$\sin(ih)+\sin((i-1)h)=2\sin\theta_i\cos\frac h2$. Write $x\in\mathbb R^N$ as
$x_i=\sqrt{p_i}f_i$. Since
$2J^\star_{i,i+1}\sqrt{p_ip_{i+1}}=\sin(ih)$ and
$-f_if_{i+1}=\frac12(f_{i+1}-f_i)^2-\frac12f_i^2-\frac12f_{i+1}^2$,
\[
 \mathfrak q(f):=x^T(I-J_N^\star)x
 =\sum_ip_if_i^2+\frac12\sum_{i<N}\sin(ih)(f_{i+1}-f_i)^2
 -\frac12\sum_{i<N}\sin(ih)(f_i^2+f_{i+1}^2),
\]
and the coefficient of $f_i^2$ in the last sum is
$\frac12(\sin(ih)+\sin((i-1)h))=cp_i$. Hence
\[
 \mathfrak q(f)=(1-c)\sum_ip_if_i^2+\frac12\sum_{i<N}\sin(ih)(f_{i+1}-f_i)^2 .
\]
Let $S$ be the set of indices with $\theta_i\in[\frac\pi4,\frac{3\pi}4]$,
that is, $i\in[\frac N4+\frac12,\frac{3N}4+\frac12]$. This interval has
length $N/2$ and contains at least $\lfloor N/2\rfloor\ge N/4$ integers,
and $p_i\ge\frac1{\sqrt2}\ge\frac12$ on $S$. Hence
$\mathfrak q(f)\ge\frac1{2N^2}\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac N4\min_Sf_i^2$, and some
$j\in S$ has $f_j^2\le16N\mathfrak q(f)$.

Fix $i$ and let $E$ be the set of edges $k$, joining $k$ and $k+1$, between
$i$ and $j$. The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives
$(f_i-f_j)^2\le\sum_{k\in E}\frac1{\sin(kh)}\sum_{k\in E}\sin(kh)(f_{k+1}-f_k)^2
\le2\mathfrak q(f)\sum_{k\in E}\frac1{\sin(kh)}$, hence
\[
 f_i^2\le2f_j^2+2(f_i-f_j)^2\le2f_j^2+4\mathfrak q(f)\sum_{k\in E}\frac1{\sin(kh)} .
\]
Since $\sin(kh)=\sin(\min(k,N-k)h)\ge2\min(k,N-k)/N$, each term is at
most $N/(2\min(k,N-k))$. Put $m'=\lfloor N/4\rfloor+1$, so that $4m'\ge N+1$.
The edges with $\min(k,N-k)>N/4$ are those with $m'\le k\le N-m'$; there are
at most $N-2m'+1\le2m'$ of them, and each contributes at most $N/(2m')$, so
together they contribute at most $N$. Let $k\in E$ with $\min(k,N-k)\le N/4$. If
$k\le N/4$, then $k<j$, so $i\le k$; if $k\ge3N/4$, then $k\ge j$, since
$j\le\frac{3N}4+\frac12$, so $k\le i-1$. Only one of the two cases occurs,
and in either case $n=\min(k,N-k)$ runs through distinct integers in
$[d,N/4]$, where $d=\min(i,N+1-i)$. These edges contribute at most
$\frac N2\sum_{n=d}^{\lfloor N/4\rfloor}\frac1n\le\frac N2(1+\log\frac Nd)$.
Thus $\sum_{k\in E}1/\sin(kh)\le\frac N2(1+\log\frac Nd)+N$. Moreover
$p_i=\sin\theta_i=\sin(\pi-\theta_i)\le\pi d/N$. With $u=d/N\in(0,1]$,
\[
 p_if_i^2\le32N\mathfrak q(f)+2\pi N\mathfrak q(f)\,u\Bigl(3+\log\frac1u\Bigr)
 \le(32+6\pi)N\mathfrak q(f)<64N\mathfrak q(f),
\]
where $u(3+\log\frac1u)$ is increasing on $(0,1]$, with derivative
$2+\log\frac1u>0$, and equals $3$ at $u=1$. For a positive definite matrix
$M$, the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality in the inner product $\langle x,y\rangle_M=x^TMy$
gives $x_i^2=\langle M^{-1}e_i,x\rangle_M^2\le(M^{-1})_{ii}\,x^TMx$ with equality at
$x=M^{-1}e_i$, so $(M^{-1})_{ii}=\sup_{x\ne0}x_i^2/x^TMx$. With
$M=I-J_N^\star$ and $x_i^2=p_if_i^2$ this proves the claim.
head: environment

label: proof:thm:reference-limit
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:reference-limit}
By the finite part, $J_N^\star$ has the orthonormal eigenvectors
$U_{\cdot j}$, $U_{ij}=\sqrt{w_i}\phi_{N,j}(x_i)$, with eigenvalues
$\cos((j+\frac12)h)$, and
$(1-\cos((j+\frac12)h))^{-1}=N^2r_{N,j}$ by \Cref{lem:trace}. Hence
$d_i=\sum_{j<N}N^2r_{N,j}U_{ij}^2$ and
\[
 D_N(t)=\sum_{j<N}r_{N,j}\,NU_{ij}^2\qquad(t\in[\tfrac{i-1}N,\tfrac iN)).
\]

{Convergence of the first $K$ terms.} The intervals
$[\cos(ih),\cos((i-1)h)]$, $1\le i\le N$, partition $[-1,1]$, have lengths
$2w_i$ and contain $x_i$; hence $\sum_iw_iF(x_i)$ is a Riemann sum of
$\frac12\int_{-1}^1F$ with mesh at most $h$, and converges to it for every
$F\in C[-1,1]$. For fixed $j$ and $N>j$, the moment matrix of $1,x,\dots,x^j$ is
positive definite: a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $j$ cannot
vanish at all $N$ distinct nodes. These matrices converge to the positive
definite moment matrix of $\tfrac12\,\mathrm d x$ on $[-1,1]$. Cholesky
factorization, and hence Gram--Schmidt with positive leading coefficients,
depends continuously on a positive definite moment matrix. Therefore
$\phi_{N,j}\to\sqrt{2j+1}\,\mathsf P_j$ coefficientwise and uniformly on
$[-1,1]$.
For
$t\in[\frac{i-1}N,\frac iN)$, $|\theta_i-\pi t|\le h$, so
$|x_i-\cos\pi t|\le h$, $|p_i-\sin\pi t|\le h$, and
$Nw_i=p_i\cdot N\sin\frac\pi{2N}$ with $N\sin\frac\pi{2N}\to\frac\pi2$. By the
uniform continuity of $\mathsf P_j$ on $[-1,1]$, for fixed $K$
\[
 D_{N,K}(t):=\sum_{j<K}r_{N,j}NU_{ij}^2\ \longrightarrow\
 D_K(t):=\sum_{j<K}\Lambda_j\upsilon_j(t)^2\quad\text{uniformly on }[0,1),
\]
since $NU_{ij}^2=Nw_i\phi_{N,j}(x_i)^2\to\frac\pi2\sin(\pi t)(2j+1)\mathsf P_j(\cos\pi t)^2=\upsilon_j(t)^2$
uniformly and $r_{N,j}\to\Lambda_j$.

{The tails.} By \Cref{lem:uniform-diagonal}, $0\le D_N\le64$, and
$0\le D_N-D_{N,K}\le D_N$. Since the columns of $U$ are unit vectors,
\[
 \|D_N-D_{N,K}\|_{L^1(0,1)}=\sum_i\frac1N\sum_{j=K}^{N-1}r_{N,j}NU_{ij}^2
 =\sum_{j=K}^{N-1}r_{N,j}\le\sum_{j\ge K}\frac2{(2j+1)^2}\le\frac1{2K-1},
\]
by the bound of \Cref{lem:trace} used in the proof of
\Cref{thm:transfer} and telescoping; hence
$\|D_N-D_{N,K}\|_2^2\le64/(2K-1)$. By \Cref{lem:legendre},
$\sum_j\Lambda_j\upsilon_j^2=2\sum_j\upsilon_j^2/\mu_j=2G_*(t,t)=l\bar l=\phi_*$, so
$0\le\phi_*-D_K\le\phi_*$ and
$\|\phi_*-D_K\|_2^2\le\|\phi_*\|_\infty\int_0^1(\phi_*-D_K)
=\|\phi_*\|_\infty\sum_{j\ge K}\Lambda_j$, where $\phi_*$ is bounded as a
continuous function on $[0,1]$. Therefore
\[
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\|D_N-\phi_*\|_2
 \le\frac8{\sqrt{2K-1}}+\Bigl(\|\phi_*\|_\infty\sum_{j\ge K}\Lambda_j\Bigr)^{1/2}
\]
for every $K$, and the right-hand side tends to zero as $K\to\infty$.

{Conclusion.} The definition of $D_N$ gives
\[
 N^{-3}\mathcal E_N(J_N^\star)=\sum_iN^{-1}(d_i/N)^2=\|D_N\|_2^2\to\|\phi_*\|_2^2=c_{\sin} .
\]
By \eqref{eq:sine-gain},
$\Delta A_N(\mathcal R_N^\star)/(N^{3/2}\epsilon_N^\star)=2N^{-3/2}\mathcal E_N(J_N^\star)^{1/2}
=2\|D_N\|_2\to2\sqrt{c_{\sin}}$, and since $\mathcal R_N^\star\in\mathfrak E_N(\mu,L)$,
$\mathscr G(\mu,L)\le2\sqrt{c_{\sin}}$.

label: lem:sine-sum
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sine-sum}
For an integer $K\ge0$ let
\[
 \Sigma_{1,K}(a)=\sum_{j=0}^Ka^{j(j+1)},\qquad
 \Sigma_{2,K}(a)=1+2\sum_{j=1}^K(-1)^ja^{j^2},\qquad
 \Sigma_{1,K}^6\Sigma_{2,K}^6=\sum_{n=0}^{12K^2+6K}C_na^n,
\]
\[
 I(\lambda)=\int_1^\infty\varpi^2e^{-\lambda\pi\varpi}\,\mathrm d\varpi
 =e^{-\lambda\pi}\Bigl(\frac1{\lambda\pi}+\frac2{(\lambda\pi)^2}
 +\frac2{(\lambda\pi)^3}\Bigr),\qquad
 M_1=\frac1{1-e^{-2\pi}},\qquad M_2=1+\frac{2e^{-\pi}}{1-e^{-3\pi}},
\]
\[
 E_K=512\sum_nC_nI\bigl(n+\tfrac32\bigr),
\]
\[
 R_K=512\Bigl[\frac{6M_1^5M_2^6\,I(\frac32+(K+1)(K+2))}{1-e^{-2(K+2)\pi}}
 +\frac{12M_1^6M_2^5\,I(\frac32+(K+1)^2)}{1-e^{-(2K+3)\pi}}\Bigr].
\]
Then $|c_{\sin}-E_K|\le R_K$, and $R_K\to0$.
head: environment
name: A finite sum for the sine energy

label: proof:lem:sine-sum
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:sine-sum}
The formula for $I(\lambda)$ follows from the antiderivative
$-e^{-cv}(v^2/c+2v/c^2+2/c^3)$ of $v^2e^{-cv}$, $c=\lambda\pi$. By
\Cref{prop:target}, $c_{\sin}=\int n_*^3$, $n_*$ is even, and for $x\le0$ the
variable $\varpi=e^{-2x}$ ranges over $[1,\infty)$ with
$\,\mathrm d x=-\,\mathrm d\varpi/(2\varpi)$; by \eqref{eq:sine-theta},
\[
 c_{\sin}=2\int_{-\infty}^0n_*^3\,\mathrm d x
 =512\int_1^\infty\varpi^2e^{-3\pi\varpi/2}\,\Sigma_1(e^{-\pi\varpi})^6
 \Sigma_2(e^{-\pi\varpi})^6\,\mathrm d\varpi .
\]
The polynomial $\Sigma_{1,K}^6\Sigma_{2,K}^6$ has degree
$6K(K+1)+6K^2$, and integrating it against $512\varpi^2e^{-3\pi\varpi/2}$ with
$a=e^{-\pi\varpi}$ gives $E_K$, since $a^ne^{-3\pi\varpi/2}=e^{-(n+3/2)\pi\varpi}$.

Let $\varpi\ge1$ and $a=e^{-\pi\varpi}\le e^{-\pi}$. Since $j(j+1)\ge2j$,
$0\le\Sigma_{1,K}\le\Sigma_1\le\sum_ja^{2j}\le M_1$; since $j^2\ge3j-2$ for
$j\ge1$, $|\Sigma_2|,|\Sigma_{2,K}|\le1+2\sum_{j\ge1}a^{3j-2}\le M_2$. The
omitted exponents of $\Sigma_1$ are $j(j+1)$, $j\ge K+1$, with consecutive
differences $2(j+1)\ge2(K+2)$; those of $\Sigma_2$ are $j^2$, $j\ge K+1$,
with differences $2j+1\ge2K+3$. Comparison with geometric series gives
\[
 |\Sigma_1-\Sigma_{1,K}|\le\frac{a^{(K+1)(K+2)}}{1-e^{-2(K+2)\pi}},\qquad
 |\Sigma_2-\Sigma_{2,K}|\le\frac{2a^{(K+1)^2}}{1-e^{-(2K+3)\pi}} .
\]
For $|X|,|x|\le M_1$ and $|Y|,|y|\le M_2$,
$X^6Y^6-x^6y^6=(X^6-x^6)Y^6+x^6(Y^6-y^6)$ and
$|X^6-x^6|=|X-x|\,|\sum_{i<6}X^ix^{5-i}|\le6M_1^5|X-x|$ give
\[
 |\Sigma_1^6\Sigma_2^6-\Sigma_{1,K}^6\Sigma_{2,K}^6|
 \le6M_1^5M_2^6|\Sigma_1-\Sigma_{1,K}|+6M_1^6M_2^5|\Sigma_2-\Sigma_{2,K}| .
\]
Integrating this bound against $512\varpi^2e^{-3\pi\varpi/2}$ gives
$|c_{\sin}-E_K|\le R_K$. Finally, $I(\lambda)\le e^{-\lambda\pi}$ for $\lambda\ge1$,
since $\frac1\pi+\frac2{\pi^2}+\frac2{\pi^3}<1$, so $R_K\to0$.

label: proof:thm:ground
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:ground}
{Ground state and square identity.}
The positive compact operator $K_m$ has a positive largest eigenvalue
$\lambda_0$. Its nonnegative kernel allows a nonnegative normalized
maximizer $\varphi$ of the Rayleigh quotient, with
$K_m\varphi=\lambda_0\varphi$. Put $j=\sqrt m\,\varphi\in L^1$ and
\[
 u_-(x)=e^{-x}\int_{-\infty}^xe^yj(y)\,\mathrm d y,\qquad
 u_+(x)=e^x\int_x^\infty e^{-y}j(y)\,\mathrm d y,\qquad u=u_-+u_+.
\]
Then $u_-'=-u_-+j$, $u_+'=u_+-j$, and $j$ is nonnegative and nonzero.
Thus $u>0$, $u'=u_+-u_-$ is continuous and locally absolutely continuous,
$|u'|\le u$, and $u''=u-2j$ almost everywhere. The functions $u_\pm$
are in $L^1\cap L^\infty$, so $u\in H^1$. Moreover,
$\sqrt m\,u=\lambda_0\varphi$, whence $2j=\kappa mu$.

Set $a=u'/u$. Then $|a|\le1$ and $a'=1-\kappa m-a^2$. For $f\in H^1$,
\[
 (f'-af)^2=f'^2+f^2-\kappa mf^2-(af^2)' .
\]
All nondifferentiated terms are integrable, and $af^2\to0$ at both
infinities by \Cref{lem:features}(i). Integration proves
\eqref{eq:ground-square}. Its right-hand side vanishes precisely when
$(f/u)'=0$, or $f=cu$.

{Simplicity and uniqueness.}
Any $H^1\cap C^1$ solution $v$ of $-v''+v=\kappa mv$ with locally
absolutely continuous derivative satisfies
$\|v\|_\mathcal H^2=\kappa\int mv^2$: integrate $(vv')'=v'^2+v^2-\kappa mv^2$
between endpoints tending to $\pm\infty$ along which $vv'\to0$.
Such endpoints exist because $vv'\in L^1$; the integrands are in $L^1$
because $v$ is bounded. The square identity therefore gives $v=cu$.
For an eigenvector $\psi$ of $K_m$ at $\lambda_0$, the convolution
$v=e^{-|\cdot|}*(\sqrt m\,\psi)$ has this regularity and satisfies
$\sqrt m\,v=\lambda_0\psi$. Thus $\psi$ is a multiple of $\varphi$,
proving simplicity as well as uniqueness of the positive solution.
The square identity proves the variational characterization of $\kappa$;
testing with $u$ excludes every larger coupling.

{Ground coordinate.}
The function $q=1-a$ lies in $[0,2]$ and satisfies
$q'=\kappa m-Q(q)$. For $R>0$,
\[
 \int_{-R}^RQ(q)=\kappa\int_{-R}^Rm-q(R)+q(-R)\le\kappa\int m+2.
\]
Hence $Q(q),q'\in L^1$, $q$ has limits at both infinities, and these
limits belong to $\{0,2\}$. A limit $q(+\infty)=0$ would give
$u'/u\ge1/2$ eventually and exponential growth of $u$; a limit
$q(-\infty)=2$ gives the same contradiction at the other end.
Thus the limits are $0$ and $2$, and integration gives
$\int Q(q)=\kappa\int m-2$. Outside a compact support, $u''=u$ and
$u\in H^1$ select $u=c_-e^x$ on the left and $u=c_+e^{-x}$ on the
right, giving the stated constant values of $q$. If $m$ is bounded,
$|q'|\le\kappa\|m\|_\infty+1$, so $q$ is Lipschitz.

label: proof:lem:filter
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:filter}
Put $M=\int m$ and $M(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xm$.

{The Volterra equation.} Let $V_0=1$ and
$V_{j+1}(x)=\frac s2\int_{-\infty}^x(1-e^{-2(x-y)})m(y)V_j(y)\,\mathrm d y$. By
induction on $j$, using $0\le1-e^{-2(x-y)}\le1$ and
$\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d y}M(y)^{j+1}=(j+1)M(y)^jm(y)$,
\[
 0\le V_j(x)\le\frac{(sM(x)/2)^j}{j!}\le\frac{(sM/2)^j}{j!} ,
\]
and, also by induction,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:volterra-terms}
 V_j(x)=\Bigl(\frac s2\Bigr)^j\int_{y_1<\dots<y_j<x}
 \prod_{i=1}^j\bigl(1-e^{-2(y_{i+1}-y_i)}\bigr)m(y_i)\,\mathrm d y_i
 \qquad(y_{j+1}=x).
\end{equation}
The series $V_s=\sum_jV_j$ converges uniformly, $1\le V_s\le e^{sM/2}$,
$V_s(x)\to1$ as $x\to-\infty$ because $M(x)\to0$, and summation of the
recursive definitions gives
$V_s(x)=1+\frac s2\int_{-\infty}^x(1-e^{-2(x-y)})m(y)V_s(y)\,\mathrm d y$. If $V$ and
$\widetilde V$ are bounded solutions, $D=V-\widetilde V$ satisfies the
homogeneous equation, and induction gives
$|D(x)|\le\|D\|_\infty(sM/2)^j/j!$ for every $j$; hence $D=0$.

{The filter.} Writing the equation as
$V_s(x)=1+\frac s2\int_{-\infty}^xmV_s-\frac s2e^{-2x}\int_{-\infty}^xe^{2y}mV_s$,
both terms are absolutely continuous, and
\[
 V_s'(x)=s\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}m(y)V_s(y)\,\mathrm d y\ge0,\qquad
 V_s''+2V_s'=smV_s\ \text{a.e.} ;
\]
the right-hand side of the first identity is continuous, so $V_s\in C^1$.
The function $r_s=V_s'/V_s$ is locally absolutely continuous and
$r_s'=V_s''/V_s-r_s^2=sm-2r_s-r_s^2$; since $(\log V_s)'=r_s$ and
$V_s(-\infty)=1$, $V_s=\exp\int_{-\infty}^xr_s$. Since $V_s$ is nondecreasing,
$V_s(y)/V_s(x)\le1$ for $y\le x$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:filter-linear-bound}
 0\le r_s(x)\le s\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}m(y)\,\mathrm d y=\frac s\kappa r_\circ(x).
\end{equation}
The linear filter satisfies $r_\circ(x)\le\kappa M(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$
and, for every $R$,
$r_\circ(x)\le\kappa e^{-2(x-R)}M+\kappa\int_R^\infty m$, so
$r_\circ(x)\to0$ as $x\to+\infty$. Hence $r_s(\pm\infty)=0$, and $r_s$ is
bounded.

{Uniqueness.} Let $\rho$ be a bounded locally absolutely continuous
solution of $\rho'=sm-2\rho-\rho^2$ with $\rho(x)\to0$ as $x\to-\infty$. The
difference $\delta=\rho-r_s$ satisfies $\delta'=-(2+\rho+r_s)\delta$, and there
is $x_0$ with $2+\rho+r_s\ge1$ on $(-\infty,x_0]$. For $a<x\le x_0$,
$|\delta(x)|=|\delta(a)|\exp(-\int_a^x(2+\rho+r_s))\le\|\delta\|_\infty e^{-(x-a)}$;
letting $a\to-\infty$ gives $\delta=0$ on $(-\infty,x_0]$, and then
$\delta(x)=\delta(x_0)\exp(-\int_{x_0}^x(2+\rho+r_s))=0$ for all $x$.

{The determinant.}
For $s>0$, dominated convergence in the Volterra equation gives
\[
 V_s(+\infty)=1+\frac s2\int_\mathbb R m(y)V_s(y)\,\mathrm d y.
\]
The function $f_-(x)=e^xV_s(x)$ is the left Jost solution for
$-\partial_x^2+sm$ at spectral parameter $z=-1$. Apply the
Fredholm--Jost identity \cite[Theorem~4.6]{GesztesyMakarov2004} with
$sm\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $\sqrt z=i$. In its notation the Birman--Schwinger
operator is $-sK_m/2$, since $(-\partial_x^2+1)^{-1}$ has kernel
$e^{-|x-y|}/2$, and the inverse transmission coefficient is the
Volterra limit above. Therefore
\[
 \det\Bigl(I+\frac s2K_m\Bigr)=V_s(+\infty),\qquad
 H_m(s)=\int_\mathbb R r_s.
\]
The case $s=0$ is immediate. The Riccati equation then gives
$\|r_s'\|_1\le sM+(2+\|r_s\|_\infty)H_m(s)$.

{The linear filter.} The function
$r_\circ(x)=\kappa e^{-2x}\int_{-\infty}^xe^{2y}m(y)\,\mathrm d y$ is locally absolutely
continuous by the product rule, with $r_\circ'=\kappa m-2r_\circ$; it is
nonnegative, and $r_\circ(\pm\infty)=0$ as shown above. By Tonelli's theorem $\int r_\circ=\frac\kappa2M$, so
$\|r_\circ'\|_1\le2\kappa M$. The function $h=q-r_\circ$ satisfies
$h'=\kappa m-Q(q)-\kappa m+2r_\circ=q^2-2h$, so as before
$h(x)=\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}q(y)^2\,\mathrm d y\ge0$, that is, $r_\circ\le q$; and
$0\le h\le q$, $h'=q'-r_\circ'\in L^1$. Together with
\eqref{eq:filter-linear-bound}, this gives $r_s\le(s/\kappa)q$. Finally, for $c>0$, $0\le\tilde m\in L^1$ and
$\varrho(x)=c\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}\tilde m(y)\,\mathrm d y$, Tonelli's theorem and
$\int_{\max(y,z)}^\infty e^{-2(2x-y-z)}\,\mathrm d x=\frac14e^{-2|y-z|}$ give
\[
 \int_\mathbb R\varrho^2
 =c^2\iint \tilde m(y)\tilde m(z)\int_{\max(y,z)}^\infty e^{-2(2x-y-z)}\,\mathrm d x\,\mathrm d y\,\mathrm d z
 =\frac{c^2}4\iint e^{-2|y-z|}\tilde m(y)\tilde m(z)\,\mathrm d y\,\mathrm d z .
\]
For $c=\kappa$ and $\tilde m=m$, $\varrho=r_\circ$, and the last double integral is
$\|K_m\|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2=\operatorname{tr} K_m^2$.

label: proof:thm:common-measure
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:common-measure}
Fix $x$ and put $I_x=(-\infty,x)$ and
\[
 G_x(t,y)=\tfrac12\bigl(e^{-|t-y|}-e^{t+y-2x}\bigr)\qquad(t,y<x).
\]
Since $(x-t)+(x-y)\ge|t-y|$, $0\le G_x\le\frac12e^{-|t-y|}$, and
$G_x(x,y)=0$. Let $\mathcal K_x$ be the operator on $L^2(I_x)$ with kernel
$\sqrt{m(t)}G_x(t,y)\sqrt{m(y)}$ and $v(t)=\sqrt{m(t)}e^{t-x}$. The kernel is
symmetric with
$\iint m(t)G_x(t,y)^2m(y)\le\frac14M^2$, so $\mathcal K_x$ is self-adjoint and
Hilbert--Schmidt, in particular compact; and $\|v\|_2^2=\int_{I_x}e^{2(t-x)}m(t)\,\mathrm d t$.

{The Green representation.} For $\phi\in L^1(I_x)$ put
$g=G_x\phi=\int_{I_x}G_x(\cdot,y)\phi(y)\,\mathrm d y$. Then
$g(t)=\frac12\int e^{-|t-y|}\phi(y)\,\mathrm d y-\frac12e^{t-2x}\int e^y\phi(y)\,\mathrm d y$. As in
the proof of \Cref{thm:ground}, $g\in C^1(I_x\cup\{x\})$, $g'$ is locally
absolutely continuous, $-g''+g=\phi$ almost everywhere, $g(x)=0$, $g,g'$
are bounded and $g(t),g'(t)\to0$ as $t\to-\infty$, and
\[
 g'(x)=-\int_{I_x}e^{y-x}\phi(y)\,\mathrm d y,
\]
since $\partial_tG_x(t,y)\to-e^{y-x}$ as $t\uparrow x$ for every $y<x$ and
$|\partial_tG_x|\le1$. Integration by parts on $[a,x]$ and $a\to-\infty$ give
$\int_{I_x}\phi g=\int_{I_x}(g'^2+g^2)$, and $g\in H^1(I_x)$.

{Positivity and the norm.} For $f\in L^2(I_x)$, $\phi=\sqrt m\,f\in L^1$
and $\langle f,\mathcal K_xf\rangle=\int\phi G_x\phi=\int_{I_x}(g'^2+g^2)\ge0$. Let
$\mathcal K_xf=\lambda f$ with $\lambda>0$ and $f\ne0$, and $g=G_x(\sqrt mf)$.
Then $\sqrt m\,g=\lambda f$, so $\int_{I_x}(g'^2+g^2)=\lambda\|f\|^2$ and
$\int_{I_x}mg^2=\lambda^2\|f\|^2$. The extension $\hat g$ of $g$ by zero on
$[x,\infty)$ lies in $H^1(\mathbb R)$ because $g(x)=0$, and \eqref{eq:ground-square}
gives
\[
 \lambda(1-\kappa\lambda)\|f\|^2=\int(\hat g'^2+\hat g^2-\kappa m\hat g^2)
 =\int\Bigl(\hat g'-\frac{u'}u\hat g\Bigr)^2\ge0 .
\]
If the right-hand side were zero, $\hat g$ would be a multiple of $u>0$
vanishing on $(x,\infty)$, so $\hat g=0$ and $f=\lambda^{-1}\sqrt m\,g=0$.
Hence $\lambda<1/\kappa$ for every positive eigenvalue. Since $\mathcal K_x$
is compact and positive, $\|\mathcal K_x\|$ is its largest eigenvalue or
zero, so $\|\mathcal K_x\|<1/\kappa$, and $I+s\mathcal K_x$ ($s\ge0$) and
$I-\kappa\mathcal K_x$ are invertible.

{Boundary values.} For $s\ge0$ put $y_s(t)=e^{t-x}V_s(t)/V_s(x)$, with
$V_s$ of \Cref{lem:filter}(ii), and put $y_{-\kappa}=u/u(x)$.
From $V_s''+2V_s'=smV_s$ and $-u''+u=\kappa mu$,
$-y_s''+(1+sm)y_s=0$ for $s\in\{-\kappa\}\cup[0,\infty)$; moreover $y_s(x)=1$,
$y_s$ is bounded on $I_x$, $y_s(t)\to0$ as $t\to-\infty$, and
\[
 y_s'(x)=1+r_s(x)\quad(s\ge0),\qquad y_{-\kappa}'(x)=\frac{u'(x)}{u(x)}=1-q(x).
\]
Let $z=e^{t-x}-sG_x(my_s)$, which is defined since $my_s\in L^1(I_x)$. Then
$-z''+z=-smy_s$, so $w=y_s-z$ satisfies $-w''+w=0$ on $I_x$, is bounded,
and $w(x)=0$; hence $w=\alpha e^t+\beta e^{-t}$ with $\beta=0$ by boundedness
and $\alpha=0$ by $w(x)=0$. Thus $y_s=e^{t-x}-sG_x(my_s)$. Multiplication
by $\sqrt m$ gives $(I+s\mathcal K_x)(\sqrt m\,y_s)=v$, so
$\sqrt m\,y_s=(I+s\mathcal K_x)^{-1}v$, and differentiation at $t=x$ gives
\[
 y_s'(x)=1+s\int_{I_x}e^{y-x}m(y)y_s(y)\,\mathrm d y
 =1+s\langle v,(I+s\mathcal K_x)^{-1}v\rangle .
\]
Hence $r_s(x)=s\langle v,(I+s\mathcal K_x)^{-1}v\rangle$ for $s\ge0$ and
$q(x)=\kappa\langle v,(I-\kappa\mathcal K_x)^{-1}v\rangle$; also
$r_\circ(x)=\kappa\int_{I_x}e^{-2(x-y)}m(y)\,\mathrm d y=\kappa\|v\|^2$.

{The measure.} Let $\sigma_x$ be the spectral measure of the positive
compact operator $\mathcal K_x$ at $v$. It has mass $\|v\|^2$, is supported
in $[0,\|\mathcal K_x\|]\subset[0,1/\kappa)$, and includes any component of
$v$ in the kernel as an atom at $0$. The spectral theorem gives
$\langle v,\Phi(\mathcal K_x)v\rangle=\int\Phi\,\mathrm d\sigma_x$ for bounded Borel $\Phi$.
Therefore
\[
 r_s(x)=s\int\frac{\,\mathrm d\sigma_x(\lambda)}{1+s\lambda},\qquad
 q(x)=\kappa\int\frac{\,\mathrm d\sigma_x(\lambda)}{1-\kappa\lambda},\qquad
 r_\circ(x)=\kappa\int\,\mathrm d\sigma_x .
\]
If $q(x)>0$, the measure $\kappa(1-\kappa\lambda)^{-1}q(x)^{-1}\,\mathrm d\sigma_x$ is a
probability measure on $[0,1/\kappa)$; its image $\mu_x$ under
$\lambda\mapsto z=\kappa\lambda$ satisfies \eqref{eq:common}, because
$\kappa r_s/(sq)=\int(1-z)(1+(s/\kappa)z)^{-1}\,\mathrm d\mu_x$ and
$r_\circ/q=\int(1-z)\,\mathrm d\mu_x$ by the three displayed identities. If
$q(x)=0$, the positive integrand $(1-\kappa\lambda)^{-1}$ forces $\sigma_x=0$,
and all filters vanish at $x$.
