label: prop:three-filter
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:three-filter}
At a point with $q>0$, let $U_i=\kappa r_{s_i}/(s_iq)$ for $i=0,1$ and
$\vartheta=1-r_\circ/q$. Then $0\le U_0\le1$ and $f(U_0)\le U_1\le U_0$.
If $0<U_0<1$ and $f(U_0)<U_1<U_0$, put
\[
 y_-=\frac{\kappa_1U_1-\kappa_0U_0}{\delta U_1},\qquad
 y_+=\frac{\kappa_1(U_0-U_1)}{\delta(1-U_1)};
\]
then $0<y_+<U_0<y_-<1$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:third-interval}
 \vartheta_-:=\frac{\kappa(1-U_0)}{\kappa+s_0y_+}
 \ \le\ \vartheta\ \le\
 \vartheta_+:=1-\frac{\kappa_0U_0}{\kappa+s_0y_-}.
\end{equation}
On the boundary of the region, $\vartheta=1$ if $U_0=0$; $\vartheta=0$ if
$U_0=1$; $\vartheta=1-U_0$ if $U_1=U_0$; and
$\vartheta=\kappa(1-U_0)/(\kappa+s_0U_0)$ if $U_1=f(U_0)$. Every point of the
region and of the interval \eqref{eq:third-interval} arises from some
probability measure in \eqref{eq:common}.
head: environment
name: The range of three filters

label: proof:prop:three-filter
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:prop:three-filter}
{Moment coordinates.}
The decreasing bijection $w=\kappa(1-z)/(\kappa+s_0z)$ has inverse
$z=\kappa(1-w)/(\kappa+s_0w)$. For the image measure $\tilde\omega$,
\[
 U_0=\int w\,\mathrm d\tilde\omega,\qquad U_1=\int f(w)\,\mathrm d\tilde\omega,
 \qquad 1-\vartheta=\int g_0(w)\,\mathrm d\tilde\omega,
 \quad g_0(w)=\frac{\kappa_0w}{\kappa+s_0w}.
\]
Every probability measure on $[0,1]$ can occur in these coordinates.
Since $f''(w)=2\kappa_0\kappa_1\delta/(\kappa_1-\delta w)^3>0$,
Jensen's inequality and $f(w)\le w$ give $f(U_0)\le U_1\le U_0$.
Equality on the lower boundary forces $\tilde\omega=\delta_{U_0}$;
on the upper boundary it forces
$\tilde\omega=(1-U_0)\delta_0+U_0\delta_1$.
These measures, including $U_0=0,1$, give all four boundary values.

{Extremizing measures.}
For an interior pair, the increasing ratios
\[
 \frac{f(y)}y=\frac{\kappa_0}{\kappa_1-\delta y},\qquad
 \frac{1-f(y)}{1-y}=\frac{\kappa_1}{\kappa_1-\delta y}
\]
take the values $U_1/U_0$ and $(1-U_1)/(1-U_0)$ at
$y_-$ and $y_+$, respectively. The strict moment inequalities give
$0<y_+<U_0<y_-<1$. Thus
\[
 \tilde\omega_-=\Bigl(1-\frac{U_0}{y_-}\Bigr)\delta_0
       +\frac{U_0}{y_-}\delta_{y_-},\qquad
 \tilde\omega_+=\frac{1-U_0}{1-y_+}\delta_{y_+}
       +\frac{U_0-y_+}{1-y_+}\delta_1
\]
are probability measures with moments $(U_0,U_1)$.

{Sharp bounds by interpolation.}
For $0<y<1$, let $P_\pm\in\operatorname{span}\{1,w,f(w)\}$ agree with $g_0$ and
its derivative at $y$, and agree with $g_0$ at $0$ for $P_-$ or at $1$
for $P_+$. Multiplication by $\kappa_1-\delta w$ maps this span
bijectively onto the quadratic polynomials; Hermite interpolation
therefore gives unique $P_\pm$. The polynomials
\[
 E_\pm=(\kappa_1-\delta w)(\kappa+s_0w)(g_0-P_\pm)
\]
have degree at most three, with zeros $0,y,y$ or $y,y,1$.
Their common value at $w=-\kappa/s_0$ is
$-\kappa_0^2\kappa s_1/s_0^2$, fixing the remaining factor. Hence
\[
 g_0-P_-=
 \frac{\kappa_0^2s_0s_1w(w-y)^2}
 {(\kappa+s_0y)^2(\kappa+s_0w)(\kappa_1-\delta w)}\ge0,
\]
\[
 g_0-P_+=
 \frac{\kappa_0\kappa s_0s_1(w-1)(w-y)^2}
 {(\kappa+s_0y)^2(\kappa+s_0w)(\kappa_1-\delta w)}\le0.
\]
The integral of $P_\pm$ depends only on $(1,U_0,U_1)$. Take $y=y_-$
in $P_-$ and $y=y_+$ in $P_+$; equality holds on the corresponding
two-point supports. Therefore
\[
 \frac{\kappa_0U_0}{\kappa+s_0y_-}
 =\int g_0\,\mathrm d\tilde\omega_-
 \le\int g_0\,\mathrm d\tilde\omega
 \le\int g_0\,\mathrm d\tilde\omega_+
 =1-\frac{\kappa(1-U_0)}{\kappa+s_0y_+}.
\]
This is \eqref{eq:third-interval}. Mixtures of $\tilde\omega_-$ and
$\tilde\omega_+$ preserve the two moments and attain every intermediate
value of $\vartheta$; the boundary measures already identified complete
the attainment assertion.
head: environment

label: lem:range
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:range}
For $(U,T)\in[0,1]^2$ put
\[
 V=\frac{U[\kappa_0+\delta T(1-U)]}{\kappa_1-\delta U},\qquad
 y_+=\frac{\kappa_1U(1-T)}{\kappa_1-\delta UT},\qquad
 y_-=\frac{\kappa_0U+\kappa_1T(1-U)}{\kappa_0+\delta T(1-U)},
\]
\[
 \vartheta_-=\frac{\kappa(1-U)}{\kappa+s_0y_+},\qquad
 \vartheta_+=1-\frac{\kappa_0U}{\kappa+s_0y_-}.
\]
All denominators are at least $\kappa$, $\kappa_1-\delta U\ge\kappa_0$ and
$\kappa_1-\delta UT\ge\kappa_0$, these functions are continuous
on $[0,1]^2$, and $V,y_\pm,\vartheta_\pm$ take values in $[0,1]$. Then
$\mathcal R_\kappa=\{(U,V,\vartheta):(U,T)\in[0,1]^2,\ \vartheta_-\le\vartheta\le\vartheta_+\}$,
and on the interior of $[0,1]^2$ the functions $y_\pm,\vartheta_\pm$ coincide
with those of \Cref{prop:three-filter} at $(U_0,U_1)=(U,V)$. The sets
$\mathcal R_\kappa$ and $\Omega_\kappa$ are compact, and the state of every $m$ as
in \Cref{lem:filter} with $\kappa(m)=\kappa$ lies in $\Omega_\kappa$ at every point.
head: environment
name: Parametrization of the state region

label: proof:lem:range
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:range}
The identity $V=(1-T)f(U)+TU$ maps the square onto the two-filter region;
on its interior, $T\mapsto V$ is an increasing affine bijection from
$(0,1)$ to $(f(U),U)$. Substitution in the formulas of
\Cref{prop:three-filter} gives
\[
 y_+=\frac{\kappa_1(U-V)}{\delta(1-V)},\qquad
 y_-=\frac{\kappa_1V-\kappa_0U}{\delta V}.
\]
These are the displayed formulas after cancellation of common factors.
Their denominators satisfy
$\kappa_1-\delta U,\kappa_1-\delta UT,\kappa_0+\delta T(1-U)\ge\kappa_0$.
The inequalities $0\le y_+\le U\le y_-\le1$ follow by clearing these
positive denominators. Hence $\kappa+s_0y_\pm\ge\kappa$, all functions
are continuous on the square, and $V,y_\pm,\vartheta_\pm\in[0,1]$.

At $T=0$, $y_+=y_-=U$ and
$\vartheta_\pm=\kappa(1-U)/(\kappa+s_0U)$; at $T=1$,
$y_+=0$, $y_-=1$, and $\vartheta_\pm=1-U$. At $U=0,1$ the common
endpoint values are $1,0$, respectively. These agree with all the
boundary cases of \Cref{prop:three-filter}, proving the range assertion
and $\vartheta_-\le\vartheta_+$ everywhere.

The continuous map
$(U,T,\lambda)\mapsto(U,V,(1-\lambda)\vartheta_-+\lambda\vartheta_+)$
maps $[0,1]^3$ onto $\mathcal R_\kappa$, so this set is compact.
Likewise, $\Omega_\kappa$ is the image of $[0,2]\times\mathcal R_\kappa$
under $(q,U_0,U_1,\vartheta)\mapsto(q,qU_0/\kappa,qU_1/\kappa,q\vartheta)$.
For $q>0$, state inclusion follows from \Cref{thm:common-measure,prop:three-filter};
for $q=0$, all filters vanish and the state is $Y_-$.

label: proof:prop:state-region
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:prop:state-region}
\Cref{lem:range} gives continuous $V,\vartheta_\pm$, their bounds,
compactness, and state inclusion. Every normalized triple in
$\mathcal R_\kappa$ is attained by a probability measure by
\Cref{prop:three-filter}; multiplying its coordinates by $q$ gives
the last assertion.

label: proof:lem:base-identity
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:base-identity}
{Calibration and root.}
For $0\le h\le q$, write $N=2(q-h)^2-(q^2-2h)g(h)$. If $q^2\le2h$,
then $N\ge0$; otherwise $g(h)\le2-h$ gives
$N\ge2(q-h)^2-(q^2-2h)(2-h)=h(2-q)^2\ge0$. Furthermore,
\[
 F_\varsigma(q,0)=\frac{(2-g(0))q^2}{2+\varsigma g(0)}\le q^2,
 \qquad F_\varsigma(q,q)=\frac{Q(q)g(q)}{2+\varsigma g(q)}\le(2-q)^2.
\]
Thus $0\le\Gamma_\varsigma\le\min\{q^2,(2-q)^2\}\le Q^2$.
Continuity follows by taking the minimum of the continuous function
$F_\varsigma(q,qu)$ over the fixed compact interval $0\le u\le1$.

For $0<q<2$, put $c=2bQ+2\kappa\omega\Gamma_\varsigma>0$.
The function $\kappa\nu^2-3Q-c/\nu$ increases strictly from $-\infty$
to $+\infty$, so the positive root is unique and
$d_\kappa=2Q+c/\nu_\kappa>2Q$. Its strict monotonicity gives joint
continuity for $0<q<2$. Since $Q\le1$ and $\Gamma_\varsigma\le Q^2$,
\[
 \nu_\kappa\le\max\{1,((3+2b+2\kappa\omega)/\kappa)^{1/2}\},
 \qquad \nu_\kappa^3\le C Q
\]
with $C$ uniform on compact $\kappa$-sets. This proves continuity at
$q=0,2$ as well.

{Pointwise identities.}
By \Cref{lem:filter}, $0\le f_\varsigma\le q$, $h_\varsigma=q-f_\varsigma$,
and $h_\varsigma'=q^2+\varsigma f_\varsigma^2-2h_\varsigma$.
Substituting $\mathcal J_\varsigma'=-g/(2+\varsigma g)$ gives
\eqref{eq:calibration-pointwise} and $\mathcal T\ge0$.
Put $\mathcal V(q)=-\kappa^{-1}\int_0^q(b+\tfrac32\nu_\kappa)$.
The cubic equation and \eqref{eq:cubic-loss} yield
\[
 n^3+bn^2+(\mathcal V\circ q)'
 =\rho(n,\nu_\kappa)-\tfrac12\nu_\kappa^3
   +\frac{(3\nu_\kappa+2b)Q}{2\kappa}
 =\rho(n,\nu_\kappa)-\omega\Gamma_\varsigma(q).
\]
Adding $\omega$ times the calibration identity gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:defect-identity}
 n^3+bn^2+\omega f_\varsigma^2+
 \bigl\{\mathcal V(q)+\omega\mathcal J_\varsigma(h_\varsigma)\bigr\}'
 =\rho(n,\nu_\kappa)+\omega\mathcal T.
\end{equation}

{Integration.}
The derivatives $q'$ and $h_\varsigma'$ are integrable by
\Cref{thm:ground,lem:filter}; $\mathcal V$ and $\mathcal J_\varsigma$
are $C^1$ with bounded derivatives. Their compositions therefore have
integrable derivatives, with endpoint changes
$-\kappa^{-1}(2b+\tfrac32\int_0^2\nu_\kappa)$ and
$\mathcal J_\varsigma(2)$, respectively. Also $n^2,n^3,f_\varsigma^2\in L^1$.
The two nonnegative terms on the right of \eqref{eq:defect-identity}
are consequently integrable. Finally, integration of
$f_\varsigma'=\kappa m-2f_\varsigma-\varsigma f_\varsigma^2$ gives
\eqref{eq:base-observable}. Integrating \eqref{eq:defect-identity}, with
$\int m=1$, proves \eqref{eq:base-deficit}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The function $b_\circ$ is positive and nondecreasing, so
$k\nu_\circ^3=3Q\nu_\circ+2b_\circ(Q)Q\ge2b_\circ(0)Q$ and, as in the proof of
\Cref{lem:base-identity}, $k\nu_\circ^2>3Q$ and
$d_\circ>\frac23k\nu_\circ^2\ge\frac23k(2b_\circ(0)Q/k)^{2/3}$. Hence
$1/d_\circ\le CQ^{-2/3}$ is integrable on $(0,2)$ and $X_2<\infty$. Since $Q\le1$
and $b_\circ(Q)\le b_\circ(1)$, $k\nu_\circ^3\le3Q\nu_\circ+2b_\circ(1)Q$; as in the proof of
\Cref{lem:base-identity}, this gives
$\nu_\circ\le\nu_{\max}:=\max\{1,((3+2b_\circ(1))/k)^{1/2}\}$ and
$\nu_\circ^3\le(3\nu_{\max}+2b_\circ(1))Q/k$, so $\nu_\circ(q)\to0$ as $q\to0$ or $q\to2$,
and $d_\circ\le k\nu_\circ^2$ is bounded. The function
$(\nu,q)\mapsto k\nu^3-3Q(q)\nu-2b_\circ(Q(q))Q(q)$ is $C^\infty$ on
$(0,\infty)\times(0,2)$, and its $\nu$-derivative at the root is
$3k\nu_\circ^2-3Q=3d_\circ>0$; by the implicit function theorem
$\nu_\circ\in C^\infty(0,2)$, and with the limits at the ends,
$\nu_\circ\in C[0,2]$. \Cref{thm:primal-map}, applied with
$\kappa=k$ and $D=d_\circ$ after the translation $x\mapsto x-X_\circ(1)$, shows
that $m_\circ$ is bounded with support $[0,X_2]$, has ground parameter $k$,
and has ground coordinate $X_\circ^{-1}$ on $[0,X_2]$. Since $\nu_\circ$ depends
on $q$ only through $Q(q)$, $d_\circ(2-q)=d_\circ(q)$, so
$X_\circ(2-q)=X_2-X_\circ(q)$, $q_\circ(X_2-x)=2-q_\circ(x)$ and
$m_\circ(X_2-x)=m_\circ(x)$. Differentiation of $k\nu^3-3Q\nu-2b_\circ(Q)Q=0$
in $Q$ gives
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\nu_\circ}{\,\mathrm d Q}=\frac{3\nu_\circ+2b_\circ(Q)+2Qb_\circ'(Q)}{3k\nu_\circ^2-3Q}
 =\frac{3\nu_\circ+2b_\circ+2Qb_\circ'}{3d_\circ}>0 ,
\]
and $Q(q_\circ(x))$ increases strictly on $(0,X_2/2)$, where $q_\circ<1$. Hence
$m_\circ=\nu_\circ(q_\circ)^2$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, zero outside $[0,X_2]$,
strictly increasing on $[0,X_2/2]$ and symmetric about $X_2/2$.

The filter $f_\circ=r_{\varsigma k}/\varsigma$ of $m_\circ$ satisfies
$f_\circ'=km_\circ-2f_\circ-\varsigma f_\circ^2$, $f_\circ=0$ on $(-\infty,0]$, and
$0\le f_\circ\le q_\circ$ by \Cref{lem:filter} with $s=\varsigma k$; it is $C^1$
because $m_\circ$ is continuous, and $f_\circ>0$ on $(0,\infty)$, since
$f_\circ(x)=\int_0^xe^{-\int_t^x(2+\varsigma f_\circ)}km_\circ(t)\,\mathrm d t$. The reflected
filter $\check f_\circ(x)=f_\circ(X_2-x)$ satisfies
$\check f_\circ'=-km_\circ+2\check f_\circ+\varsigma\check f_\circ^2$ and
$0\le\check f_\circ\le q_\circ(X_2-x)=2-q_\circ$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
{Monotonicity of $h_c$.} On $[0,X_2]$, $q_\circ'=km_\circ-Q(q_\circ)$, so
$h_c=q_\circ-f_\circ$ has the derivative
\[
 h_c'=2f_\circ+\varsigma f_\circ^2-Q(q_\circ),\qquad h_c'(0)=0 .
\]
On $(0,X_2)$ the functions $q_\circ$ and $m_\circ$ are locally Lipschitz, so
$f_\circ'$ and $h_c'$ are locally absolutely continuous, and
\[
 h_c''+(2+2\varsigma f_\circ)h_c'
 =(2+2\varsigma f_\circ)(km_\circ-Q(q_\circ))-Q'(q_\circ)q_\circ'
 =(2q_\circ+2\varsigma f_\circ)q_\circ' ,
\]
using $Q'(q)=2-2q$ and $km_\circ-Q(q_\circ)=q_\circ'$. The function $h_c'$ is
continuous on $[0,X_2]$, and by this equation
$|h_c''|\le(2+2\varsigma\|f_\circ\|_\infty)|h_c'|+(4+2\varsigma\|f_\circ\|_\infty)\|q_\circ'\|_\infty$
almost everywhere on $(0,X_2)$; so $h_c'$ is Lipschitz on $[0,X_2]$, and
variation of constants on $[0,x]$ gives
\[
 h_c'(x)=\int_0^x\exp\Bigl(-\int_t^x(2+2\varsigma f_\circ)\Bigr)
 \bigl(2q_\circ(t)+2\varsigma f_\circ(t)\bigr)q_\circ'(t)\,\mathrm d t>0
 \qquad(0<x\le X_2),
\]
because $q_\circ>0$ and $q_\circ'=d_\circ(q_\circ)>0$ on $(0,X_2)$. For $x\ge X_2$,
$q_\circ=2$, $m_\circ=0$, $h_c=2-f_\circ$ and $h_c'=2f_\circ+\varsigma f_\circ^2>0$, and
$f_\circ(+\infty)=0$ by \Cref{lem:filter}. Hence $h_c$ is continuous and
strictly increasing on $[0,\infty)$, $h_c(0)=0$, $h_c(x)\to2$ as $x\to\infty$.

{The potential.} Define $g_\circ$ on $[0,2)$ by
$g_\circ(h_c(x))=f_\circ(x)+\check f_\circ(x)$ and put $g_\circ(2)=0$. Since
$f_\circ(x)\to0$ and $\check f_\circ(x)=f_\circ(X_2-x)\to0$ as $x\to\infty$,
$g_\circ$ is continuous on $[0,2]$. The bounds
$\check f_\circ\le2-q_\circ$ and $f_\circ\ge0$ give
$0\le g_\circ(h_c)\le f_\circ+2-q_\circ=2-h_c$. For $x\ge X_2$,
$\check f_\circ(x)=f_\circ(X_2-x)=0$, so $g_\circ(h)=2-h$ for
$h\ge h_c(X_2)=2-f_\circ(X_2)$. On $(0,X_2)$, $g_\circ$ is $C^1$ as a function of
$h$, since $h_c'>0$ there, and
\[
 1+g_\circ'(h_c)=\frac{h_c'+f_\circ'+\check f_\circ'}{h_c'}
 =\frac{2\check f_\circ+\varsigma\check f_\circ^2-Q(q_\circ)}{h_c'},
\]
because $f_\circ'+\check f_\circ'=(\check f_\circ-f_\circ)(2+\varsigma(f_\circ+\check f_\circ))$.
The numerator $\check P:=2\check f_\circ+\varsigma\check f_\circ^2-Q(q_\circ)$ at $x$ equals
$h_c'(X_2-x)>0$, by $\check f_\circ(x)=f_\circ(X_2-x)$ and
$Q(q_\circ(x))=Q(q_\circ(X_2-x))$. Hence $h+g_\circ(h)$ is nondecreasing on $[0,2]$:
strictly increasing on $[0,h_c(X_2)]$ and constant $2$ on $[h_c(X_2),2]$.

{Comparison of the two filters.} Let $m_1,m_2\ge0$ be bounded on
$(-\infty,x]$, vanish near $-\infty$, and let $f_1,f_2$ solve
$f_i'=km_i-2f_i-\varsigma f_i^2$ with $f_i(-\infty)=0$. Then
$\delta=f_2-f_1$ satisfies $\delta'=k(m_2-m_1)-c\delta$ with
$c=2+\varsigma(f_1+f_2)\ge2$, and, since $\delta$ is bounded,
\[
 \delta(x)=k\int_{-\infty}^x\exp\Bigl(-\int_t^xc\Bigr)\bigl(m_2(t)-m_1(t)\bigr)\,\mathrm d t .
\]
Fix $0<x<X_2/2$, and take $m_1=m_\circ$ and $m_2(\tau)=m_\circ(2x-\tau)$. By
translation invariance and the symmetry of $m_\circ$, the filter of $m_2$
at $x$ is $f_\circ$ at $X_2-x$, that is, $f_2(x)=\check f_\circ(x)$, while
$f_1(x)=f_\circ(x)$. For $\tau<x$ write $\tau=x-t$ with $t>0$; then
$m_2(\tau)-m_1(\tau)=m_\circ(x+t)-m_\circ(x-t)$. If $x+t\le X_2/2$, this is
nonnegative by monotonicity; if $x+t>X_2/2$, then
$m_\circ(x+t)=m_\circ(X_2-x-t)$ with $x-t<X_2-x-t<X_2/2$, so it is again
nonnegative. For $0<t<\min\{x,X_2/2-x\}$ it is positive. Hence
$\check f_\circ(x)>f_\circ(x)$ for $0<x<X_2/2$, and by reflection
$\check f_\circ(x)<f_\circ(x)$ for $X_2/2<x<X_2$.
head: environment

label: proof:thm:contact
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:contact}
{The derivative.} Put $A=q-h$ and $B=q^2-2h$, so that
$F_\varsigma=(2A^2-Bg_\circ(h))/(2+\varsigma g_\circ(h))$. Where $g_\circ$ is
differentiable,
\[
 \partial_hF_\varsigma
 =\frac{(-4A+2g_\circ-Bg_\circ')(2+\varsigma g_\circ)-\varsigma g_\circ'(2A^2-Bg_\circ)}{(2+\varsigma g_\circ)^2}
 =\frac{2\bigl[(g_\circ-2A)(2+\varsigma g_\circ)-g_\circ'(B+\varsigma A^2)\bigr]}{(2+\varsigma g_\circ)^2}.
\]
Let $h=h_c(x)$, $\xi=q_\circ(x)$, $f=f_\circ(x)$ and
$\check f=\check f_\circ(x)$ for $0<x<X_2$. Write
$\Delta_g=2+\varsigma(f+\check f)$ and
$\Xi=(2-\xi)f+\xi\check f+\varsigma f\check f-Q(\xi)$.
Use $h=\xi-f$, $g_\circ=f+\check f$,
$h_c'g_\circ'=(\check f-f)\Delta_g$, and
\[
 B+\varsigma A^2=h_c'+2(q-\xi)(\xi+\varsigma f)
 +(1+\varsigma)(q-\xi)^2.
\]
Substitution and collection of the factor $q-\xi$ give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:contact-sign}
 \partial_hF_\varsigma(q,h_c(x))
 =\frac{2(q-\xi)}{\Delta_gh_c'}
 \bigl[(1+\varsigma)(f-\check f)(q-\xi)-2\Xi\bigr].
\end{equation}

{Positivity of $\Xi$.} Let $\epsilon_\xi=Q(\xi)/(1+\sqrt{1+\varsigma Q(\xi)})$,
the positive solution of $2\epsilon+\varsigma\epsilon^2=Q(\xi)$. The function
$y\mapsto2y+\varsigma y^2$ is increasing on $[0,\infty)$, and
$2f+\varsigma f^2-Q(\xi)=h_c'>0$, $2\check f+\varsigma\check f^2-Q(\xi)=\check P>0$;
hence $f=\epsilon_\xi+\alpha_1$, $\check f=\epsilon_\xi+\alpha_2$ with
$\alpha_1,\alpha_2>0$. Substituting and using $2\epsilon_\xi+\varsigma\epsilon_\xi^2=Q(\xi)$,
\[
 \Xi=(2-\xi)\alpha_1+\xi\alpha_2+\varsigma\epsilon_\xi(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)+\varsigma\alpha_1\alpha_2>0 .
\]

{The case $0<q\le1$ on $[0,q]$.} Let $h=h_c(x)\in(0,q]$ with
$0<x<X_2$. If $\xi=q$, \eqref{eq:contact-sign} gives $\partial_hF_\varsigma=0$. If $\xi<q$, then $\xi<1$, so $x<X_2/2$ and $f<\check f$; the
bracket in \eqref{eq:contact-sign} is negative and $q-\xi>0$, so
$\partial_hF_\varsigma<0$. If $\xi\ge1$, then $f\ge\check f$ and $q-\xi\le0$,
so the bracket is at most $-2\Xi<0$ and $\partial_hF_\varsigma\ge0$, with
equality only if $\xi=q$. If $q<\xi<1$, then $\xi-q\le\xi-h=f$ because
$h\le q$, and $\check f>f$; the bracket equals
$(1+\varsigma)(\xi-q)(\check f-f)-2\Xi\le(1+\varsigma)f(\check f-f)-2\Xi$, and
\[
 2\Xi-(1+\varsigma)f(\check f-f)
 =\alpha_1\bigl[4-2\xi+(3\varsigma+1)\epsilon_\xi\bigr]
 +\alpha_2\bigl[2\xi+(\varsigma-1)f\bigr]+(\varsigma+1)\alpha_1^2>0 .
\]
Here $2\xi+(\varsigma-1)f\ge\xi+\varsigma f>0$ by $f\le\xi$; so $\partial_hF_\varsigma>0$.
On $[h_c(X_2),2]$, where $g_\circ(h)=2-h$, the numerator of $F_\varsigma$ is
$h(2-q)^2$ and $\partial_hF_\varsigma=(2+2\varsigma)(2-q)^2/(2+\varsigma(2-h))^2>0$. The
function $F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ is continuous on $[0,q]$ and continuously
differentiable away from the two points $0$ and $h_c(X_2)$; it is
therefore strictly decreasing on $[0,h^*]$ and strictly increasing on
$[h^*,q]$, where $h^*=h_c(x^*)$, $q_\circ(x^*)=q$. Here $h^*=q-f_\circ(x^*)<q$.

{Points $h>q$.} Let $0<q\le1$, $0<a\le2-q$, $G=g_\circ(q)$ and
$g=g_\circ(q+a)$. Since $h+g_\circ(h)$ is nondecreasing, $g\ge G-a$, and
$g\ge0$. The identity
$2g_\circ(h)+\varsigma g_\circ(h)^2-Q(h)=\check P+2(2-\xi)f+(1+\varsigma)f^2+2\varsigma f\check f$
at $h=h_c(x)$, $0\le x\le X_2$,
and the identity
$2(2-h)+\varsigma(2-h)^2-Q(h)=(1+\varsigma)(2-h)^2$ on the tail give
$2G+\varsigma G^2\ge Q(q)$. Now $q-(q+a)=-a$ and $q^2-2(q+a)=-Q-2a$ with
$Q=Q(q)$, so
\[
 F_\varsigma(q,q+a)=\varphi(g),\qquad \varphi(\gamma)=\frac{2a^2+(Q+2a)\gamma}{2+\varsigma\gamma},
 \qquad F_\varsigma(q,q)=\frac{QG}{2+\varsigma G}.
\]
If $g\ge G$, then
$(2+\varsigma G)(2+\varsigma g)[\varphi(g)-F_\varsigma(q,q)]=2a^2(2+\varsigma G)+2ag(2+\varsigma G)+2Q(g-G)>0$.
If $g<G$, note $\varphi'(\gamma)=2(Q+2a-\varsigma a^2)/(2+\varsigma\gamma)^2$. When
$Q+2a-\varsigma a^2<0$, $\varphi(g)>\varphi(G)>F_\varsigma(q,q)$ by the previous case
with $g$ replaced by $G$. When $Q+2a-\varsigma a^2\ge0$, $\varphi$ is
nondecreasing; for $a\le G$,
\[
 \varphi(g)-F_\varsigma(q,q)\ge\varphi(G-a)-\frac{QG}{2+\varsigma G}
 =\frac{2a(2G+\varsigma G^2-Q)}{(2+\varsigma G)(2+\varsigma(G-a))}\ge0,
\]
while for $a>G$, $\varphi(g)\ge\varphi(0)=a^2>G^2\ge QG/(2+\varsigma G)$, the last
inequality by $2G+\varsigma G^2\ge Q$. In all cases
$F_\varsigma(q,q+a)\ge F_\varsigma(q,q)>F_\varsigma(q,h^*)$. Hence $h^*$ is the unique
minimizer of $F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ on $[0,2]$ for $0<q\le1$.

{The case $1<q<2$.} On $[0,h_c(X_2)]$ put
$\mathcal U(h)=2-h-g_\circ(h)$. For $0\le x\le X_2$,
\[
 \mathcal U(h_c(x))=2-(q_\circ-f_\circ)-(f_\circ+\check f_\circ)
 =2-q_\circ(x)-f_\circ(X_2-x)=h_c(X_2-x),
\]
so $\mathcal U$ is an involution of $[0,h_c(X_2)]$, and
$g_\circ(\mathcal U(h_c(x)))=f_\circ(X_2-x)+\check f_\circ(X_2-x)=g_\circ(h_c(x))$. For $h\in[0,h_c(X_2)]$, substitution of
$\mathcal U(h)=2-h-g_\circ(h)$ and $g_\circ(\mathcal U(h))=g_\circ(h)$ gives
$F_\varsigma(q,h)=F_\varsigma(2-q,\mathcal U(h))$.
Since $F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ increases strictly on $[h_c(X_2),2]$ for every $q$,
every minimizer of $F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ on $[0,2]$ lies in $[0,h_c(X_2)]$, and
\[
 \min_{[0,2]}F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)=\min_{[0,h_c(X_2)]}F_\varsigma(2-q,\mathcal U(\cdot))
 =\min_{[0,2]}F_\varsigma(2-q,\cdot).
\]
For $1<q<2$, $0<2-q<1$, so the unique minimizer of $F_\varsigma(2-q,\cdot)$ is
$h_c(X_\circ(2-q))=h_c(X_2-X_\circ(q))$, and the unique minimizer of
$F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ is $\mathcal U(h_c(X_2-X_\circ(q)))=h_c(X_\circ(q))$.

{The value.} At the minimizer $h=q-f$, $f=f_\circ(x)$, $\check f=\check f_\circ(x)$,
$q_\circ(x)=q$: $A=f$, $B=2f-Q(q)$, and
$2f^2-(2f-Q)(f+\check f)=Q(f+\check f)-2f\check f$. Since $h=q-f\in[0,q]$ minimizes
$F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)$ on $[0,2]\supset[0,q]$,
$\Gamma_\varsigma(q)=\min_{[0,2]}F_\varsigma(q,\cdot)=F_\varsigma(q,q-f)$, which gives
\eqref{eq:contact}; with the equality of the minima over $[0,2]$ for $q$ and
$2-q$ proved above, this gives $\Gamma_\varsigma(2-q)=\Gamma_\varsigma(q)$.

label: lem:J-value
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:J-value}
In the setting of \Cref{thm:contact}, with $g=g_\circ$, $X_2=X_\circ(2)$ and
$f_{\rm end}=f_\circ(X_2)$,
\[
 \mathcal J_\varsigma(2)=\int_0^{X_2/2}\Bigl(2\Gamma_\varsigma(q_\circ)-f_\circ^2-\check f_\circ^2\Bigr)\,\mathrm d x
 -\frac{\varsigma f_{\rm end}-2\log(1+\varsigma f_{\rm end}/2)}{\varsigma^2} .
\]
head: environment
name: The calibration constant

label: proof:lem:J-value
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:J-value}
For $0<x<X_2$, $h_c(x)$ is the minimizer of $F_\varsigma(q_\circ(x),\cdot)$, so
\eqref{eq:calibration-pointwise}, which is an algebraic identity in
$(q,h_\varsigma,f_\varsigma)$ given the two state equations and holds along $m_\circ$
with $(q,f_\varsigma,h_\varsigma)=(q_\circ,f_\circ,h_c)$, gives
$(\mathcal J_\varsigma(h_c))'=\Gamma_\varsigma(q_\circ)-f_\circ^2$. Integration over $[0,X_2]$, with
$h_c(0)=0$ and $\mathcal J_\varsigma(0)=0$, gives
$\mathcal J_\varsigma(h_c(X_2))=\int_0^{X_2}(\Gamma_\varsigma(q_\circ)-f_\circ^2)\,\mathrm d x$. By the symmetry
$q_\circ(X_2-x)=2-q_\circ(x)$, $\Gamma_\varsigma(q_\circ(X_2-x))=\Gamma_\varsigma(q_\circ(x))$, and
$\int_{X_2/2}^{X_2}f_\circ^2=\int_0^{X_2/2}\check f_\circ^2$, so the integral equals
the first term of the claim. On $[h_c(X_2),2]=[2-f_{\rm end},2]$,
$g_\circ(h)=2-h$, and the substitution $w=2-h$ gives
\[
 \mathcal J_\varsigma(2)-\mathcal J_\varsigma(h_c(X_2))=-\int_0^{f_{\rm end}}\frac{w\,\mathrm d w}{2+\varsigma w}
 =-\Bigl[\frac w\varsigma-\frac2{\varsigma^2}\log\Bigl(1+\frac{\varsigma w}2\Bigr)\Bigr]_0^{f_{\rm end}} .
\qedhere
\]

label: proof:prop:exact-reference
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:prop:exact-reference}
The condition \eqref{eq:self-consistent} makes the defining cubics for
$\nu_\circ$ and $\nu_k$ identical. Uniqueness of the positive root and
continuity at $0,2$ give $\nu_\circ=\nu_k$, hence $d_\circ=d_k$ and
$X_\circ(q)=X_k(q)+X_\circ(1)$. This proves the stated translation.

Suppose $\int m_\circ=1$. Then $m_\circ\in\mathcal M^1_c$ and
$\kappa(m_\circ)=k$ by \Cref{thm:contact}. Along its support,
$n=\nu_k(q_\circ)$ and $h_\varsigma=h_c$ minimizes $F_\varsigma(q_\circ,\cdot)$;
therefore both defects in \eqref{eq:base-deficit} vanish. They also
vanish outside: on the left $(q,f,h)=(0,0,0)$; on the right $q=2$,
$n=\nu_k(2)=0$ and $g_\circ(h)=2-h$, which gives
$F_\varsigma(2,h)=0=\Gamma_\varsigma(2)$. Thus
$E(m_\circ)=\mathcal B_k(m_\circ)$.

For every density in the stated class, \eqref{eq:base-deficit} gives
$E(m)\ge\mathcal B_k(m)$. By \eqref{eq:base-value} and \eqref{eq:base-observable},
the prescribed ground parameter and determinant force
$\mathcal B_k(m)=\mathcal B_k(m_\circ)=E(m_\circ)$. The reference itself
belongs to the class and attains this value.

The comparison density $\bar m_\kappa$ is bounded, compactly supported,

label: def:comparison-profile
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:comparison-profile}
A {comparison profile} at $\kappa>0$ is a continuous
$\nu:[0,2]\to[0,\infty)$, positive on $(0,2)$, such that
$d=\kappa\nu^2-Q$ is positive on $(0,2)$, $1/d\in L^1(0,2)$, and, for a
constant $C_\nu$,
\[
 \frac{\nu^2}d+\frac Q{d\nu}+\frac{\nu^3}Q\le C_\nu\qquad\text{on }(0,2).
\]
Its density $\bar m$ is the density of \Cref{thm:primal-map} with $D=d$,
that is, $\bar m(X(q))=\nu(q)^2$, $X(q)=\int_1^qd^{-1}$. Its left filters are
those of \Cref{lem:filter}, and its {right filters}, as functions of
$q$, are $R_s(q)=\check r_s(-X(q))$ and $R_\circ(q)=\check r_\circ(-X(q))$, where
$\check r_s,\check r_\circ$ are the left filters of $\check m(x)=\bar m(-x)$.
head: environment
name: Comparison profiles

label: lem:right-filters
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:right-filters}
Let $\nu$ be a comparison profile at $\kappa$ with density $\bar m$. Then
$\bar m$ has ground parameter $\kappa$, and $R_s,R_\circ$ are absolutely
continuous on $[0,2]$ and satisfy
\[
 d\frac{\,\mathrm d R_s}{\,\mathrm d q}=-s\nu^2+2R_s+R_s^2,\qquad
 d\frac{\,\mathrm d R_\circ}{\,\mathrm d q}=-\kappa\nu^2+2R_\circ,\qquad R_s(2)=R_\circ(2)=0,
\]
\[
 0\le R_s\le\frac s\kappa(2-q),\qquad 0\le R_\circ\le2-q,\qquad
 R_\circ(q)=\kappa\int_{X(q)}^\infty e^{-2(y-X(q))}\bar m(y)\,\mathrm d y .
\]
Let $\bar v_s$ solve $-\bar v''+(1+s\bar m)\bar v=0$ with $\bar v_s=e^{-x}$ for
$x\ge X(2)$. Then $R_s(q)=-\bar v_s'/\bar v_s-1$ at $x=X(q)$, and for
$x\le X(0)$, $\bar v_s(x)=c_s^-e^{-x}+c_s^+e^x$ with $c_s^-=\exp H_{\bar m}(s)$.
If $\bar m$ is symmetric about $0$, then, with $\bar r_s,\bar r_\circ$ the left filters
of $\bar m$ (functions of $x$), $R_s(q)=\bar r_s(X(2-q))$ and
$R_\circ(q)=\bar r_\circ(X(2-q))$.

parameter $\kappa$ and ground coordinate $q(x)=X^{-1}(x)$ there. The reflection
$(Rf)(x)=f(-x)$ is unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ and $K_{\check m}=RK_{\bar m}R$, so
$\kappa(\check m)=\kappa$. With $u$ the ground state of $\bar m$, the function
$\check u(x)=u(-x)$ is positive, lies in $H^1\cap C^1$, has a locally absolutely
continuous derivative and solves $-\check u''+\check u=\kappa\check m\check u$ almost
everywhere; by the uniqueness statement of \Cref{thm:ground}, the ground
coordinate of $\check m$ is $\check q(x)=1-\check u'(x)/\check u(x)=1+u'(-x)/u(-x)=2-q(-x)$.
\Cref{lem:filter}, applied to $\check m$, gives $0\le\check r_s\le\frac s\kappa\check q$
and $0\le\check r_\circ\le\check q$, that is, the two bounds. The filter
equations $\check r_s'=s\check m-2\check r_s-\check r_s^2$ evaluated at
$-x$, with $\check m(-x)=\bar m(x)=\nu(q(x))^2$ and $\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d x}=d(q)\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d q}$
on $(X(0),X(2))$, give the differential equations; the composition of the
Lipschitz function $\check r_s$ (its derivative is bounded because $\check m$
is) with the absolutely continuous function $-X$ is absolutely continuous
on $[0,2]$. The filters of $\check m$ vanish to the
left of its support $[-X(2),-X(0)]$, which gives $R_s(2)=R_\circ(2)=0$; the
convolution formula for $\check r_\circ$ gives the formula for $R_\circ$.

The function $Y=e^x\check V_s$, with $\check V_s$ the function $V_s$ of \Cref{lem:filter}(ii) for
$\check m$, solves $-Y''+(1+s\check m)Y=0$ and equals $e^x$ to the left of
the support of $\check m$; so $\bar v_s(x)=Y(-x)$, and
$-\bar v_s'(x)/\bar v_s(x)=Y'(-x)/Y(-x)=1+\check r_s(-x)$. To the right of
the support of $\check m$, $\check V_s''+2\check V_s'=0$, so
$\check V_s=\alpha+\beta e^{-2x}$ with $\alpha=\check V_s(+\infty)=\exp H_{\check m}(s)$,
and $Y=\alpha e^x+\beta e^{-x}$; since $K_{\check m}$ is unitarily equivalent
to $K_{\bar m}$ by the reflection $f(x)\mapsto f(-x)$, $\alpha=\exp H_{\bar m}(s)$,
and $\bar v_s(x)=\alpha e^{-x}+\beta e^x$ for $x\le X(0)$. If $\bar m$ is
symmetric, $\check m=\bar m$ and $-X(q)=X(2-q)$.
head: environment

label: lem:comparison-general
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:comparison-general}
Let $\nu$ be a comparison profile at $\kappa$ with density $\bar m$ and right
filters $R_s,R_\circ$, and let $m\ge0$ be integrable with $E(m)<\infty$,
$\kappa(m)=\kappa$, ground coordinate $q$ and left filters $r_s,r_\circ$. Define
$a_s,a_\circ$ by the formulas of \Cref{thm:comparisons} with $\nu,d,R_s,R_\circ$
in place of $\nu_\kappa,d_\kappa,R_s,R_\circ$. Then
$-sQ/(2d)\le a_s\le0$, $-\kappa Q/d\le a_\circ\le0$, and
\[
 H_m(s)-H_{\bar m}(s)=\int a_s(q,r_s)\bigl(n^2-\nu(q)^2\bigr)\,\mathrm d x,
 \qquad
 S(m)-S(\bar m)=\int a_\circ(q,r_\circ)\bigl(n^2-\nu(q)^2\bigr)\,\mathrm d x .
\]
head: environment
name: Comparison with a comparison profile

label: proof:lem:comparison-general
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:comparison-general}
{Bounds and integrability.}
The inequalities $r_s\le sq/\kappa$ and
$R_s\le s(2-q)/\kappa$ imply
$2\kappa r_sR_s\le sQ(r_s+R_s)$, including when either factor vanishes.
Thus $-sQ/(2d)\le a_s\le0$. Similarly,
$2r_\circ R_\circ\le Q(r_\circ+R_\circ)$ and
$r_\circ+R_\circ\le2$ give $-\kappa Q/d\le a_\circ\le0$.
The profile bounds imply $|a_s|+|a_\circ|\le C\nu$ and
$\nu^3\le C Q(q)\in L^1(\mathbb R)$. Since
$\nu n^2\le\nu^3/3+2n^3/3$, both claimed integrands are integrable.

{Determinant potential.}
Let $L_s(q)=\log(e^{X(q)}\bar v_s(X(q)))$. By \Cref{lem:right-filters},
$dL_s'=-R_s$ and $L_s(2)=0$. On the triangle
$\Delta_s=\{0\le q\le2,\ 0\le r\le sq/\kappa\}$ define
\[
 W_s(q,r)=L_s(q)+\log\frac{2+r+R_s(q)}2.
\]
On $0<q<2$, the right-filter equation gives
\[
 \partial_qW_s=-\frac{rR_s+s\nu^2}{d(2+r+R_s)},\qquad
 \partial_rW_s=\frac1{2+r+R_s}.
\]
These derivatives are bounded on $\Delta_s$ because
$rR_s\le s^2Q/\kappa^2$, $Q/d\le C_\nu\nu$, and
$\nu^2/d\le C_\nu$. The potential is continuous on the closed triangle,
so integration along segments makes it Lipschitz there. Its endpoint
values are
\[
 W_s(0,0)=\log c_s^-=H_{\bar m}(s),\qquad
 W_s(2,r)=\log(1+r/2),
\]
where the first identity follows from
$\bar v_s=c_s^-e^{-x}+c_s^+e^x$ on the left of the support.
Along $m$, substitution of $q'=\kappa n^2-Q$ and
$r_s'=sn^2-2r_s-r_s^2$ gives, for $0<q<2$,
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d x}W_s(q,r_s)=-r_s+a_s(q,r_s)(n^2-\nu^2).
\]
Indeed, the coefficient of $n^2$ is
$-(sQ+\kappa r_sR_s)/(d(2+r_s+R_s))=a_s$; the remaining term is
$-r_s-a_s\nu^2$, using $d=\kappa\nu^2-Q$.

The composition is locally absolutely continuous. On the level sets
$q=0,2$, one has $q'=0$, and hence $n=0$, almost everywhere. On $q=0$
also $r_s=0$; on $q=2$, differentiating $\log(1+r_s/2)$ gives $-r_s$.
Locality of derivatives of absolutely continuous functions justifies
these identities on the level sets. The derivative formula therefore
holds almost everywhere, with the endpoint convention $a_s=0$.
Its right-hand side is integrable, and $(q,r_s)$ tends to $(0,0)$ and
$(2,0)$ at the two infinities. Integration proves the determinant identity.

{Second-trace potential.}
Put
\[
 G_\circ(q)=\frac\kappa2\int_q^2\frac{\nu^2R_\circ}{d},\qquad
 W_\circ(q,r)=\frac{r^2}4+\frac{rR_\circ(q)}2+G_\circ(q).
\]
The integral is finite, and on $\Delta_\circ=\{0\le q\le2,\ 0\le r\le q\}$,
\[
 \partial_rW_\circ=\frac{r+R_\circ}2,\qquad
 \partial_qW_\circ=
 \frac{2rR_\circ-\kappa\nu^2(r+R_\circ)}{2d}.
\]
The same profile bounds, with $rR_\circ\le Q$ and $r+R_\circ\le2$,
make these derivatives bounded; thus $W_\circ$ is Lipschitz on
$\Delta_\circ$. The state equations yield
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d x}W_\circ(q,r_\circ)
 =-r_\circ^2+a_\circ(q,r_\circ)(n^2-\nu^2).
\]
The coefficient of $n^2$ is
$\kappa[2r_\circ R_\circ-Q(r_\circ+R_\circ)]/(2d)=a_\circ$;
the constant term follows from $d=\kappa\nu^2-Q$.
At $q=0$, $r_\circ=0$; at $q=2$, $W_\circ=r_\circ^2/4$ and its derivative
is $-r_\circ^2$. The same level-set argument extends the formula almost
everywhere. Its endpoint values are $G_\circ(0)$ and $0$.

Finally, integration of $(\bar r_\circ^2)'$ and Fubini's theorem give
\[
 S(\bar m)=\frac\kappa2\int\bar m\bar r_\circ
 =\frac\kappa2\int\bar mR_\circ
 =\frac\kappa2\int_0^2\frac{\nu^2R_\circ}{d}=G_\circ(0).
\]
Integrating the derivative of $W_\circ$ proves the second identity.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:filter-continuity}
For $s>0$ let $\bar r_s(q),\bar r_\circ(q)$ denote the left filters of $\bar m_\kappa$ at
the point $X_\kappa(q)$, $q\in[0,2]$, and put
\[
 w_s=q-\frac\kappa s\bar r_s,\qquad w_\circ=q-\bar r_\circ .
\]
Then $\bar r_s,\bar r_\circ$ are jointly continuous in
$(q,\kappa)\in[0,2]\times(0,\infty)$, and on every compact $\kappa$-set
$0\le w_s,w_\circ\le Cq^{7/3}$. If $\Gamma_\varsigma$ is symmetric, the right
filters are $R_s(q)=\bar r_s(2-q)$ and $R_\circ(q)=\bar r_\circ(2-q)$.
head: environment
name: Continuity of the comparison filters

label: proof:lem:filter-continuity
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:filter-continuity}
Fix a compact set $\mathsf K\subset(0,\infty)$ and $\kappa\in\mathsf K$. Along
$\bar m_\kappa$, $x=X_\kappa(q)$ and $\frac{\,\mathrm d q}{\,\mathrm d x}=d_\kappa(q)$ on $(0,2)$;
$\bar r_s$ is Lipschitz in $x$, and $X_\kappa$ is absolutely continuous, so
$\bar r_s(q)$ is absolutely continuous on $[0,2]$ with $\bar r_s(0)=0$ and
\[
 \frac{\,\mathrm d\bar r_s}{\,\mathrm d q}=G_\kappa(q,\bar r_s),\qquad
 G_\kappa(q,r)=\frac{s\nu_\kappa(q)^2-2r-r^2}{d_\kappa(q)} .
\]
Its values lie in $[0,R_{\max}]$, $R_{\max}=2s/\min\mathsf K$. For
$r,r'\in[0,R_{\max}]$,
$|G_\kappa(q,r)-G_\kappa(q,r')|\le\ell_\kappa(q)|r-r'|$ with
$\ell_\kappa=(2+2R_{\max})/d_\kappa$, and
$|G_\kappa(q,r)-G_{\kappa'}(q,r)|\le\epsilon_{\kappa,\kappa'}(q)$ with
$\epsilon_{\kappa,\kappa'}=s|\nu_\kappa^2/d_\kappa-\nu_{\kappa'}^2/d_{\kappa'}|+(2R_{\max}+R_{\max}^2)|1/d_\kappa-1/d_{\kappa'}|$.
The function $e=|\bar r_s^{(\kappa)}-\bar r_s^{(\kappa')}|$ satisfies
$e(q)\le\int_0^q\ell_\kappa e+\int_0^2\epsilon_{\kappa,\kappa'}$, so Gronwall's
inequality gives
$\sup_qe\le\exp(\int_0^2\ell_\kappa)\int_0^2\epsilon_{\kappa,\kappa'}$. As
$\kappa'\to\kappa$, $\epsilon_{\kappa,\kappa'}\to0$ pointwise on $(0,2)$ by
\Cref{lem:local-profile}, with the integrable majorant
$3s/\min\mathsf K+CQ^{-2/3}$; hence $\bar r_s$ is continuous in $\kappa$
uniformly in $q$, and being continuous in $q$ for each $\kappa$, it is
jointly continuous. The same argument, with
$G_\kappa(q,r)=(\kappa\nu_\kappa^2-2r)/d_\kappa$, applies to $\bar r_\circ$.

By \Cref{lem:filter}, $0\le w_s\le q$, and along $\bar m_\kappa$
\[
 w_s'=q'-\frac\kappa s\bar r_s'=\Bigl(1+\frac s\kappa\Bigr)q^2-2\Bigl(1+\frac{sq}\kappa\Bigr)w_s
 +\frac s\kappa w_s^2 ,
\]
since
$q'-\frac\kappa s(s\bar m-2\bar r_s-\bar r_s^2)=-Q(q)+\frac{2\kappa}s\bar r_s+\frac\kappa s\bar r_s^2$,
which for $\bar r_s=\frac s\kappa(q-w_s)$ equals
$-Q(q)+2(q-w_s)+\frac s\kappa(q-w_s)^2$. For $0\le w\le q$,
$-2(1+\frac{sq}\kappa)w+\frac s\kappa w^2\le w(\frac s\kappa(w-2q)-2)\le0$, so
$\frac{\,\mathrm d w_s}{\,\mathrm d q}\le(1+\frac s\kappa)q^2/d_\kappa\le Cq^2Q^{-2/3}$, and
$w_s(0)=0$ gives $w_s\le Cq^{7/3}$ for $q\le1$, hence for $q\le2$ after
enlarging $C$. Likewise $w_\circ'=q^2-2w_\circ\le q^2$ gives $w_\circ\le Cq^{7/3}$.
The last assertion is \Cref{lem:right-filters} with \Cref{lem:local-profile}.

label: lem:symmetric-values
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symmetric-values}
Let $m\ge0$ be integrable and not zero, with support in $[x_-,2x_c-x_-]$
and symmetric about $x_c$, let $\kappa=\kappa(m)$, and let $r_s,r_\circ$ be its left filters.
Then
\[
 H_m(s)=2\int_{x_-}^{x_c}r_s\,\mathrm d x+\log(1+r_s(x_c)),\qquad
 S(m)=2\int_{x_-}^{x_c}r_\circ^2\,\mathrm d x+r_\circ(x_c)^2 .
\]
head: environment
name: Spectral values of a symmetric density

label: proof:lem:symmetric-values
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:symmetric-values}
Translate so that $x_c=0$. Let $u_L=e^xV_s$, with $V_s$ of
\Cref{lem:filter}(ii); it solves $-u''+(1+sm)u=0$, equals $e^x$
to the left of the support, and $u_L'/u_L=1+r_s$, $u_L(x)=e^x\exp\int_{-\infty}^xr_s$.
Since $m$ is even, $u_R(x)=u_L(-x)$ solves the same equation and equals
$e^{-x}$ to the right of the support. The Wronskian
$W=u_L'u_R-u_Lu_R'$ is constant. At $x=0$, $u_R(0)=u_L(0)$ and
$u_R'(0)=-u_L'(0)$, so $W=2u_L'(0)u_L(0)=2(1+r_s(0))\exp(2\int_{x_-}^0r_s)$,
using $r_s=0$ on $(-\infty,x_-]$. To the right of the support,
$V_s=\alpha+\beta e^{-2x}$ with $\alpha=V_s(+\infty)=\exp H_m(s)$
(\Cref{lem:filter}), so $u_L=\alpha e^x+\beta e^{-x}$, $u_R=e^{-x}$ and
$W=2\alpha$. Comparing the two expressions gives the first identity.

For the second, write $S(m)=\frac{\kappa^2}4\iint m(x)m(y)e^{-2|x-y|}$ and
split $\mathbb R^2$ into the four quadrants of the signs of $x,y$. For the
quadrant $x,y<0$, the identity of \Cref{lem:filter}(i) with $c=\kappa$ and
$\tilde m=m\mathbf1_{(-\infty,0)}$, for which
$\kappa\int_{-\infty}^xe^{-2(x-y)}\tilde m(y)\,\mathrm d y$ is $r_\circ(x)$ on $(-\infty,0]$ and
$r_\circ(0)e^{-2x}$ on $[0,\infty)$, gives
$\int_{-\infty}^0r_\circ^2+\int_0^\infty r_\circ(0)^2e^{-4x}\,\mathrm d x=\int_{-\infty}^0r_\circ^2+r_\circ(0)^2/4$. For the quadrant
$x<0<y$, the integral is
$\frac{\kappa^2}4\int_{x<0}e^{2x}m\int_{y>0}e^{-2y}m=\frac{\kappa^2}4(r_\circ(0)/\kappa)^2$,
because $\int_{y>0}e^{-2y}m(y)\,\mathrm d y=\int_{x<0}e^{2x}m(x)\,\mathrm d x=r_\circ(0)/\kappa$ by
symmetry. By symmetry the quadrant $x,y>0$ equals the first and the
quadrant $y<0<x$ equals the second. Summation gives the claim.

label: proof:prop:certificate-mechanism
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:prop:certificate-mechanism}
Let $m\in\mathcal M^1_c$ with ground parameter $\kappa$ and state $Y$.
Then $E(m)<\infty$, and $Y(x)\in\Omega_\kappa$ by \Cref{lem:range}.
On the level sets $q=0,2$, absolute continuity gives $q'=0$ almost
everywhere, and the ground equation then gives $n=0$. The hypotheses
therefore imply $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,n)\ge0$ almost everywhere.

The terms $\rho(n,\nu_\kappa(q))$ and $a(n^2-\nu_\kappa^2)$ are integrable
by \Cref{lem:base-identity,thm:comparisons}. Since $Y'$ is integrable and
$Y$ lies in the compact set $\Omega_\kappa$, the chain rule gives
\[
 (\Psi\circ Y)'=\mathsf b_\Psi n^2-\mathsf d_\Psi\in L^1,\qquad
 \int_\mathbb R(\Psi\circ Y)'=\Psi(Y_+)-\Psi(Y_-)=0.
\]
For the price, let $\Phi(y)=\int_0^y\eta$. This function is Lipschitz,
with $\Phi'=\eta$ outside the finite discontinuity set of $\eta$.
The chain rule applies off its preimage under $q$; on that preimage,
both $q$ and $\Phi\circ q$ have derivative zero almost everywhere on
each level set. Hence
\[
 (\Phi\circ q)'=\eta(q)q'\in L^1,\qquad
 \int_\mathbb R\eta(q)q'=\Phi(2)-\Phi(0)=\int_0^2\eta.
\]
Also $\int Q(q)=\kappa-2$. Rewrite \eqref{eq:residual} as
\[
 \rho=\mathscr R_\kappa+a(n^2-\nu_\kappa^2)
 -\frac{\eta(q)q'}\kappa-\frac\tau\kappa Q(q)-(\Psi\circ Y)' .
\]
Every term is integrable. Integrating and discarding
$\mathscr R_\kappa\ge0$, then using \Cref{thm:comparisons}, gives
\[
 \int\rho\ge\sum_i\xi_i[H_m(s_i)-H_{\bar m_\kappa}(s_i)]
 +\chi[S(m)-S(\bar m_\kappa)]-\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\eta
 -\frac{\tau(\kappa-2)}\kappa.
\]
Combine this with $E(m)\ge\mathcal B_\kappa(m)+\int\rho$ from
\eqref{eq:base-deficit}.

label: proof:thm:master
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:master}
Since $d_\kappa=\kappa\nu_\kappa^2-Q$,
$\frac{\eta}\kappa(\kappa n^2-Q)=\eta(n^2-\nu_\kappa^2)+\frac{\eta d_\kappa}\kappa$, and
$\mathsf b_\Psi n^2=\mathsf b_\Psi(n^2-\nu_\kappa^2)+\mathsf b_\Psi\nu_\kappa^2$. Hence
\[
 \mathscr R_\kappa(Y,n)=-\bigl[y(n^2-\nu_\kappa^2)-\rho(n,\nu_\kappa)\bigr]
 +\frac{\eta d_\kappa+\tau Q}\kappa+\mathsf b_\Psi\nu_\kappa^2-\mathsf d_\Psi,\qquad
 y=a-\eta-\mathsf b_\Psi ,
\]
and $\inf_{n\ge0}\mathscr R_\kappa=-\mathcal C(\nu_\kappa,y)+(\eta d_\kappa+\tau Q)/\kappa
+\mathsf b_\Psi\nu_\kappa^2-\mathsf d_\Psi$. The replacement changes $\mathsf b_\Psi$ to
$\mathsf b_\Psi-\kappa F'(q)$ and $\mathsf d_\Psi$ to $\mathsf d_\Psi-Q F'(q)$, because the
first components of $\mathsf b$ and $\mathsf d$ are $\kappa$ and $Q$. Thus $y$ is
unchanged, the right side changes by
$F'(q)(d_\kappa-\kappa\nu_\kappa^2+Q)=0$, and $\mathcal P_\kappa$ changes by
$F(2)-F(0)=0$. For the last claim,
$(\eta d_\kappa+\tau Q)/\kappa=\nu_\kappa ed_\kappa/\kappa$, and
\[
 \int\bar m_\kappa=\int_0^2\frac{\nu_\kappa^2}{d_\kappa}\,\mathrm d q
 =\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\frac{d_\kappa+Q}{d_\kappa}\,\mathrm d q=\frac1\kappa\Bigl(2+\int_0^2\frac Q{d_\kappa}\,\mathrm d q\Bigr)
\]
gives $\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\eta+\frac{\tau(\kappa-2)}\kappa
=\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\nu_\kappa e-\frac\tau\kappa\int_0^2\frac Q{d_\kappa}+\frac{\tau(\kappa-2)}\kappa
=\frac1\kappa\int_0^2\nu_\kappa e+\tau\bigl(1-\int\bar m_\kappa\bigr)$; here $Q/d_\kappa\le\nu_\kappa/(2b)$
is integrable (\Cref{lem:local-profile}).

label: thm:certificate-transfer
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:certificate-transfer}
Let $\Theta$ be a dual certificate admissible at $k$. There is
$\delta_*>0$ such that $\Theta$ is admissible at every $\kappa$ with
$|\kappa-k|<\delta_*$, and
\[
 \sup_{J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N}\bigl|\ell_{\kappa(m_J)}(\Theta;m_J)-\ell_*(\Theta)\bigr|
 \longrightarrow0\qquad(N\to\infty).
\]
head: environment
name: Transfer of an admissible certificate

label: proof:thm:certificate-transfer
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:certificate-transfer}
{Admissibility near $k$.} By \Cref{lem:regular-criterion}(ii), and
since $e_{\mathsf C}$ and $\psi$ are continuous, for each side, cell $\mathsf C$ and end
$\sigma$, the bracket in \eqref{eq:witness} is a continuous function on the
compact set $\mathsf C\times[0,1]^2\times[k/2,2k]$, hence uniformly continuous.
Its maximum over $\mathsf C\times[0,1]^2$ at $\kappa=k$ is negative, so there is
$\delta_{\mathsf C,\sigma}>0$ such that the maximum is negative for
$|\kappa-k|<\delta_{\mathsf C,\sigma}$. There are finitely many pairs
$(\mathsf C,\sigma)$; $\delta_*$ is the smallest of these numbers and $k/2$.

{The value.} Write $\kappa_J=\kappa(m_J)$. By \Cref{thm:transfer},
$\sup_J|\kappa_J-k|\le4\delta_N/\Lambda_0^2\to0$, and every $m_J$ has
$\int m_J=1$. Compare the terms of \eqref{eq:dual-value} at
$(\kappa_J,m_J)$ with those of \eqref{eq:dual-target-value}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item By \Cref{thm:transfer}, $|H_{m_J}(s_i)-H_*(s_i)|\le\frac{s_i}2\delta_N$ and
$|S(m_J)-\frac{k^2}6|=|\frac{\kappa_J^2}4\operatorname{tr} K_{m_J}^2-\frac{k^2}4\cdot\frac23|
\le\frac{|\kappa_J^2-k^2|}4+\frac{k^2}2\delta_N$, using $\operatorname{tr} K_{m_J}^2\le1$.
\item In $\mathcal B_{\kappa_J}(m_J)$: $\kappa\mapsto\int_0^2\nu_\kappa\,\mathrm d q$ is continuous
by joint continuity and boundedness of $\nu_\kappa$ (\Cref{lem:local-profile});
$\mathcal J_\varsigma(2)$ does not depend on $\kappa$; and by
\eqref{eq:base-observable}, $S_\varsigma(m_J)=\kappa_J/\varsigma-2H_{m_J}(\varsigma\kappa_J)/\varsigma^2$,
where
$|H_{m_J}(\varsigma\kappa_J)-H_*(\varsigma k)|\le\frac\varsigma2|\kappa_J-k|+\frac{\varsigma k}2\delta_N$,
because $0\le\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d s}H_m(s)=\sum_j\lambda_j/(2+s\lambda_j)\le\frac12\int m$.
\item The price \eqref{eq:closed-price-main} is continuous in $\kappa$: by
\Cref{lem:regular-criterion}(ii), $\hat\nu_\kappa(t)$ is jointly continuous on
$[0,1]\times[k/2,2k]$, hence uniformly continuous; and
$\int\bar m_\kappa=\int_0^2\nu_\kappa^2/d_\kappa\,\mathrm d q$ is continuous by dominated
convergence with the majorant $3/k$ for $\kappa\ge k/2$.
\item $H_{\bar m_\kappa}(s)$ and $S(\bar m_\kappa)$ are continuous in $\kappa$. The left
filters of $\bar m_\kappa$ vanish to the left of its support; on the support
$\,\mathrm d x=\,\mathrm d q/d_\kappa$; and to the right of it they solve $r'=-2r-r^2$, respectively
$r'=-2r$, whose solutions with initial value $r_0$ have
$\int_0^\infty r=\log(1+r_0/2)$, respectively $\int_0^\infty r^2=r_0^2/4$. By
\Cref{lem:filter}, with $\kappa(\bar m_\kappa)=\kappa$,
\[
 H_{\bar m_\kappa}(s)=\int_0^2\frac{\bar r_s}{d_\kappa}\,\mathrm d q+\log\Bigl(1+\frac{\bar r_s(2)}2\Bigr),
 \qquad
 S(\bar m_\kappa)=\int_0^2\frac{\bar r_\circ^2}{d_\kappa}\,\mathrm d q+\frac{\bar r_\circ(2)^2}4 .
\]
By \Cref{lem:filter-continuity} and its proof, $\bar r_s$ and $\bar r_\circ$ are
bounded on $[0,2]\times[k/2,2k]$ and continuous in $\kappa$ uniformly in $q$, and
by \Cref{lem:local-profile} $d_\kappa^{-1}$ is continuous into $L^1(0,2)$; hence
both quantities are continuous in $\kappa$.
\end{enumerate}
The value is a continuous function of $\kappa$ and of these quantities, with
coefficients fixed by $\Theta$; since $\sup_J|\kappa_J-k|\to0$ and $\delta_N\to0$, the
differences tend to zero uniformly in $J$.

body_md:
\label{proof:thm:dual}
We first show, for every $\kappa>0$ at which $\Theta$ is admissible, that
$E(m)\ge\ell_\kappa(\Theta;m)$ for all $m\in\mathcal M^1_c$ with $\kappa(m)=\kappa$. Let
$Y\in\Omega_\kappa$ with $0<q<2$. There
are a side and $t\in(0,1]$ with $q=q_{\mathrm s}(t)$, a cell $\mathsf C\ni t$, and,
by \Cref{lem:regular-criterion}(iii), $(U,T)\in[0,1]^2$ and
$\vartheta\in[\vartheta_-,\vartheta_+]$ such that $Y$ has the normalized coordinates
$(U,V,\vartheta)$. By \eqref{eq:witness},
$\psi(\mathfrak b_\sigma-e)-\mathfrak c_\sigma-e(1-\mathfrak l)<0$ at $(t,U,T)$ for both
$\sigma$; by convexity in $\vartheta$ (\Cref{lem:regular-criterion}(iii)),
\eqref{eq:closed-criterion} holds at $\vartheta$, hence \eqref{eq:master} holds at
$Y$, and by \Cref{thm:master} $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,n)\ge0$ for all $n\ge0$. At
$q\in\{0,2\}$, $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,0)=0$ by \Cref{lem:regular-criterion}(iv), and
$\Psi\in C^1(\mathbb R^4)$ with $\Psi(Y_-)=\Psi(Y_+)$. By
\Cref{prop:certificate-mechanism} and \eqref{eq:centered-price}, every
$m\in\mathcal M^{1}_c$ with $\kappa(m)=\kappa$ satisfies $E(m)\ge\ell_\kappa(\Theta;m)$.
For $m\in\mathcal A_{\mathrm{obs}}(\varsigma)$ one has $\kappa(m)=k$ and
$\mathbf o_\varsigma(m)=\mathbf o_\varsigma^*$, so
$S_\varsigma(m)=k/\varsigma-2H_*(\varsigma k)/\varsigma^2$,
$\mathcal B_k(m)=\mathcal B_*$, $S(m)=k^2/6$, and $\ell_k(\Theta;m)=\ell_*(\Theta)$.
This proves (i).

By \Cref{thm:certificate-transfer}, there is $\delta_*>0$ such that
$\Theta$ is admissible at every $\kappa$ with $|\kappa-k|<\delta_*$, and
$\ell_{\kappa(m_J)}(\Theta;m_J)\to\ell_*(\Theta)$ uniformly over
$J\in\overline{\mathcal Y}_N$ as $N\to\infty$, where $m_J$ is the packed density of
\Cref{thm:packing}. By \Cref{thm:transfer}, $|\kappa(m_J)-k|<\delta_*$
for all large $N$, and then
$N^{-3}\mathcal E_N(J)=E(m_J)\ge\ell_{\kappa(m_J)}(\Theta;m_J)$. This proves the
first claim of (ii); the second follows from the definition of
$\underline{\mathsf e}$, and the third from \Cref{thm:gain}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:regular-criterion}
Let $\Theta$ be a dual certificate and $\kappa>0$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item With $v=t$ on the left side, $f_\circ=\varphi_\circ$, $q_\circ-f_\circ=h_c=\epsilon_\circ$
and $\check f_\circ(t)=\varphi_\circ(2-t)$ at $q_\circ=t^3$; $\Gamma_\varsigma(q)/Q(q)=\gamma(t)$ at
$q=t^3$; $\nu_\kappa(t^3)=t\hat\nu(t)$, $d_\kappa(t^3)=t^2\mathfrak d(t)$, and
$\frac{\,\mathrm d x}{\,\mathrm d t}=\mathfrak p$ along $\bar m_\kappa$; the left filters of $\bar m_\kappa$ at
$q=t^3$ are $\bar r_s=\varrho_s(t)=\frac s\kappa(t^3-w_s(t))$ and
$\bar r_\circ=\varrho_\circ(t)=t^3-w_\circ(t)$, and at $q=2-t^3$ they are $\varrho_s(2-t)$ and
$\varrho_\circ(2-t)$. Consequently, on the left side
\[
 \bar U_i=1-\frac{w_{s_i}}{t^3},\quad \bar\vartheta=\frac{w_\circ}{t^3},\quad
 \widehat R_i=\frac{\varrho_{s_i}(2-t)}{h_t},\quad \widehat R_\circ=\frac{\varrho_\circ(2-t)}{h_t},
\]
and on the right side
\[
 \bar U_i=\frac{\kappa\varrho_{s_i}(2-t)}{s_ih_t},\quad \bar\vartheta=1-\frac{\varrho_\circ(2-t)}{h_t},\quad
 \widehat R_i=\frac{s_i}\kappa\Bigl(1-\frac{w_{s_i}}{t^3}\Bigr),\quad \widehat R_\circ=1-\frac{w_\circ}{t^3}.
\]
\item The functions $z_\circ,\mathfrak p_\circ,\gamma,\hat\nu,\mathfrak d,\mathfrak p$ are $C^\infty$ on
$[0,1]$, and the restrictions of $\varphi_\circ,\varrho_s,\varrho_\circ$ to $[0,1]$ and to
$[1,2]$ are $C^\infty$ on these closed intervals; $\epsilon_\circ,w_s,w_\circ$ vanish to order seven at
$t=0$, and $\epsilon_\circ/t^3$, $w_s/t^3$, $w_\circ/t^3$ are $C^\infty$ on $[0,1]$. The
functions $\hat\nu,\mathfrak d,\widehat R_i,\widehat R_\circ,\bar U_i,\bar\vartheta$ are jointly
continuous in $(t,\kappa)\in[0,1]\times(0,\infty)$, $\hat\nu>0$, $\mathfrak d>0$,
$\bar U_i,\bar\vartheta,\widehat R_\circ\in[0,1]$, $\widehat R_i\in[0,s_i/\kappa]$, and
$\varphi_\circ,\epsilon_\circ,\gamma\ge0$. All quotients
$\mathscr D(\cdot)$ above are polynomials. Consequently $\mathfrak b_\sigma$, $\mathfrak c_\sigma$ and
$\mathfrak l$ are continuous in $(t,U,T,\kappa)\in[0,1]^3\times(0,\infty)$.
\item For $0<t\le1$, the normalized states in $\Omega_\kappa$ over $q=q_{\mathrm s}(t)$
are exactly the points $(U,V,\vartheta)$ with $(U,T)\in[0,1]^2$ and
$\vartheta\in[\vartheta_-,\vartheta_+]$. With
$\Psi=\Psi_{\rm raw}-\Psi_{\rm raw}(\bar Y(q))$ and $\eta=-\tau Q/d_\kappa+\nu_\kappa e$,
the criterion \eqref{eq:master} at such a state, divided by $\nu_\kappa^3$, reads
\begin{equation}\label{eq:closed-criterion}
 \psi\bigl(\mathfrak b-e\bigr)-\mathfrak c-e(1-\mathfrak l)\le0,
\end{equation}
where $\mathfrak b,\mathfrak c$ are the expressions above at the given $\vartheta$. Both
are affine in $\vartheta$, so the maximum of the left side over
$\vartheta\in[\vartheta_-,\vartheta_+]$ is attained at $\vartheta_\pm$.
\item The function $F(q)=\Psi_{\rm raw}(\bar Y(q))$ belongs to $C^1[0,2]$ with
$F(0)=F(2)=F'(0)=F'(2)=0$; extended by zero it belongs to $C^1(\mathbb R)$, and
$\Psi\in C^1(\mathbb R^4)$ with $\Psi(Y_-)=\Psi(Y_+)=0$. At $q\in\{0,2\}$,
$\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,0)=0$ for all $Y\in\Omega_\kappa$.
\end{enumerate}

name: The normalized criterion

label: proof:lem:regular-criterion
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:regular-criterion}
{The reference density.} At $q=t^3$, $Q=Q_t$, and dividing
$k\nu^3-3Q\nu-2b_\circ(Q)Q=0$ by $kt^3$ shows that $\nu_\circ(t^3)=tz_\circ(t)$. By
\Cref{lem:jets}, $3z_\circ^2-\frac{3th_t}k=\frac{6th_t}k+\frac{6b_\circ h_t}{kz_\circ}>0$ at the root,
and the coefficients are $C^\infty$ in $t\in[0,1]$, with
$2b_\circ(Q_t)h_t/k>0$; the implicit function theorem shows that $z_\circ$ is
$C^\infty$ and positive on $[0,1]$. Then
$d_\circ=k\nu_\circ^2-Q=t^2(kz_\circ^2-th_t)=t^2(2th_t+2b_\circ h_t/z_\circ)$ by the cubic, and
along $m_\circ$, $\frac{\,\mathrm d x}{\,\mathrm d t}=\frac{3t^2}{d_\circ}=\mathfrak p_\circ$. By
\Cref{thm:contact}, $m_\circ$ and $q_\circ$ are symmetric; in the coordinate $v$,
with $x$ the corresponding point of $[0,X_\circ(2)]$, $\frac{\,\mathrm d x}{\,\mathrm d v}=\mathfrak p_\circ$ on both
halves, because $\frac{\,\mathrm d q}{\,\mathrm d v}=3t^2$ there. The filter equation of $f_\circ$
in the variable $v$ is the equation for $\varphi_\circ$, with the initial value
$f_\circ(0)=0$; so $f_\circ=\varphi_\circ$, and $\check f_\circ$ at $v$ is $\varphi_\circ$ at $2-v$.
The coefficient $\mathfrak p_\circ(kt^2z_\circ^2-2\varphi-\varsigma\varphi^2)$ is $C^\infty$ on each closed
half, so $\varphi_\circ$ is $C^\infty$ on $[0,1]$ and on $[1,2]$. The function
$h_c=q_\circ-f_\circ$ satisfies, by $q_\circ'=km_\circ-Q$ and the filter equation,
$h_c'=(1+\varsigma)q_\circ^2-2(1+\varsigma q_\circ)h_c+\varsigma h_c^2$ (the computation of
\Cref{lem:filter-continuity} with $s/\kappa=\varsigma$), which in the variable $t$ is
the equation for $\epsilon_\circ$; so $h_c=\epsilon_\circ$. Write
$\epsilon_\circ'=\alpha(t)\epsilon_\circ+\mathfrak p_\circ(1+\varsigma)t^6$ with
$\alpha=\mathfrak p_\circ(-2-2\varsigma t^3+\varsigma\epsilon_\circ)$ bounded; variation of constants
from $\epsilon_\circ(0)=0$ gives $|\epsilon_\circ(t)|\le Ct^7$, so
$\epsilon_\circ(0)=\epsilon_\circ'(0)=\epsilon_\circ''(0)=0$ and $\epsilon_\circ/t^3$ is $C^\infty$ by
\Cref{lem:cubic-quotient}. By \eqref{eq:contact} and $f_\circ=q-h_c$,
\[
 \frac{Q(f_\circ+\check f_\circ)-2f_\circ\check f_\circ}{Q}
 =q+\check f_\circ-\frac{2\check f_\circ}{2-q}+\frac{h_c(2\check f_\circ-Q)}{Q}
 =\frac{q(2-q-\check f_\circ)+(h_c/q)(2\check f_\circ-Q)}{2-q},
\]
which divided by $2+\varsigma(f_\circ+\check f_\circ)$ is $\gamma$; so
$\Gamma_\varsigma(t^3)/Q_t=\gamma(t)$, a $C^\infty$ function on $[0,1]$, independent of
$\kappa$, with $\gamma\ge0$.

{The comparison density.} Dividing \eqref{eq:base-root} by
$\kappa t^3$ shows $\nu_\kappa(t^3)=t\hat\nu(t)$; as for $z_\circ$, $\hat\nu$ is $C^\infty$
and positive on $[0,1]$, and jointly continuous in $(t,\kappa)$ by the
argument in the proof of \Cref{lem:base-identity} applied to the cubic in
$z$, whose constant term $2(b+\kappa\omega\gamma)h_t/\kappa$ is positive. The cubic gives
$\kappa\hat\nu^2-th_t=2th_t+2(b+\kappa\omega\gamma)h_t/\hat\nu=\mathfrak d>0$ and
$d_\kappa=t^2\mathfrak d$. By \Cref{lem:local-profile}, $\bar m_\kappa$ is symmetric,
and $\frac{\,\mathrm d x}{\,\mathrm d v}=\mathfrak p$ on both halves as for $m_\circ$. The filter
equations in $v$ are those for $\varrho_s,\varrho_\circ$, so $\bar r_s=\varrho_s$ and
$\bar r_\circ=\varrho_\circ$, and these are $C^\infty$ on each closed half. The
functions $w_s=t^3-\frac\kappa s\varrho_s$ and $w_\circ=t^3-\varrho_\circ$ satisfy the equations
of (F) by the computation in the proof of \Cref{lem:filter-continuity}, and
vanish to order seven by the argument used for $\epsilon_\circ$; hence $w_s/t^3$ and
$w_\circ/t^3$ are $C^\infty$ on $[0,1]$. By \Cref{lem:filter-continuity},
$R_s(q)=\bar r_s(2-q)$ and $R_\circ(q)=\bar r_\circ(2-q)$; at $q=t^3$ the point $2-q$
corresponds to $v=2-t$. This gives (i) and the smoothness in (ii).

{Ranges and continuity.} By \Cref{lem:filter}, $f_\circ\ge0$ and
$h_c=q_\circ-f_\circ\ge0$, and $\gamma=\Gamma_\varsigma/Q\ge0$ by \Cref{lem:base-identity};
also $0\le\bar r_s\le\frac s\kappa q$
and $0\le\bar r_\circ\le q$, and by \Cref{lem:right-filters}, $0\le R_s\le\frac s\kappa(2-q)$ and
$0\le R_\circ\le2-q$; these give the ranges. Joint continuity in $(t,\kappa)$
follows from \Cref{lem:filter-continuity}: away from the end $t=0$ of a
side, the functions are continuous functions of $\bar r_s,\bar r_\circ$, $q$
and $1/q$, $1/(2-q)$; at $t=0$, the bounds $0\le w_s,w_\circ\le Ct^7$, uniform on
compact $\kappa$-sets, give the continuity of $1-w_s/t^3$ and $w_\circ/t^3$ with
the value $1$, respectively $0$, at $t=0$. Since $(2-q)^2$ divides $P$,
and $q$ divides $P$ when $l=1$, the polynomials $P'q$, $Pq$, $P'q^l$,
$Pq^{l-1}$, $Pq^l$, $Pq^{l+1}$ are divisible by $q$ and by $2-q$; so all
quotients $\mathscr D(\cdot)$ are polynomials. All denominators in
$\mathfrak b_\sigma,\mathfrak c_\sigma,\mathfrak l$ are positive and continuous: $\hat\nu$, $\mathfrak d$,
$2+s_iqU_i/\kappa+(2-q)\widehat R_i\ge2$, and those of $V,\vartheta_\pm$
(\Cref{lem:range}). This proves (ii).

{Coefficients of the potential.} For a term $\Psi_P$ of $\Psi_{\rm raw}$
write its derivative along a density as $\mathsf b_Pn^2-\mathsf d_P$ by
\eqref{eq:state-flow}, and put $b_P=-\mathsf b_P/\nu$ and
$c_P=(\mathsf b_P\nu^2-\mathsf d_P)/\nu^3$ with $\nu=\nu_\kappa(q)$. For $P(q)h$,
$(P(q)h)'=P'(\kappa n^2-Q)h+P(q^2-2h)$, so $\mathsf b_P=\kappa P'h$ and
$\mathsf b_P\nu^2-\mathsf d_P=P'hd_\kappa+P(q^2-2h)$. With $h=q\vartheta$, $\nu=t\hat\nu$,
$d_\kappa=t^2\mathfrak d$ and $q/t^3=\mathscr Dq$, this is \eqref{eq:regular-h}. For
$\Psi_P=P(q)\mathsf M$, $\mathsf M=u_0^iu_1^j$, with $u_l'=n^2-2u_l-s_lu_l^2$,
\[
 \mathsf b_P=\kappa P'\mathsf M+P(\partial_{u_0}\mathsf M+\partial_{u_1}\mathsf M),\qquad
 \mathsf d_P=P'Q\mathsf M+P\sum_{l'=0}^1\partial_{u_{l'}}\mathsf M\,(2u_{l'}+s_{l'}u_{l'}^2).
\]
With $u_{l'}=q\upsilon_{l'}$, $\mathsf M=q^l\mathsf m$, $\partial_{u_0}\mathsf M+\partial_{u_1}\mathsf M=q^{l-1}\mathsf m_1$
and, by Euler's identity $\sum\upsilon_{l'}\partial_{\upsilon_{l'}}\mathsf m=l\mathsf m$,
$\sum\partial_{u_{l'}}\mathsf M(2u_{l'}+s_{l'}u_{l'}^2)=2lq^l\mathsf m+q^{l+1}\mathsf m_2$. Hence
$\mathsf b_P\nu^2-\mathsf d_P=P'q^l\mathsf md_\kappa+Pq^{l-1}\mathsf m_1\nu^2-2lPq^l\mathsf m-Pq^{l+1}\mathsf m_2$,
and division by $\nu^3=t^3\hat\nu^3$ gives \eqref{eq:regular-u}.

{The spectral coefficients.} With $r_{s_i}=s_iqU_i/\kappa$,
$R_{s_i}=(2-q)\widehat R_i$, $r_\circ=q(1-\vartheta)$ and $R_\circ=(2-q)\widehat R_\circ$,
\[
 s_iQ+\kappa r_{s_i}R_{s_i}=s_iQ(1+U_i\widehat R_i),\qquad
 2r_\circ R_\circ-Q(r_\circ+R_\circ)=Q\bigl[2(1-\vartheta)\widehat R_\circ-q(1-\vartheta)-(2-q)\widehat R_\circ\bigr],
\]
and $Q/(d_\kappa\nu)=(2-t^3)/(\mathfrak d\hat\nu)$ on both sides, since $Q=t^3(2-t^3)$.
Hence, with $a=\xi_0a_{s_0}+\xi_1a_{s_1}+\chi a_\circ$ and
$\eta/\nu=-\tau(2-t^3)/(\mathfrak d\hat\nu)+e$, the quantity $(a-\eta)/\nu$ equals the
first three terms of $\mathfrak b_\sigma$ minus $e$.

{Centering.} The function $\bar Y(q)$ is absolutely continuous on
$[0,2]$, and $\frac{\,\mathrm d\bar Y}{\,\mathrm d q}=(\mathsf b\nu^2-\mathsf d)(\bar Y)/d_\kappa$ is
continuous on $(0,2)$. Hence $F\in C^1(0,2)$ with
\[
 F'(q)=\frac{\mathsf b_{\rm raw}(\bar Y)\nu^2-\mathsf d_{\rm raw}(\bar Y)}{d_\kappa}
 =\frac{\nu^3}{d_\kappa}\sum_P\bar c_P .
\]
By (ii), $\sum_P\bar c_P$ is bounded on each side, and
$\nu^3/d_\kappa=\nu\cdot\nu^2/d_\kappa\le\frac3{2\kappa}\nu\to0$ at $q\to0,2$; so $F'$
extends continuously by $0$, and $F\in C^1[0,2]$. At $Y_-=0$ every term of
$\Psi_{\rm raw}$ vanishes, and at $q=2$ the factor $(2-q)^2$ vanishes, so
$F(0)=F(2)=0$ and $\Psi(Y_\pm)=0$. For $\Psi=\Psi_{\rm raw}-F(q)$,
$\mathsf b_\Psi=\mathsf b_{\rm raw}-\kappa F'$ and $\mathsf d_\Psi=\mathsf d_{\rm raw}-QF'$, so
\[
 -\frac{\mathsf b_\Psi}\nu=\sum_P\Bigl(b_P+\frac{\kappa\hat\nu^2}{\mathfrak d}\bar c_P\Bigr),
 \qquad
 \frac{\mathsf b_\Psi\nu^2-\mathsf d_\Psi}{\nu^3}=\sum_Pc_P-\frac{F'd_\kappa}{\nu^3}=\sum_P(c_P-\bar c_P),
\]
using $\kappa\nu^2-Q=d_\kappa$ and $\nu^2/d_\kappa=\hat\nu^2/\mathfrak d$.

{The criterion.} By \Cref{lem:range}, the normalized states over
$q=q_{\mathrm s}(t)$ are the stated points. By the previous two steps,
$(a-\eta-\mathsf b_\Psi)/\nu=\mathfrak b-e$ and
\[
 \frac{\eta d_\kappa+\tau Q}{\kappa\nu^3}+\frac{\mathsf b_\Psi\nu^2-\mathsf d_\Psi}{\nu^3}
 =\frac{ed_\kappa}{\kappa\nu^2}+\mathfrak c=e\frac{\mathfrak d}{\kappa\hat\nu^2}+\mathfrak c=e(1-\mathfrak l)+\mathfrak c ,
\]
since $\mathfrak d=\kappa\hat\nu^2-t(2-t^3)$. For $0<q<2$, $\nu>0$, and
$\mathcal C(\nu,y)=\nu^3\psi(y/\nu)$ (\Cref{lem:conjugate}); dividing \eqref{eq:master}
by $\nu^3$ gives \eqref{eq:closed-criterion}. The functions $\vartheta\mapsto\mathfrak b$,
$\vartheta\mapsto\mathfrak c$ are affine, $\psi$ is convex, so the left side of
\eqref{eq:closed-criterion} is convex in $\vartheta$ and its maximum over an interval is
attained at an end point. This proves (iii).

{The ends.} At $q\in\{0,2\}$, $\nu_\kappa=Q=0$, $a=0$, and
$\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,0)=-\mathsf d_\Psi(Y)=-\nabla\Psi_{\rm raw}(Y)\cdot\mathsf d(Y)$. At $q=0$,
$Y=Y_-$ and $\mathsf d(Y_-)=0$. At $q=2$, the first component of $\mathsf d$ is
$Q(2)=0$, and the partial derivatives of $\Psi_{\rm raw}$ in $u_0,u_1,h$ contain
the factor $(2-q)^2$. Hence $\mathscr R_\kappa(Y,0)=0$. Finally $F'(0)=F'(2)=0$
and $F(0)=F(2)=0$, so the extension of $F$ by zero is $C^1$ on $\mathbb R$, and
$\Psi\in C^1(\mathbb R^4)$. This proves (iv).

body_md:
\label{lem:jets}
Let $f,g,a,b,C,A,B\in C^N$ on an interval and $0\le j\le N$. Then
\[
 (fg)_j=\sum_{i=0}^jf_ig_{j-i},\qquad
 (1/f)_0=\frac1{f_0},\quad (1/f)_j=-\frac1{f_0}\sum_{i=1}^jf_i(1/f)_{j-i}\quad(f\ne0),
\]
\[
 (e^f)_0=e^{f_0},\quad j(e^f)_j=\sum_{i=1}^jif_i(e^f)_{j-i};\qquad
 z=\sqrt f>0:\quad z_0=\sqrt{f_0},\quad z_j=\frac{f_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}z_iz_{j-i}}{2z_0}\ (j\ge1) .
\]
If $z>0$ solves $z^3-az-b=0$ with $a\ge0$, $b>0$, then $3z^2-a=2a+3b/z>0$,
$z\in C^N$ by the implicit function theorem, and at each point $t$, with
$s_l=\sum_{i=1}^{l-1}z_iz_{l-i}$ and the normalized derivatives $a_i,b_i,z_i$ at $t$,
\[
 z_j=\frac{b_j+\sum_{i=1}^ja_iz_{j-i}-3z_0s_j-\sum_{i=1}^{j-2}z_is_{j-i}}{2a_0+3b_0/z_0}
 \qquad(j\ge1).
\]
If $y'=C+Ay+By^2$, then
$(j+1)y_{j+1}=C_j+\sum_{i=0}^jA_iy_{j-i}+\sum_{i=0}^jB_i(y^2)_{j-i}$ for
$j<N$. Moreover, for every real $c$, with $\tilde C=C+Ac+Bc^2$,
$\tilde A=A+2Bc$, $\varrho_0=y_0-c$ and $\varrho_j=y_j$ ($j\ge1$),
$(j+1)y_{j+1}=\tilde C_j+\sum_{i=0}^j\tilde A_i\varrho_{j-i}+\sum_{i=0}^jB_i(\varrho^2)_{j-i}$,
where $(\varrho^2)_l=\sum_{i=0}^l\varrho_i\varrho_{l-i}$; in particular, for $c=y_0$, $\varrho_0=0$.
Evaluating these formulas in jet enclosures on a set $S$ gives jet
enclosures on $S$.

label: proof:lem:jets
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:jets}
The formulas for products, reciprocals, exponentials and square roots
are the standard recurrences of Taylor arithmetic \cite[Chapter~13]{GriewankWalther}.
For the cubic, $z_0^3=a_0z_0+b_0$ gives $3z_0^2-a_0=2a_0+3b_0/z_0>0$, and
comparing the coefficients of order $j$ in $z^3=az+b$, with
$z^3=z_0^3+3z_0^2u+3z_0u^2+u^3$ for $u=z-z_0$, gives the formula, since the
coefficient of $u^2$ is $s_j$ and that of $u^3$ is $\sum_{i=1}^{j-2}z_is_{j-i}$. The
equation $y'=F$ gives $(j+1)y_{j+1}=F_j$, and $C+Ay+By^2=\tilde C+\tilde A(y-c)+B(y-c)^2$.
Each formula expresses the jet at $t$ through jets at the same $t$ (and $c$,
which may be taken equal to $y(t)$); so evaluation in enclosures valid on
$S$ gives enclosures valid on $S$.

label: lem:cubic-root
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cubic-root}
For $a\ge0$ and $b>0$ the equation $z^3-az-b=0$ has a unique positive root
$z(a,b)$, and $\max\{\sqrt a,\sqrt[3]b\}\le z(a,b)\le\sqrt a+\sqrt[3]b$. The
root increases in $a$ and in $b$. If $X$ is an interval containing
$z(a,b)$ with $3x^2-a>0$ on $X$ and $m\in X$, then
$z(a,b)\in m-(m^3-am-b)/(3X^2-a)$, the quotient being taken over $X$.
head: environment
name: The positive cubic root

label: proof:lem:cubic-root
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:cubic-root}
The positive roots are the zeros of $z^2-a-b/z$, which increases strictly
from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$ on $(0,\infty)$. At the root, $z^3=az+b\ge b$ and
$z^2=a+b/z\ge a$. If $z>\sqrt a+\sqrt[3]b$, then
$z^2-a>2\sqrt a\sqrt[3]b+\sqrt[3]{b^2}\ge\sqrt[3]{b^2}$ and
$z(z^2-a)>\sqrt[3]b\cdot\sqrt[3]{b^2}=b$, which is impossible. Implicit
differentiation gives $\partial_az=z/(3z^2-a)>0$ and
$\partial_bz=1/(3z^2-a)>0$. Finally, by the mean value theorem,
$m^3-am-b=(3\xi^2-a)(m-z)$ for some $\xi$ between $m$ and $z$, so
$\xi\in X$ and $z=m-(m^3-am-b)/(3\xi^2-a)$.

label: lem:quadrature
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:quadrature}
Let $f\in C^N([c-h,c+h])$, $N\ge2$, and $M_N\ge\sup|f_N|$ on
$[c-h,c+h]$. Then
\[
 \Bigl|\int_{c-h}^{c+h}f(t)\,\mathrm d t
 -\sum_{\substack{0\le j<N\\j\text{ even}}}\frac{2h^{j+1}}{j+1}f_j(c)\Bigr|
 \le\frac{2h^{N+1}}{N+1}M_N .
\]
head: environment
name: Quadrature

label: proof:lem:quadrature
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:quadrature}
By Taylor's formula with Lagrange remainder,
$f(t)=\sum_{j<N}f_j(c)(t-c)^j+f_N(\xi_t)(t-c)^N$ with $|f_N(\xi_t)|\le M_N$.
The integral of $(t-c)^j$ over $[c-h,c+h]$ is $2h^{j+1}/(j+1)$ for even
$j$ and zero for odd $j$, and $\int|t-c|^N=2h^{N+1}/(N+1)$.

label: lem:flow-step
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:flow-step}
Let $F(t,y)=C(t)+A(t)y+B(t)y^2$ with $C,A,B\in C^{N+1}([a,a+h])$, $N\ge1$.
Let $Y_0$ be an interval, $m\in\mathbb R$, $r\ge\sup_{y\in Y_0}|y-m|$, and let
$Y$ be a closed interval such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:picard}
 y_0+\theta F(t,y)\in Y\qquad\text{for all }y_0\in\operatorname{hull}(Y_0\cup\{m\}),\
 \theta\in[0,h],\ t\in[a,a+h],\ y\in Y .
\end{equation}
Then for every $y_0\in\operatorname{hull}(Y_0\cup\{m\})$ the solution of $y'=F(t,y)$,
$y(a)=y_0$, exists on $[a,a+h]$ and stays in $Y$. Let $z$ be the solution
with $z(a)=m$, $R\ge\sup_{[a,a+h]}|z_{N+1}|$ and
$L\ge\sup\{A(t)+2B(t)y:t\in[a,a+h],y\in Y\}$. Then every solution with
$y(a)\in Y_0$ satisfies, for $0\le v\le h$,
\[
 \Bigl|y(a+v)-\sum_{j=0}^Nz_j(a)v^j\Bigr|\le Rv^{N+1}+re^{Lv},\qquad y(a+v)\in Y .
\]
The number $R$ may be taken as an upper bound for the modulus of the
interval obtained from either recurrence of \Cref{lem:jets} with the jet
enclosures of $C,A,B$ on $[a,a+h]$ and with $y_0$ replaced by $Y$,
respectively with $\varrho_0=0$ and $c$ replaced by $Y$.
head: environment
name: A validated flow step

label: proof:lem:flow-step
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:flow-step}
Let $\pi_Y$ be the nearest-point projection onto $Y$. The equation
$\tilde y'=F(t,\pi_Y(\tilde y))$ has a bounded globally Lipschitz
right-hand side and therefore a solution on $[a,a+h]$.
For fixed $t$, condition \eqref{eq:picard} places every value
$y_0+(t-a)F(\tau,\pi_Y(\tilde y(\tau)))$, $a\le\tau\le t$, in $Y$.
Their average is $\tilde y(t)$ and also belongs to the interval $Y$.
Thus the projection is inactive, and $\tilde y$ is the unique solution
of the original equation on the whole step.

Taylor's formula gives
$z(a+v)=\sum_{j\le N}z_j(a)v^j+z_{N+1}(\xi)v^{N+1}$ with $\xi\in[a,a+v]$. At every
$t\in[a,a+h]$ the normalized derivatives of $z$ satisfy the recurrence of
\Cref{lem:jets} with the normalized derivatives of $C,A,B$ at $t$ and
with $z(t)\in Y$ (in the shifted form with $c=z(t)\in Y$); by \Cref{lem:jets}
the interval recurrence with the enclosures on $[a,a+h]$ and $Y$ contains
$z_{N+1}(t)$, which justifies the
choice of $R$. For a solution $y$ with $y(a)\in Y_0$, the difference
$e=y-z$ satisfies $e'=F(t,y)-F(t,z)=[A+B(y+z)]e=[A+2B\tfrac{y+z}2]e$, and
$\frac{y+z}2\in Y$ by convexity, so $A+B(y+z)\le L$ and
$|e(a+v)|=|e(a)|\exp\int_a^{a+v}[A+B(y+z)]\le re^{Lv}$, for either sign of $L$.

label: lem:cubic-quotient
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cubic-quotient}
Let $f\in C^{N+4}([0,\beta])$ with $f(0)=f'(0)=f''(0)=0$, and let
$g(t)=f(t)/t^3$ for $t>0$, $g(0)=f_3(0)$. Then $g\in C^{N+1}([0,\beta])$,
\[
 g_j(t)=\frac{(j+3)!}{2\,j!}\int_0^1(1-v)^2v^jf_{j+3}(vt)\,\mathrm d v\qquad(0\le j\le N+1),
\]
the weight $\frac{(j+3)!}{2j!}(1-v)^2v^j$ being nonnegative with integral one, and
for $0\le t\le\beta$ and $j\le N$
\[
 g_j(t)\in\sum_{l=j}^N\binom ljf_{l+3}(0)t^{l-j}
 +\binom{N+1}jt^{N+1-j}\,\mathrm{hull}\,f_{N+4}([0,\beta]) .
\]
head: environment
name: Removing a cubic zero

label: proof:lem:cubic-quotient
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:cubic-quotient}
Taylor's formula with integral remainder at $0$ gives
$f(t)=\frac{t^3}2\int_0^1(1-v)^2f'''(vt)\,\mathrm d v$, so
$g(t)=\frac12\int_0^1(1-v)^2f'''(vt)\,\mathrm d v$, and differentiation under the
integral gives $g^{(j)}(t)=\frac12\int_0^1(1-v)^2v^jf^{(j+3)}(vt)\,\mathrm d v$, which
is the formula, with $\int_0^1(1-v)^2v^j\,\mathrm d v=2j!/(j+3)!$. Hence $g_l(0)=f_{l+3}(0)$
and $g_{N+1}(t)$ lies in the hull of the values of $f_{N+4}$ on $[0,t]$.
Taylor's formula for $g_j$ at $0$ of order $N-j$, whose remainder
coefficient is $\binom{N+1}jg_{N+1}(\xi)$, gives the last claim.

label: lem:translation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:translation}
Let $p(q)=\sum_{j=0}^na_jq^j$ and $c\in\mathbb R$. Starting with $b_j=a_j$, for
$r=n-1,\dots,0$ replace $b_j$ by $b_j+cb_{j+1}$ for $j=r,\dots,n-1$ in
this order. Then $b_j=\sum_{i=j}^n\binom ija_ic^{i-j}$ and
$p(q)=\sum_jb_j(q-c)^j$.
head: environment
name: Polynomial translation

label: proof:lem:translation
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:translation}
After the pass with index $r$, the invariant is
$b_j=a_j$ for $j<r$ and
$b_j=\sum_{i=j}^n\binom{i-r}{j-r}a_ic^{i-j}$ for $j\ge r$.
It holds before the first pass with $r=n$. Processing $j$ in increasing
order uses the previous-pass value of $b_{j+1}$; Pascal's identity
therefore proves the invariant at the next pass, including $j=r$.
At $r=0$ it is the stated coefficient formula. The expansion of
$q^i=((q-c)+c)^i$ gives the polynomial identity.

label: lem:box-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:box-bound}
Let $\Phi\in C^2$ on $\mathsf B=I_U\times I_T\times I_t$, let $(c_U,c_T)\in I_U\times I_T$,
$t_c\in I_t$, and $d_U=I_U-c_U$, $d_T=I_T-c_T$, $d_t=I_t-t_c$ as intervals.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(0)] $\max_{\mathsf B}\Phi$ is at most the upper end of any enclosure of $\Phi$
on $\mathsf B$.
\item If $\Phi_U\ge0$ on $\mathsf B$, then $\max_{\mathsf B}\Phi$ is attained on
$U=\sup I_U$; if $\Phi_U\le0$, on $U=\inf I_U$; likewise for $T$.
\item With $\beta_0=\Phi(c,t_c)+\Phi_t(c,t_c)d_t+\frac12\max\{0,\sup_{I_t}\Phi_{tt}(c,\cdot)\}d_t^2$,
$\Phi(c,t)\le\sup\beta_0$ for $t\in I_t$, where $c=(c_U,c_T)$; hence
$\beta=\min\{\sup\beta_0,\sup\Phi(c,I_t)\}$, with $\Phi(c,I_t)$ any enclosure of
$\Phi(c,\cdot)$ on $I_t$, satisfies $\beta\ge\Phi(c,t)$ for $t\in I_t$.
\item Let $\beta\ge\Phi(c,t)$ for $t\in I_t$, let $G_U,G_T$ enclose
$\Phi_U(c,t),\Phi_T(c,t)$ for $t\in I_t$, and $H$ enclose the Hessian in $(U,T)$
on $\mathsf B$. Then $\max_{\mathsf B}\Phi$ is at most each of
\[
\begin{gathered}
 \sup\Bigl(\beta+G_Ud_U+G_Td_T+\tfrac12\sup H_{UU}\,d_U^2+H_{UT}d_Ud_T+\tfrac12\sup H_{TT}\,d_T^2\Bigr),\\
 \sup\bigl(\beta+\Phi_U(\mathsf B)d_U+\Phi_T(\mathsf B)d_T\bigr).
\end{gathered}
\]
\item If moreover $\alpha_U=-\sup H_{UU}>0$, $\alpha_T=-\sup H_{TT}>0$,
$\gamma=\sup|H_{UT}|$, $\alpha_U\alpha_T>\gamma^2$ and $g_U=\sup|G_U|$,
$g_T=\sup|G_T|$, then
$\max_{\mathsf B}\Phi\le\beta+\frac{\alpha_Tg_U^2+\alpha_Ug_T^2+2\gamma g_Ug_T}{2(\alpha_U\alpha_T-\gamma^2)}$.
If $I_U$ is a point and $\alpha_T>0$, then $\max_{\mathsf B}\Phi\le\beta+g_T^2/(2\alpha_T)$, and
symmetrically; if both $I_U,I_T$ are points, $\max_{\mathsf B}\Phi\le\beta$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Upper bounds on a box

label: proof:lem:box-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:box-bound}
(0) is the definition of an enclosure. (i) For fixed $(T,t)$, $\Phi$ is
monotone in $U$. (ii) Taylor's formula in $t$ at fixed $c$ gives
$\Phi(c,t)=\Phi(c,t_c)+\Phi_t(c,t_c)(t-t_c)+\frac12\Phi_{tt}(c,\xi)(t-t_c)^2$ with $\xi\in I_t$,
which is at most
$\Phi(c,t_c)+\Phi_t(c,t_c)(t-t_c)+\frac12\max\{0,\sup_{I_t}\Phi_{tt}(c,\cdot)\}(t-t_c)^2$, and
$t-t_c\in d_t$.
(iii) For fixed $t$, Taylor's formula in $(U,T)$ at $c$ with the Hessian at
an intermediate point, and the bounds $\Phi_{UU}(U-c_U)^2\le\sup H_{UU}(U-c_U)^2$,
$\Phi_{TT}(T-c_T)^2\le\sup H_{TT}(T-c_T)^2$, give the first bound; the mean value
theorem gives the second. (iv) With $v_U=|U-c_U|$, $v_T=|T-c_T|$, the
first expansion gives
$\Phi-\beta\le g_Uv_U+g_Tv_T-\frac12(\alpha_Uv_U^2-2\gamma v_Uv_T+\alpha_Tv_T^2)$. The matrix
$M=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}\alpha_U&-\gamma\\-\gamma&\alpha_T\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ is
positive definite, and the maximum of $g\cdot v-\frac12v^TMv$ over $v\in\mathbb R^2$
is $\frac12g^TM^{-1}g$, which is the displayed bound. If $I_U$ is a point,
$v_U=0$ and $\max_{v_T\in\mathbb R}(g_Tv_T-\frac12\alpha_Tv_T^2)=g_T^2/(2\alpha_T)$; the case of a point
$I_T$ is symmetric; if both are points, $\Phi(U,T,t)=\Phi(c,t)\le\beta$.

label: proof:thm:primal-map
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:primal-map}
{The coordinate.} Put $B=\|D\|_\infty$. The function $X$ is
absolutely continuous and strictly increasing on $[0,2]$, with
$X(q_2)-X(q_1)\ge(q_2-q_1)/B$, and has finite values $X(0),X(2)$. Its
inverse $q$, extended by $0$ on $(-\infty,X(0)]$ and by $2$ on
$[X(2),\infty)$, is Lipschitz with constant $B$. Let $\mathsf N\subset(0,2)$ be
the null set where $X$ is not differentiable with $X'=1/D$; since $X$ is
absolutely continuous, $X(\mathsf N)$ is a null set. At every $x\in(X(0),X(2))$
outside $X(\mathsf N)$ at which $q$ is differentiable, differentiation of
$X(q(x))=x$ gives $q'(x)=D(q(x))$. By the definition of $m$,
$q'=D(q)=\kappa m-Q(q)$ almost everywhere on $(X(0),X(2))$, and outside this
interval $q'=0=\kappa m-Q(q)$. The change of variables for the absolutely
continuous increasing $X$ gives
$\int_{X(0)}^{X(2)}\phi(q(x))\,\mathrm d x=\int_0^2\phi(p)D(p)^{-1}\,\mathrm d p$ for measurable
$\phi\ge0$, which proves \eqref{eq:primal-masses}; also $m\le(B+1)/\kappa$.

{The ground state.} Put $u(x)=\exp\int_0^x(1-q)$. Then $u>0$,
$u'=(1-q)u$ is locally absolutely continuous, and
$u''=(-q'+(1-q)^2)u=(1-\kappa m)u$ almost everywhere, since
$(1-q)^2=1-Q(q)$. On $(-\infty,X(0)]$, $u=c_-e^x$, and on $[X(2),\infty)$,
$u=c_+e^{-x}$; so $u,u'\in L^2$ and $u\in H^1$. The computation in the proof
of \Cref{thm:ground}, which uses only $u>0$, $|u'/u|\le1$ and
$-u''+u=\kappa mu$, gives for every $f\in H^1$
\[
 \int(f'^2+f^2)-\kappa\int mf^2=\int\Bigl(f'-\frac{u'}uf\Bigr)^2\ge0,
\]
with equality for $f=u$. For the feature operator $\mathcal K_m$,
$\langle \mathcal K_mf,f\rangle_\mathcal H=\int m(x)\langle f,v_x\rangle_\mathcal H^2\,\mathrm d x=2\int mf^2$ by
\Cref{lem:features}(i), so
$\lambda_0(K_m)=\|\mathcal K_m\|=\sup_{f\ne0}2\int mf^2/\|f\|_\mathcal H^2$. The displayed
inequality gives $\lambda_0(K_m)\le2/\kappa$, and equality at $f=u$ gives
$\lambda_0(K_m)\ge2/\kappa$. Hence $\kappa(m)=\kappa$. The ground state $u_m$ of
\Cref{thm:ground} also gives equality in this identity, with the same
$\kappa$, so $u=cu_m$ and the ground coordinate of $m$ is $1-u'/u=q$.

label: lem:contraction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:contraction}
Let $\varrho>0$, let $F$ be continuously differentiable on the cube
$K=\{\|a\|_\infty\le\varrho\}$ in $\mathbb R^d$, and let $C$ be a $d\times d$ matrix with
\[
 \theta_F:=\sup_{a\in K}\|I-C\,DF(a)\|_\infty<1,
 \qquad \varepsilon_F:=\|CF(0)\|_\infty,\qquad \varepsilon_F+\theta_F\varrho\le\varrho ,
\]
where $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the maximum norm and the induced matrix norm. Then
$F$ has exactly one zero $a_*$ in $K$; the iterates $a^{(0)}=0$,
$a^{(j+1)}=a^{(j)}-CF(a^{(j)})$ lie in $K$, and
$\|a^{(j)}-a_*\|_\infty\le\theta_F^j\varepsilon_F/(1-\theta_F)$.

name: Exact feasibility by contraction

label: proof:lem:contraction
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:contraction}
For $G(a)=a-CF(a)$, the mean value inequality gives
$\|G(a)-G(b)\|_\infty\le\theta_F\|a-b\|_\infty$ and
$\|G(a)\|_\infty\le\varepsilon_F+\theta_F\varrho\le\varrho$ on $K$.
The contraction theorem \cite[Theorem~2.1]{TeschlODE} gives a unique
fixed point, the stated iterates, and the error bound, since
$\|G(0)\|_\infty=\varepsilon_F$.
Moreover, $\|I-CDF(0)\|_\infty<1$ makes $CDF(0)$ invertible by a
Neumann series; hence $C$ is invertible, and fixed points of $G$ are
exactly zeros of $F$.

label: prop:primal-jacobian
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:primal-jacobian}
Let $\phi_0,\dots,\phi_d$ be polynomials, $\phi_a=\phi_0+\sum_ia_i\phi_i$,
$\kappa>0$, and let $m_a$ be the density of \Cref{thm:primal-map} with
the symmetric speed $D_a(t^3)=t^2e^{\phi_a(t)}$, $D_a(2-q)=D_a(q)$. On the
left side write $Q=t^3(2-t^3)$, $X_a'(t)=3e^{-\phi_a(t)}$ for $\,\mathrm d x/\,\mathrm d t$, and
$n_a=t\hat n_a$, $\hat n_a=\sqrt{(e^{\phi_a}+t(2-t^3))/\kappa}$, for $\sqrt{m_a}$. Then the
masses, the energy, $H_{m_a}(s)$ for $s>0$, and $S(m_a)$ are continuously
differentiable in $a\in\mathbb R^d$, with
\begin{align}
 \partial_i\int m_a&=-\frac2\kappa\int_0^1X_a'Q\phi_i\,\mathrm d t,
 &\partial_i\int\sqrt{m_a}&=-\int_0^1X_a'\frac{D_a+2Q}{\kappa n_a}\phi_i\,\mathrm d t,
 \label{eq:primal-jacobian-mass}\\
 \partial_iH_{m_a}(s)&=-2\int_0^1X_a'\frac{sQ/\kappa+r_sR_s}{2+r_s+R_s}\phi_i\,\mathrm d t,
 &\partial_iS(m_a)&=\int_0^1X_a'\bigl[2r_\circ R_\circ-Q(r_\circ+R_\circ)\bigr]\phi_i\,\mathrm d t,
 \label{eq:primal-jacobian-spec}
\end{align}
where $r_s,r_\circ$ are the left filters of $m_a$ and $R_s,R_\circ$ its right
filters, as functions of $t$ on the left side, and $D_a=t^2e^{\phi_a}$;
also $\int m_a^{j/2}=2\int_0^1X_a'n_a^j\,\mathrm d t$ for $j=1,2,3$. Moreover $E(m_a)\le E(m_0)\exp\bigl(\|a\|_\infty\sum_i\|\phi_i\|_\infty\bigr)$, the
norms being taken on $[0,1]$.
head: environment
name: Derivatives of the primal family

label: proof:prop:primal-jacobian
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:prop:primal-jacobian}
{The family.} On a cube $\|a\|_\infty\le\varrho$, $c\le e^{\phi_a}\le C$ on
$[0,1]$ for constants $0<c\le C$. Hence $D_a\le C$,
$\int_0^2D_a^{-1}\,\mathrm d q=2\int_0^13t^2(t^2e^{\phi_a})^{-1}\,\mathrm d t=2\int_0^1X_a'\,\mathrm d t<\infty$, and
\Cref{thm:primal-map} applies; $m_a$ is symmetric, $\sqrt{m_a}=n_a$ and
$\,\mathrm d x=X_a'\,\mathrm d t$ on the left half. Moreover $n_a$ is a comparison profile at
$\kappa$ (\Cref{def:comparison-profile}): with $\nu=n_a$ and $d=D_a$,
$\nu^2/d=\hat n_a^2e^{-\phi_a}$, $Q/(d\nu)=(2-t^3)/(e^{\phi_a}\hat n_a)$ and
$\nu^3/Q=\hat n_a^3/(2-t^3)$ are bounded on the cube.

{Masses and energy.} By \eqref{eq:primal-masses} and symmetry,
$\int m_a^{j/2}=2\int_0^1X_a'n_a^j\,\mathrm d t$ for $j=1,2,3$. The integrands are
$C^\infty$ in $(t,a)$, and $\partial_iX_a'=-X_a'\phi_i$,
$\partial_i(n_a^2)=t^2e^{\phi_a}\phi_i/\kappa=D_a\phi_i/\kappa$, so
\[
 \partial_i(X_a'n_a^j)=X_a'n_a^j\Bigl[-1+\frac{jD_a}{2(D_a+Q)}\Bigr]\phi_i ,
\]
using $n_a^2=(D_a+Q)/\kappa$. For $j=2$ this is $-X_a'Q\phi_i/\kappa$; for $j=1$ it is
$-X_a'n_a\frac{D_a+2Q}{2(D_a+Q)}\phi_i=-X_a'\frac{D_a+2Q}{2\kappa n_a}\phi_i$, where
$(D_a+2Q)/n_a=t(e^{\phi_a}+2t(2-t^3))/\hat n_a$ is bounded. Differentiation under
the integral, justified by these bounded continuous derivatives, gives
\eqref{eq:primal-jacobian-mass}. For $j=3$ the bracket equals
$(D_a-2Q)/(2(D_a+Q))\in[-1,\frac12]$; along $\lambda\mapsto\lambda a$,
\[
 \Bigl|\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d\lambda}\log(X_{\lambda a}'n_{\lambda a}^3)\Bigr|
 \le\Bigl|\sum_ia_i\phi_i\Bigr|\le\|a\|_\infty\sum_i\|\phi_i\|_\infty ,
\]
and integration over $\lambda\in[0,1]$ and then over $t$ gives the energy bound.

{Filters.} In the variable $v\in[0,2]$ of \Cref{lem:regular-criterion}
(with $t=v$ or $t=2-v$), the filter $r_s$ of $m_a$ solves
$\frac{\,\mathrm d r}{\,\mathrm d v}=X_a'(sn_a^2-2r-r^2)$, $r(0)=0$, with values in
$[0,\frac s\kappa\cdot2]$. On each closed half the right-hand side is $C^\infty$ in
$(v,r,a)$; by differentiable dependence on parameters
\cite[Theorem~2.11]{TeschlODE}, applied on $[0,1]$ and then on $[1,2]$ with
the initial value at $v=1$ obtained from the first half, $r_s$ is
continuously differentiable in $a$, uniformly in $v$. The same holds for
$r_\circ$. By symmetry, the right filters at $q$ are the left filters at
$2-q$, that is, at $2-v$.

{Spectral derivatives.} Fix $a$, $i$ and $\epsilon\ne0$ small, and apply
\Cref{lem:comparison-general} with the comparison profile $\nu=n_a$ (density
$m_a$) and $m=m_{a+\epsilon e_i}$, whose ground parameter is $\kappa$. In the
ground coordinate $q$ of $m$, $\,\mathrm d x=\,\mathrm d q/D_{a+\epsilon e_i}(q)$ on its support, and
$n^2-\nu(q)^2=(D_{a+\epsilon e_i}(q)-D_a(q))/\kappa$; outside the support both
vanish. Hence
\[
 \frac{H_{m_{a+\epsilon e_i}}(s)-H_{m_a}(s)}\epsilon
 =\int_0^2a_s^{(a)}\bigl(q,r_s^{(a+\epsilon e_i)}(q)\bigr)
 \frac{1-e^{-\epsilon\phi_i}}{\kappa\epsilon}\,\mathrm d q ,
\]
where $a_s^{(a)}$ is the coefficient of the profile $n_a$, $r_s^{(a')}(q)$ is
the filter of $m_{a'}$ at its ground coordinate $q$, and $\phi_i$ is
evaluated at the $t$ corresponding to $q$; here
$(D_{a+\epsilon e_i}-D_a)/D_{a+\epsilon e_i}=1-e^{-\epsilon\phi_i}$. As $\epsilon\to0$,
$r_s^{(a+\epsilon e_i)}\to r_s^{(a)}$ uniformly, $(1-e^{-\epsilon\phi_i})/\epsilon\to\phi_i$
boundedly, $a_s^{(a)}(q,\cdot)$ is continuous, and
$|a_s^{(a)}|\le sQ/(2D_a)$ is integrable in $q$. Dominated convergence gives
\[
 \partial_iH_{m_a}(s)=\frac1\kappa\int_0^2a_s^{(a)}(q,r_s)\phi_i\,\mathrm d q
 =-\int_0^2\frac{sQ/\kappa+r_sR_s}{D_a(2+r_s+R_s)}\phi_i\,\mathrm d q ,
\]
and the substitution $\,\mathrm d q/D_a=X_a'\,\mathrm d t$ on each half, with the symmetry
that exchanges $r_s$ and $R_s$, gives \eqref{eq:primal-jacobian-spec}. The
same argument with $a_\circ$, for which $a_\circ/\kappa=[2r_\circ R_\circ-Q(r_\circ+R_\circ)]/(2D_a)$,
gives the formula for $\partial_iS$. The right-hand sides are continuous in $a$,
since the filters are, with the integrable majorants above; hence the
partial derivatives are continuous and the functions are continuously
differentiable.
