body_md:
\label{lem:gradients}
For $s>0$ let $V_L$ be the function $V_s$ of \Cref{lem:filter}(ii) for $m$,
$V_R(x)=V_L(-x)$, $u_L=e^xV_L$, $u_R=e^{-x}V_R$, $W=u_L'u_R-u_Lu_R'$ and
$G_s(x,y)=u_L(\min(x,y))u_R(\max(x,y))/W$. Let $u$ be the ground state of
$m$ (\Cref{thm:ground}). For real $h\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ write $\mathcal K_h$ as in
\Cref{sec:embedding}, and put $W_2(x)=\int e^{-2|x-y|}m(y)\,\mathrm d y$. Let
$v_1,\dots,v_d\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ and $m_\epsilon=m+\sum_l\epsilon_lv_l$ for
$\epsilon\in\mathbb R^d$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item There is $\epsilon_0>0$ such that $m_\epsilon\ge0$ for $|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$, and
$(\epsilon,s)\mapsto H_{m_\epsilon}(s)$ is real analytic on
$\{|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0\}\times(0,\infty)$. For $d=1$, $v=v_1$ and $s>0$,
\[
 \partial_\epsilon H_{m_\epsilon}(s)\big|_{\epsilon=0}=s\int G_s(x,x)v,\qquad
 \partial_\epsilon\partial_sH_{m_\epsilon}(s)\big|_{\epsilon=0}
 =\int\bigl[G_s(x,x)+s\partial_sG_s(x,x)\bigr]v,
\]
with $\partial_sG_s(x,x)=-\int G_s(x,y)^2m(y)\,\mathrm d y$ and
$0<G_s(x,y)\le\frac12e^{-|x-y|}$.
\item The function $\epsilon\mapsto\kappa(m_\epsilon)$ is continuously differentiable
near $0$, and for $d=1$,
$\partial_\epsilon\kappa(m_\epsilon)|_{\epsilon=0}=-\kappa\int u^2v/\int u^2m$.
\item For $d=1$, $\partial_\epsilon\operatorname{tr} K_{m_\epsilon}^2|_{\epsilon=0}=2\int W_2v$.
\item The functions $G_s(x,x)$, $\partial_sG_s(x,x)$, $u^2$ and $W_2$ are
continuous on $\mathbb R$, and as $x\to+\infty$, with constants depending on $s$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 G_s(x,x)&=\tfrac12+C_se^{-2x}+o(n),&\qquad
 \partial_sG_s(x,x)&=C_s'e^{-2x}+o(n),\\
 u(x)^2&=C_ue^{-2x}+o(n),&\qquad
 W_2(x)&=C_2e^{-2x}+o(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{enumerate}

name: Gradients of the observations

label: proof:lem:gradients
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:lem:gradients}
{Solutions.} Let $s>0$ and $r_s$ be the filter of $m$. By
\Cref{lem:filter}(ii), $V_L$ is $C^1$ with locally absolutely continuous
derivative and $V_L''+2V_L'=smV_L$, so $-u_L''+(1+sm)u_L=0$ almost
everywhere, and $u_L'/u_L=1+r_s$. Since $m$ is even, $u_R(x)=u_L(-x)$
solves the same equation, and $u_R'/u_R(x)=-(1+r_s(-x))$. Hence $W$ is
constant, $u_L'/u_L\ge1$ and $-u_R'/u_R\ge1$; so $u_L(y)\le u_L(x)e^{y-x}$
for $y\le x$, $u_R(y)\le u_R(x)e^{x-y}$ for $y\ge x$, and, evaluating $W$ at
$x$, $W=u_Lu_R(u_L'/u_L-u_R'/u_R)\ge2u_L(x)u_R(x)$. Hence for $y\le x$,
$0<G_s(x,y)=u_L(y)u_R(x)/W\le u_L(y)/(2u_L(x))\le\frac12e^{-(x-y)}$, and, since
$G_s(x,y)=G_s(y,x)$, the same bound holds for $y\ge x$. By the substitution
$y\mapsto-y$ in the equation of \Cref{lem:filter}(ii),
$V_R(x)=1+\frac s2\int_x^\infty(1-e^{-2(y-x)})m(y)V_R(y)\,\mathrm d y$, so
$1\le V_R\le e^{s\int m/2}$ and $|V_R(x)-1|\le\frac s2e^{s\int m/2}\int_x^\infty m$.

{(i).} Let $\mathsf S=\bigcup_l\operatorname{supp} v_l$, a compact set, and
$c_{\mathsf S}=\min_{\mathsf S}m>0$ ($m$ is continuous and positive). For
$|\epsilon|\sum_l\|v_l\|_\infty<c_{\mathsf S}/2$, $m_\epsilon\ge c_{\mathsf S}/2$ on $\mathsf S$ and
$m_\epsilon=m$ elsewhere; this defines $\epsilon_0$. By
\Cref{lem:features}(ii),(iii), the operators $\mathcal K_m$ and $\mathcal K_{v_l}$ are
trace class, $A(\epsilon,s)=\frac s2(\mathcal K_m+\sum_l\epsilon_l\mathcal K_{v_l})=\frac s2\mathcal K_{m_\epsilon}$
is positive for $|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$, $s\ge0$, and its nonzero eigenvalues are those
of $\frac s2K_{m_\epsilon}$, so $H_{m_\epsilon}(s)=\log\det(I+A(\epsilon,s))$. The trace-class determinant is analytic in its operator argument,
and its logarithmic derivative at an invertible $I+A$ is
$D\log\det(I+A)[B]=\operatorname{tr}((I+A)^{-1}B)$
\cite[Chapter~3]{SimonTrace}. Here $A(\epsilon,s)$ is a polynomial
family in trace norm and $\det(I+A)>0$ for real $|\epsilon|<\epsilon_0$
and $s\ge0$, so $H_{m_\epsilon}(s)$ is jointly real analytic.
With $d=1$ and
$B=\frac s2\mathcal K_v$,
\[
 \partial_\epsilon H|_{\epsilon=0}=\frac s2\operatorname{tr}\Bigl[\Bigl(I+\frac s2\mathcal K_m\Bigr)^{-1}\mathcal K_v\Bigr]
 =\frac s2\int v(x)\Bigl\langle\Bigl(I+\frac s2\mathcal K_m\Bigr)^{-1}v_x,v_x\Bigr\rangle_\mathcal H\,\mathrm d x ,
\]
the trace commuting with the Bochner integral (\Cref{lem:features}(ii)).

Fix $x$ and put $\mathsf g=\sqrt2G_s(\cdot,x)$. By the bounds above and
$|u_L'/u_L|,|u_R'/u_R|\le1+\|r_s\|_\infty$, $\mathsf g$ and $\mathsf g'$ are bounded by
multiples of $e^{-|t-x|}$, so $\mathsf g\in\mathcal H$. On $(-\infty,x)$ and on
$(x,\infty)$, $\mathsf g$ is a multiple of $u_L$, respectively $u_R$, so
$-\mathsf g''+(1+sm)\mathsf g=0$ there; $\mathsf g$ is continuous at $x$, and
$\mathsf g'(x+)-\mathsf g'(x-)=\sqrt2(u_Lu_R'-u_L'u_R)(x)/W=-\sqrt2$. Consequently
$-\mathsf g''+(1+sm)\mathsf g=\sqrt2\delta_x$ distributionally.
Its weak form is
\[
 \langle \mathsf g,h\rangle_\mathcal H+s\int m\mathsf gh=\sqrt2h(x)=\langle v_x,h\rangle_\mathcal H
 \qquad(h\in\mathcal H).
\]
Here the extension from smooth test functions follows by density and
the bound $|\int m\mathsf gh|\le\|m\|_1\|\mathsf g\|_\infty\|h\|_\infty$.
By \Cref{lem:features}(i),(ii), this is
$(I+\tfrac s2\mathcal K_m)\mathsf g=v_x$.
Therefore
$\langle (I+\frac s2\mathcal K_m)^{-1}v_x,v_x\rangle_\mathcal H=\langle \mathsf g,v_x\rangle_\mathcal H=\sqrt2\mathsf g(x)=2G_s(x,x)$,
which gives the first formula. Since
$\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm d s}(I+\frac s2\mathcal K_m)^{-1}=-(I+\frac s2\mathcal K_m)^{-1}\frac12\mathcal K_m(I+\frac s2\mathcal K_m)^{-1}$,
\[
 \partial_s\bigl(2G_s(x,x)\bigr)=-\tfrac12\langle \mathcal K_m\mathsf g,\mathsf g\rangle_\mathcal H
 =-\int m\mathsf g^2=-2\int G_s(\cdot,x)^2m .
\]
Hence $|\partial_sG_s(x,x)|\le\frac14\int m$, and by the mean value theorem the
difference quotients of $s\mapsto sG_s(x,x)$ are bounded uniformly in $x$
on compact $s$-intervals; since $v$ has compact support, dominated
convergence gives
$\partial_s\partial_\epsilon H|_{\epsilon=0}=\int[G_s(x,x)+s\partial_sG_s(x,x)]v$, and for the real
analytic $H$ this is $\partial_\epsilon\partial_sH|_{\epsilon=0}$.

{(ii).} On the fixed space $\mathcal H$, the family
$\mathcal K_{m_\epsilon}=\mathcal K_m+\sum_l\epsilon_l\mathcal K_{v_l}$
is analytic in trace norm by \Cref{lem:features}(ii).
The eigenvalue $\lambda_0=2/\kappa$ is simple and isolated
(\Cref{thm:ground}). Analytic perturbation theory for an isolated simple
eigenvalue \cite[Chapter~VII, \S1]{Kato1995} gives a differentiable
eigenvalue and eigenprojection; the spectral gap ensures that this
branch remains the largest eigenvalue for small real $\epsilon$.
Its normalized eigenvector at $0$ is $e=u/\|u\|_\mathcal H$, so
\[
 D\lambda_0(m)[v]=\langle \mathcal K_ve,e\rangle_\mathcal H
 =\frac{2\int vu^2}{\|u\|_\mathcal H^2},\qquad
 \|u\|_\mathcal H^2=\kappa\int mu^2.
\]
Differentiating $\kappa=2/\lambda_0$ yields
$D\kappa(m)[v]=-\kappa\int u^2v/\int mu^2$. The same argument applies
to all the finitely many directions, which proves (ii).

{(iii).} $\operatorname{tr} K_{m_\epsilon}^2=\iint m_\epsilon(x)m_\epsilon(y)e^{-2|x-y|}$
(\Cref{lem:filter}(i)) is a quadratic polynomial in $\epsilon$ with linear
coefficient $2\int vW_2$.

{(iv).} The function $G_s(x,x)=u_L(x)u_R(x)/W$ is continuous;
$G_s(x,y)$ is continuous in $x$ for fixed $y$ and bounded by $\frac12$, so
$\partial_sG_s(x,x)=-\int G_s(x,y)^2m(y)\,\mathrm d y$ is continuous by dominated
convergence; $u^2$ is continuous; and $W_2$ is continuous by dominated
convergence. Let $x\to+\infty$. With
$\alpha=V_L(+\infty)=1+\frac s2\int mV_L=e^{H_m(s)}$ and
$\beta=-\frac s2\int e^{2y}m(y)V_L(y)\,\mathrm d y$, the equation of
\Cref{lem:filter}(ii) gives
\[
 V_L(x)=\alpha+\beta e^{-2x}-\frac s2\int_x^\infty mV_L+\frac s2e^{-2x}\int_x^\infty e^{2y}mV_L
 =\alpha+\beta e^{-2x}+O(\mathsf J(x)),
\]
and $V_L'(x)=se^{-2x}\int_{-\infty}^xe^{2y}mV_L=-2\beta e^{-2x}+O(\mathsf J(x))$. Also
$V_R=1+O(\mathsf J)$ and $V_R'(x)=-s\int_x^\infty e^{-2(y-x)}mV_R=O(\mathsf J)$. Since
$u_L=e^xV_L$ and $u_R=e^{-x}V_R$,
$W=(V_L+V_L')V_R+V_L(V_R-V_R')\to2\alpha$, and $W$ is constant, so $W=2\alpha$.
Hence
\[
 G_s(x,x)=\frac{V_L(x)V_R(x)}{2\alpha}=\frac12+\frac\beta{2\alpha}e^{-2x}+O(\mathsf J(x)).
\]
Consider $\partial_sG_s(x,x)=-\int G_s(x,y)^2m(y)\,\mathrm d y$. With $C''=e^{s\int m}$,
$u_L(x)^2\le C''e^{2x}$ and $u_R(y)^2\le C''e^{-2y}$, so the part $y>x$ is at most
\[
 u_L(x)^2W^{-2}\int_x^\infty u_R^2m\le(C'')^2W^{-2}\int_x^\infty m ;
\]
and the part $y<x$ equals
$-u_R(x)^2W^{-2}\bigl(\int_\mathbb R u_L^2m-\int_x^\infty u_L^2m\bigr)$, where
$\int_\mathbb R u_L^2m<\infty$, $\int_x^\infty u_L^2m\le C''\int_x^\infty e^{2y}m$ and
$u_R(x)^2=e^{-2x}(1+O(\mathsf J))$. Hence
$\partial_sG_s(x,x)=-W^{-2}\int u_L^2m\,e^{-2x}+O(\mathsf J(x))$. For the ground
state, the proof of \Cref{thm:ground} gives
$u(x)=e^{-x}\int_{-\infty}^xe^yj+e^x\int_x^\infty e^{-y}j$ with $j=\kappa mu/2$, $u$
bounded. Hence $e^xu(x)=c_u+\delta(x)$ with $c_u=\int_\mathbb R e^yj$ and
\[
 |\delta(x)|\le\int_x^\infty e^yj+e^{2x}\int_x^\infty e^{-y}j\le2\int_x^\infty e^yj
 \le\kappa\|u\|_\infty e^{-x}\int_x^\infty e^{2y}m\le\kappa\|u\|_\infty e^x\mathsf J(x),
\]
so $u(x)^2=e^{-2x}(c_u+\delta)^2=c_u^2e^{-2x}+O(\mathsf J(x))$. Finally, with
$C_2=\int e^{2y}m(y)\,\mathrm d y$,
\[
 W_2(x)-C_2e^{-2x}=e^{2x}\int_x^\infty e^{-2y}m(y)\,\mathrm d y-e^{-2x}\int_x^\infty e^{2y}m(y)\,\mathrm d y,
\]
whose modulus is at most $\mathsf J(x)$. By \eqref{eq:tail-J}, every $O(\mathsf J)$
is $o(n)$.

label: proof:thm:no-touching
title: Proof
body_md:
\label{proof:thm:no-touching}
Suppose, to the contrary, that for some $\varepsilon>0$ every $m'=m+v$ with
$v\in C_c^\infty$, $\|v\|_\infty<\varepsilon$, $m'\ge0$, $\int m'=\int\sqrt{m'}=1$ and
$\mathbf O(m')\in U$ satisfies $E(m')\ge\Phi(\mathbf O(m'))$.

{A feasible curve.} Let $\mathfrak m_0(v)=\int v$ and
$\mathfrak m_1(v)=\int v/(2n)$ on $C_c^\infty$. The function $1/(2n)$ is continuous
and unbounded, since $n$ is continuous, positive and tends to $0$ at
$\pm\infty$; so there are points $a,b$ with $1/(2n(a))\ne1/(2n(b))$. Let
$w_1,w_2\in C_c^\infty$ be nonnegative with integral one, supported in
intervals around $a$ and $b$ so short that the oscillation of $1/(2n)$ on
each is less than $\frac13|1/(2n(a))-1/(2n(b))|$; then $\mathfrak m_0(w_i)=1$ and
$\mathfrak m_1(w_1)\ne\mathfrak m_1(w_2)$. Let $v\in C_c^\infty$ with
$\mathfrak m_0(v)=\mathfrak m_1(v)=0$, let $\mathsf S$ be the union of the supports of
$v,w_1,w_2$, and $c_{\mathsf S}=\min_{\mathsf S}m>0$. For $|\epsilon|+|z|$ small,
$m_{\epsilon,z}=m+\epsilon v+z(w_1-w_2)\ge c_{\mathsf S}/2$ on $\mathsf S$, and
$F(\epsilon,z)=\int_{\mathsf S}(\sqrt{m_{\epsilon,z}}-\sqrt m)$ is $C^\infty$, with $F(0,0)=0$,
$\partial_\epsilon F(0,0)=\mathfrak m_1(v)=0$ and
$\partial_zF(0,0)=\mathfrak m_1(w_1)-\mathfrak m_1(w_2)\ne0$. The implicit function theorem
gives a $C^\infty$ function $z(\epsilon)$ with $z(0)=0$, $z'(0)=0$ and
$F(\epsilon,z(\epsilon))=0$. The densities $m_\epsilon=m_{\epsilon,z(\epsilon)}$ satisfy
$\int m_\epsilon=1+\epsilon\mathfrak m_0(v)+z\mathfrak m_0(w_1-w_2)=1$ and $\int\sqrt{m_\epsilon}=1$, and
$\|m_\epsilon-m\|_\infty\to0$ as $\epsilon\to0$.

{Differentiability.} By \Cref{lem:gradients}(i)--(iii), applied with
the two directions $v$ and $w_1-w_2$, each coordinate of
$\mathbf O(m_{\epsilon,z})$ is continuously differentiable in $(\epsilon,z)$ near $0$; if
the scales are functions $\sigma_j(\kappa)$, the same holds by the chain rule,
because $H$ and $\partial_sH$ are real analytic in $(\epsilon,z,s)$ and
$\sigma_j(\kappa(m))>0$. In particular $\mathbf O(m_\epsilon)\to\mathbf O(m)$, so for small $|\epsilon|$,
$\|m_\epsilon-m\|_\infty<\varepsilon$, $\mathbf O(m_\epsilon)\in U$, and
$g(\epsilon)=E(m_\epsilon)-\Phi(\mathbf O(m_\epsilon))\ge0$, while $g(0)=0$. Also
$E(m_{\epsilon,z})=\int(m_{\epsilon,z})^{3/2}$ is $C^1$ with $\partial_\epsilon E|_0=\frac32\int nv$, since
$m_{\epsilon,z}=m$ outside $\mathsf S$ and $m_{\epsilon,z}\ge c_{\mathsf S}/2$ on $\mathsf S$. Since
$z'(0)=0$, $g$ is differentiable at $0$ with $g'(0)=\ell(v)$, where
\[
 \ell(v)=\int\Bigl(\tfrac32n-\mathfrak g\Bigr)v,\qquad
 \mathfrak g=c_\kappa u^2+c_{\rm tr}W_2
 +\sum_j\bigl\{a_j\sigma_jG_{\sigma_j}(x,x)+b_j\bigl[G_{\sigma_j}(x,x)+\sigma_j\partial_sG_{\sigma_j}(x,x)\bigr]\bigr\},
\]
with constants $c_\kappa,c_{\rm tr},a_j,b_j$ determined by the partial derivatives of
$\Phi$ at $\mathbf O(m)$, by $\int u^2m$, and, for moving scales, by $\sigma_j'$ and the
derivatives of $H_m$ in $s$; these last terms are multiples of $u^2$, and
are included in $c_\kappa$. Omitted coordinates of $\mathbf O$ correspond to zero
constants. Since $g\ge0$ near $0$ and $g(0)=0$, $\ell(v)=g'(0)=0$.

{The pointwise identity.} The functionals $\mathfrak m_0,\mathfrak m_1$ are linearly
independent, since $\mathfrak m_0(w_1-w_2)=0\ne\mathfrak m_1(w_1-w_2)$ and $\mathfrak m_0(w_1)=1$.
Choose $\varphi_0,\varphi_1\in C_c^\infty$ with $\mathfrak m_i(\varphi_l)=\delta_{il}$. For every
$v\in C_c^\infty$, $v-\mathfrak m_0(v)\varphi_0-\mathfrak m_1(v)\varphi_1$ lies in
$\ker\mathfrak m_0\cap\ker\mathfrak m_1$, so
$\ell(v)=\alpha\mathfrak m_0(v)+\zeta\mathfrak m_1(v)$ with $\alpha=\ell(\varphi_0)$, $\zeta=\ell(\varphi_1)$. The
function $\frac32n-\mathfrak g-\alpha-\zeta/(2n)$ is continuous (\Cref{lem:gradients}(iv))
and integrates to zero against every $v\in C_c^\infty$; hence, for every $x$,
\[
 \tfrac32n(x)=\alpha+\frac\zeta{2n(x)}+\mathfrak g(x).
\]

{The contradiction.} By \Cref{lem:gradients}(iv), as $x\to+\infty$,
$\mathfrak g(x)=c_0+c_1e^{-2x}+o(n(x))$ with constants $c_0=\frac12\sum_j(a_j\sigma_j+b_j)$ and
$c_1$; in particular $\mathfrak g$ is bounded near $+\infty$. Multiplying the
identity by $n(x)\to0$ gives $\zeta/2=\lim_{x\to\infty}n(x)[\frac32n-\alpha-\mathfrak g]=0$.
Then $\frac32n=\alpha+c_0+c_1e^{-2x}+o(n)$, and $x\to\infty$ gives $\alpha+c_0=0$. Then
$\frac32ne^{2x}=c_1+o(ne^{2x})$, and $n(x)e^{2x}\to0$ by \eqref{eq:tail-J} gives
$c_1=0$. Finally $\frac32n=o(n)$ contradicts $n>0$.
